Developing research suggests that ancient interbreeding wasn't random — it was socially patterned, directional and far more complicated than the headlines suggest.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Deep in a limestone cave on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, two very different sets of humans left behind nearly identical traces of their lives — similar stone tools, the remains of the same prey animals, the same types of seashells pierced and strung into ornaments. They may have been separated by thousands of years and may not have directly interacted. Yet the overlap between them was striking enough that researchers studying the site had to look twice.

The site, Üçağızlı II, offers one of the clearest examples of a conundrum that scientists have long wrestled with: Neanderthals and modern humans (Homo sapiens) didn't just collide and go their separate ways. They inhabited the same areas, and, as dozens of genetic studies have confirmed, had sex, across tens of thousands of years and on multiple continents. The DNA of nearly every person alive outside Africa today carries the proof: Roughly 2% of the non-African genome is Neanderthal.

And yet, there is not a single archaeological site that shows them living together. Knowing that modern humans and Neanderthals mated is not the same as understanding how it happened. Who approached whom? Were these interactions consensual? Were they the result of violence or trade alliances? Who raised these hybrid babies? And what does the genetic record tell us about the social lives of two different kinds of humans navigating each other's existence for the first time?

Some of the answers, it turns out, are written on the X chromosome — and they are stranger than expected.

The first high-coverage Neanderthal genome was sequenced in 2010, and for the next 15 years, researchers kept noticing something puzzling: Neanderthal DNA was less common from the X chromosomes in people alive today.

One of the two sex chromosomes in humans, the X chromosome represents about 5% of the DNA in cells. Most females carry a pair of X chromosomes in each cell, while most males have one X and one Y.

Everywhere else in our genome, traces of long-ago breeding between Neanderthals and modern humans showed up in roughly consistent proportions. But on the X chromosome, there was far less Neanderthal DNA.

In people today, the X chromosome (bottom right) has less Neanderthal DNA than the non-sex chromosomes do.

The leading explanation was negative selection — the idea that Neanderthal gene variants unique to the X chromosome were somehow incompatible with modern-human biology and had been gradually eliminated from the gene pool over thousands of generations. It was a reasonable hypothesis, given that incompatibilities elsewhere in the genome did lead to the weeding out of Neanderthal DNA on other chromosomes over time.

To understand why the negative selection explanation didn't explain the X chromosome data, however, it helps to know what different parts of the genome actually do. Some stretches of DNA are protein-coding regions; they contain the instructions for building proteins, the molecular machinery that does most of the work inside cells. Others are regulatory sequences that don't build proteins themselves but help control when and how much of a protein gets produced. And then there are still other stretches of DNA that don’t appear to code for proteins or directly regulate gene expression, though researchers suspect at least some have functions we don’t yet fully understand.

Alexander Platt, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Pennsylvania's Perelman School of Medicine, hypothesized that if the problem was that Neanderthal gene variants on the X chromosome were inherently harmful, modern-human X gene variants would have been advantageous in Neanderthals. As a result, X chromosomal DNA extracted from Neanderthal skeletons should show an excess of modern-human DNA in stretches of the genome where they'd provide measurable benefit. They reasoned that this excess would likely appear in protein-coding genes or the regulatory regions that control their expression, not noncoding DNA.

But that's not what they found. Instead, Neanderthal X chromosomes carried more modern-human DNA in the noncoding regions of the genome than in coding regions. This pattern didn't reflect selection for better gene variants. It was a signature of reproduction ‪—‬ a record of who was passing chromosomes to whom.

In a typical pregnancy, the mother contributes an X chromosome via the egg, and the father contributes either an X or a Y via the sperm cell. So, while an individual is guaranteed to inherit their mother's X, they don't necessarily carry their father's — males exclusively inherit their mother's X. That pattern differs from the other 22 pairs of chromosomes, which mothers and fathers contribute to equally. Across a population, then, two-thirds of X chromosomes are inherited from mothers and one-third from fathers.

This fact makes the X chromosome a particularly sensitive recorder of who was reproducing with whom.

Tracking the flow of X chromosomes can reveal trends in Neanderthal-human mating. If Neanderthal males paired with modern-human females more often than Neanderthal females paired with modern-human males, you'd see more modern-human X chromosomes flow into the Neanderthal gene pool.

X data suggests that when the two types of humans mated, the mother was usually a Homo sapiens.

When the team ran simulations to explore this idea, the data suggested what Platt described as a persistent, recurring mating preference: Males with more Neanderthal ancestry tended to reproduce with females with more modern-human ancestry. And this trend held across at least two distinct mating periods separated by around 200,000 years, said Platt.

This finding gave the researchers a new window into the timeline of mating between Neanderthals and modern humans. Platt's team identified at least two distinct pulses: one roughly 45,000 years ago, which produced the majority the Neanderthal DNA that lives on in non-African genomes today, and an earlier period over 200,000 years ago, whose genetic traces survived not in modern-human populations but in Neanderthals.

The pattern of Neanderthal males having offspring with H. sapiens females appears in both periods, separated by more than 150,000 years.

What the X chromosome data alone cannot say is why the pattern exists. It documents who reproduced with whom. It says nothing about who wanted whom.

That distinction matters, because the same genetic signature can emerge from very different causes, and some have nothing to do with sexual preference.

Rajiv McCoy, a geneticist at Johns Hopkins University, pointed out that biology alone could produce a genetic signal like this one. When closely related species interbreed, the success of a pregnancy can depend not just on whose genes are inherited but on which parent belongs to which group.

Even if Neanderthal genes work fine in a modern-human genetic background, hybrid pregnancies may simply have been more likely to succeed when the Neanderthal was the father rather than the mother. That's not because of either parent's sexual preferences, but because of how their respective biologies interacted in the womb, McCoy told Live Science.

Researchers have recently proposed a few mechanisms that fit neatly with this theory. One study suggests that Neanderthal red blood cells restricted fetuses' growth in the womb. Another proposed that Neanderthal mothers carrying hybrid offspring may have been more prone to preeclampsia, a life-threatening pregnancy complication. Nothing in the existing data definitively rules such causes, McCoy said.

Neanderthal males were more likely to produce hybrid offspring that contributed to our gene pool than were Neanderthal females.

In practice, the two explanations are hard to separate. "Our models have no way of distinguishing mating from mating that produces a viable and fertile offspring," McCoy said. If hybrid pregnancies failed more often when the mother was Neanderthal, the genetic record would look similar to a world where Neanderthal females mated less often with H. sapiens males. Sexual encounters that didn't result in offspring left no genetic trace.

For now, the question of what drove that bias — social preference, or biology — remains open. Whatever barriers existed between the groups, they clearly weren't absolute. Multiple distinct episodes of interbreeding over thousands of years, McCoy noted, is itself evidence that the fertility of hybrid individuals was "sufficiently intact to leave a lasting mark."

Bridget Alex, a researcher in human evolutionary biology at Harvard University who has spent her career reconstructing the timing and geography of Neanderthal-H. sapiens overlap, cautioned that all this is hampered by one fact: no direct archaeological evidence reveals how the two groups interacted.

"Despite a century and a half of Neanderthal research," she told Live Science, "no one's ever found a Neanderthal and Homo sapiens fossil in the same exact layer dated to the same exact period at the same exact site."

Instead, we have a regional and variable patchwork shaped by conditions that shifted over thousands of years and hundreds to thousands of miles.

Neanderthals inhabited a territory stretching from Siberia to Iberia to Southwest Asia between roughly 250,000 and 40,000 years ago. Modern humans were evolving in Africa during much of that span and came out repeatedly, in multiple waves, meeting Neanderthals in different times and places, with likely very different outcomes each time, Alex said.

"It's not like the Neanderthals living in what's now Spain could call up the ones in what's now Uzbekistan and be like, 'OK, what's our policy with modern humans? Do we kill them, have sex with them, ignore them?'" she said. "My assumption has always been that interactions would vary across time and space depending on the particular environmental conditions, social conditions, and just the whims of a particular group."

Grotte Mandrine contains artifacts from tens of thousands of years of Neanderthal occupation — and a single layer suggestive of Homo sapiens occupation.

At Grotte Mandrin, a cave in the Rhône Valley in southern France, archaeologists found one of the most illuminating records of what those encounters may have looked like. Ludovic Slimak, a paleoanthropologist at the University of Toulouse who has spent years excavating the site, described it as something genetics alone can't offer: "an extraordinarily precise archaeological sequence of Neanderthals and [Homo] sapiens occupying exactly the same place," he told Live Science in an email.

Neanderthal artifacts fill layer after layer of radiocarbon and luminescence dating up to about 57,000 years ago. And then, in one thin layer dated to between 56,800 and 51,700 years ago, there's a set of different stone tools and a single tooth that appear to belong to H. sapiens. Then, in layers immediately above, beginning around 51,700 years ago, Neanderthal artifacts appear again. That group of modern humans arrived, lived briefly in a continent otherwise inhabited entirely by Neanderthals, and then disappeared.

"What strikes me most is not mixture but proximity without fusion," Slimak told Live Science in an email. In other words, the two groups left no trace of cultural exchange or shared practice.There were "two human populations occupying the same landscape, probably encountering one another, while remaining culturally and biologically very different," Slimak said.

Genetics also paints a portrait of two very different social architectures. Two sites exemplify the trends: At Sunghir, a burial site in Russia dating to around 34,000 years ago, two H. sapiens adolescents were interred head to head beneath thousands of ivory beads and mammoth-bone spears. Ancient DNA analysis showed they were not immediate family members, yet they were buried together in an elaborate ceremony that implies a social world much wider than their immediate group.

Graves from more than 30,000 years ago in Sunghir in Russia show that two adolescents buried together were not closely related, suggesting Homo sapiens had wider and more flexible social networks than Neanderthals.

In contrast, at Chagyrskaya, a cave site in Siberia, Neanderthals buried in what appears to be a single community layer included a father and his teenage daughter, and a second pair of individuals who shared roughly a quarter of their DNA.

While these are just two sites, they reflect a broader trend that shows up repeatedly in genetic data: Human groups tended to operate through what Alex described as a nested structure: Tens of thousands of years ago, small groups of perhaps 20 or 30 individuals maintained broader ties through ceremonies, intermarriage between human groups and exchange with other groups.

In contrast, data from Neanderthal sites reveal that they tended to cluster in small, tightly knit groups that remained relatively separate from other Neanderthal populations.

Homozygosity, or DNA regions where a person inherited two copies of the same gene variant, is an inverse measure of genetic diversity. Adapted from Skov et al, 2022.

Unlike modern humans, Neanderthals didn't regularly mate with individuals in other communities, Alex said. The result, written in their genomes, is that individuals within a single Neanderthal group were often closely related. Their genomes show low genetic diversity across the board, — "kind of suggesting they're always a population on the verge," Alex said, "like an endangered species."

Still, there had to be some out-group mating. At sites where researchers have extracted genomes from several Neanderthal individuals, the pattern is consistent: Male Neanderthals were more closely related to each other than female Neanderthals were to each other. Females, by contrast, seemed more likely to have come from elsewhere. This is the signature of a "patrilocal" social structure in which males stay in their birth groups and females move between them.

Neanderthals' insularity sharpens a key question: If Neanderthal groups weren't regularly folding in Neanderthal females from distant communities, they would probably be even less likely to incorporate female H. sapiens. So how did modern-human women end up producing offspring with Neanderthal men at all?

Fernando Villanea, a population geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder, thinks the question may be framed backward. The image of Neanderthal males raising hybrid children with modern-human females within Neanderthal communities, he argues, probably inverts what actually happened.

Something the genomes of late Neanderthals — those living toward the end of their long history in Eurasia — make clear is that they were roughly 10 times more inbred than the modern human ancestors who were then expanding out of Africa in large numbers, he noted. That level of inbreeding isn't usually a choice; it reflects how small and fragmented Neanderthal populations likely were.

We need to imagine scenarios where a majority of modern human groups traveling into Eurasia are encountering a vanishing minority of Neanderthals.

Archaeological and paleoclimatic data fill in the context: The ecosystems Neanderthals were best adapted to were shrinking as the planet entered a warmer, more humid period. Modern humans, who had evolved in hotter, wetter African environments, were simply better suited to Europe's new conditions, experts think.

The resulting numerical imbalance changes how scientists think about mating between Neanderthals and modern humans.

"We need to imagine scenarios where a majority of modern human groups traveling into Eurasia are encountering a vanishing minority of Neanderthals," Villanea told Live Science.

In the crucial period between roughly 50,000 and 44,000 years ago, when much of the interbreeding that left a trace in our DNA took place, Neanderthal DNA made up 5% of the modern human genome. Given how heavily humans outnumbered Neanderthals at the time, "that's a lot of matings occurring between the two." The most likely story, Villanea proposes, is "human groups absorbing surviving Neanderthal individuals and raising their children in a mostly human group."

His 2018 study in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution established that this happened across multiple distinct episodes — and the later ones are particularly telling. Some ancient H. sapiens genomes from Europe around 40,000 years ago, according to the study, carry Neanderthal ancestry from individuals who lived just a few generations after archaeologists can no longer find any physical trace of Neanderthals in the region at all.

Even the very last Neanderthal survivors were still contributing to the H. sapiens gene pool. A 2024 study by Leonardo Iasi and colleagues similarly determined that almost 90% of total Neanderthal ancestry in humans today came from a main pulse roughly 50,000 to 45,000 years ago, likely in the Middle East, with the rest trickling in from more sporadic encounters scattered across Eurasia.

That paints a picture of meetings becoming rarer and rarer as Neanderthals disappeared, with hybridization continuing whenever they did meet up. "This, to me, says deliberate integration of Neanderthal individuals into human groups," Villanea said.

We know that some hybrid Neanderthal-H. sapiens survived because "we still carry the legacy of their existence," Alex said. However, we know they didn't thrive, because the Neanderthal ancestry of our ancestral populations eroded quickly.

While some hybrids survived, they likely suffered from health problems.

Most genes work in concert with other genes across the genome. When Neanderthal-specific variants entered the modern-human genome, it was like trying to put gears from one machine into a slightly different one; the parts didn't quite fit together. As a result, natural selection removed the Neanderthal variants rapidly. Villanea's calculations, based on the rate at which chromosomes recombine during cell division, suggest the drop from the original approximately 5% Neanderthal DNA roughly 50,000 to 45,000 years ago to the roughly 2% carried today happened in around 10 human generations.

"That's very fast," he said. "In real-life terms, that means a lot of hybrids did not survive to reproduce, and the ones that did probably had to deal with life-long health problems."

Platt's team looked at genetic evidence from multiple sites across Eurasia and found that the genetic purge ran in the opposite direction, too. Modern-human DNA was also being selected out of Neanderthal genomes.

Neither had inherently superior genes, Platt concluded. The gene variants were simply optimized for the separate evolutionary histories of their respective lineages, hundreds of thousands of years of independent adaptation that made certain combinations disadvantageous, if not fatal.

If Neanderthal males and modern-human females really were producing more surviving offspring than the reverse pairing, where did those children end up?

Villanea was cautious about reading too much into the X chromosome pattern on its own to answer that question. The imbalance Platt found is real, he said — not a statistical quirk. But "there is nothing in the X chromosome data that says it's based on human or Neanderthal mating preference," as Platt proposes.

The same pattern could, in theory, emerge from Neanderthal males leaving their birth groups to find mates, but as archaeological evidence suggests, this was not typical behavior. More likely, he argues, is something biological.

Hybrid children were likely raised in Homo sapiens groups.

In Peromyscus maniculatus and Peromyscus polionotus — two closely related species of North American deer mouse — a phenomenon called genomic imprinting causes hybrid offspring to develop differently in the womb depending on which species was the father and which was the mother. This pattern has nothing to do with behavior or preference. A similar process in early humans could have made Neanderthal father-H. sapiens mother pairings more likely to produce surviving offspring than the reverse, without either group consciously choosing anything.

"We simply don't know enough yet," Villanea said.

Distinguishing between these explanations — social behavior versus biological incompatibility — will require more Neanderthal genomes from the critical period of contact, ideally spanning multiple geographic regions, experts said.

There's another clue in genetic evidence from a 2026 study of 27 late Neanderthals who lived between 50,000 and 40,000 years ago in what is now Belgium and France. None of those individuals showed any sign of recent ancestry from modern humans, even as H. sapiens from the same era demonstrably carried Neanderthal DNA.

If hybrid children had been raised in Neanderthal groups and went on to reproduce there, those groups' genomes should retain traces of those events ‪—‬ but they don't.

As for whether modern-human groups were patrilocal — with males staying, females moving — the answer is considerably more variable than in Neanderthals. Modern-human communities across cultures show a range of patterns, with both sexes leaving their birth groups depending on circumstance, Alex said. That flexibility may have been part of what made human groups better able to absorb outside individuals.

Neither genetics nor archaeology has yet been able to answer the question at the center of this story: whether these encounters were by choice, by circumstance, or by force. Platt's team set it aside deliberately, and Alex is careful about it, too.

"We still wouldn't know if it was consensual or coerced," she said.

It's worth being specific about what different scenarios would look like archaeologically. If Neanderthal and modern-human individuals mingled through peaceful alliances, we might expect to find toolmaking techniques or symbolic objects crossing between groups at contact sites — precisely the kind of evidence that is absent at Grotte Mandrin, where, as Slimak noted, the two groups' technical traditions remained entirely distinct.

Slimak, writing from Grotte Mandrin in the middle of his excavation season, urged even more restraint. The genetic data, he said, are "consistent with an asymmetry" — gene flow moved more successfully through Neanderthal males and H. sapiens females than the reverse — but that is where the certainty ends.

The data says nothing about culture, desire, attraction or intent. "That entire social world has been added afterwards," he said.

The same signal, he pointed out, could emerge from a variety of histories — female mobility, demographic imbalance, alliance, exchange, capture, differential survival among hybrids. And these factors could contribute alone or in combination. Even the categories available for describing female movement may be too blunt. A single instance of migration, in traditional societies, can involve marriage, family strategy, alliance, obligation and violence all at once, in combinations that leave no trace for archaeology to disentangle.

"We may identify that a woman came from elsewhere," Slimak said. "We cannot recover her consent."

However, the convergence of genetics, demography and archaeology does reveal a structural picture, if not a sociological one.

The interbreeding was directional and repeated, patterned in ways that map onto the social organization of both groups — and driven in large part, Villanea's model suggests, by the sheer demographic weight of a growing human population folding in what remained of a disappearing one. Neanderthal males, in dwindling and insular communities, appear to have been the ones whose genes crossed into the larger H. sapiens world. Their children, in all likelihood, were raised as humans.

"Genes do not preserve past loves," Slimak said. "They preserve what was transmitted. And between transmission and lived experience lies almost the whole of human society."

#6567. Your Brain May Be Creating ‘Psychic’ Moments—Meaning Your Subconscious Tunes Into Hidden Cues, a Study Finds

A 1966 mining disaster in Wales is famous for its alleged premonitions. New research suggests what those strange “gut feelings” could mean.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

On the morning of October 21, 1966, the Welsh mining village of Aberfan was struck by one of Britain’s most harrowing peacetime disasters. After days of heavy rain, a slag heap collapsed off a colliery (a coal mine and its connected equipment) and tore down the hillside, submerging a school beneath a torrent of black sludge; 116 children died.

Warnings had come in more than one form. For years, villagers had raised concerns about the coal waste heaps perched above their homes. But some said the signs were stranger—uncanny, even. The day before the disaster, eight-year-old Paul Davies drew a picture of men digging into a hillside, with the words “The End” scrawled above the figures. That same week, ten-year-old Eryl Mai Jones told her mother she’d dreamt that “something black” had descended over the school.

Both children died the next day in the deluge.

A study by psychologist Olafur S. Palsson, PhD, suggests that so-called anomalous experiences—events that seem to go beyond what conventional science can explain—are not rare, but in fact quite common. Additionally, people who report experiencing premonitions, déjà vu, superstitious intuition, and out-of-body sensations often share distinct psychological attributes.

These “strange-but-true” perceptions correlate strongly with a cognitive trait Palsson terms subconscious connectedness: the degree of interaction between conscious awareness and subconscious thought. The research, published in the peer-reviewed journal Psychology of Consciousness: Theory, Research, and Practice in 2025, found that individuals high in subconscious connectedness were significantly more likely to report frequent anomalous experiences, including:

“Some people have a much closer connection with the non-conscious or subconscious parts of their mind,” said Palsson, professor emeritus at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. “Their conscious and subconscious mind influence each other to an unusually high degree in everyday life.”

Using a newly developed metric called the Thought Impact Scale, Palsson surveyed more than 2,000 adults in the U.S. to assess “interactions between conscious aware thinking and nonconscious mental functions.” Respondents rated how much they agree with statements (on a Likert scale) about their various mental experiences and psychological traits, including automatic thoughts, intuitive insight, emotional resonance, spontaneous mental imagery, as well as the frequency of unusual experiences such as telepathic impressions, precognitive dreams, and uncanny coincidences. A clear pattern emerged: individuals with high subconscious connectedness reported such experiences far more often than those with low scores.

Like extroversion or neuroticism, the trait varies from person to person, but stays relatively stable over time in each person. What changes, Palsson suggests, is how the trait manifests—the ways in which people interpret intuition, memory, or coincidence. For those with stronger subconscious input, the mind may simply register more of what others discard, Palsson suggests.

“Anomalous experiences are something most people have at least occasionally,” says Palsson. “Our studies showed that 84 percent to 86 percent of adults repeatedly have at least one type of such experience. Neuroscientists suggest that the brain’s default mode network—active during daydreaming and introspection—may play a role in generating these impressions. Heightened connectivity between regions of the brain responsible for memory, emotion, and prediction could explain the intensity or vividness of so-called premonitions.”

Might psychic foresight, hunches, or “gut feelings” confer some sort of evolutionary edge? Perhaps these anomalous experiences allow humans to make better sense of subtle patterns, according to Palsson. Or, perhaps premonitions and uncanny experiences point to something more banal: they might be explained by selective recall (remembering accurate predictions while ignoring those that never came true). Consider the confirmation bias and the “availability heuristic”—our tendency to remember emotionally charged events and forget the mundane. Most of our dreams are forgotten; the one that coincides with tragedy becomes unforgettable.

Premonition might be less about glimpsing the future than about perceiving—consciously or not—subtle cues the mind is already processing. And in that sense, the inexplicable becomes part of how we navigate the world, not what’s outside it.

Adrienne Bernhard is a Los Angeles-born, New York-based freelance writer and former assistant to the deputy editor at The New Yorker. She has written for the Financial Times, The Wall Street Journal, the BBC, Smithsonian, The Atlantic, the Boston Review, and New Criterion, among others.

#6566. For Talarico and Hinojosa, Whataburger Is a Perfectly Texas Place to Celebrate

Like so many Texans on so many nights, Senator-elect James Talarico and Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa ended their evening at Whataburger.

Late Tuesday night, after Talarico flipped a Senate seat for the Democrats and Hinojosa was elected the first Democratic governor of the state in more than three decades, the two sat down at an Austin-area location of Whataburger, the iconic regional fast food chain, to clink plastic orange-and-white-striped cups.

It was a fitting setting for the pair, who played critical roles in the blue wave that swept the country in the midterm elections on Tuesday night. Talarico, who defeated scandal-plagued Republican Ken Paxton, went on the offensive against billionaires, prevailing with a positive, populist message against a party funded by Elon Musk and other ultrawealthy donors.

Hinojosa, the first Latina to be elected governor for Texas, targeted corruption and data centers in her race against Republican incumbent Greg Abbott. Both Talarico and Hinojosa will be the first Democrats in more than 30 years to serve Texas in their respective roles.

But even in the midst of a polarizing political moment for the nation, loving Whataburger is bigger than politics in Texas. Since opening its first location in Corpus Christi, Texas, in 1950, the chain, with its signature A-frame buildings, has become a social center for small towns, a place for a budget-friendly meal for families, and a crucial hangout for high schoolers figuring out where else they’ll go that night or stopping for a late-night breakfast before heading home.

Instead of popping Champagne, it’s poignant that Talarico and Hinojosa celebrated with oversize sodas. You can still get a double-burger Whatameal for under $15. These aren't the first Democrats to harness the tangy-sweet appeal of Whataburger's much-beloved Fancy Ketchup. In 2018, the campaign for senate-hopeful Beto O'Rourke shared video of him skateboarding outside a Whataburger before going inside to eat.

Today’s prices are squarely in line with the affordability politics that resonated with voters this cycle. And Talarico and Hinojosa’s Whataburger cheers was a fitting end to a campaign that wove food and politics together. While casting himself as a David against Paxton’s Goliath, Talarico absorbed attacks that claimed he was vegan. While the Senator-elect had urged residents to cut down on beef consumption, he denied the dietary restriction, countering by posting pictures of himself chowing down on barbecue.

Paxton still tried to label his opponent as “Tofu Talarico,” and Trump imagined a scenario where Talarico excuses himself to vomit after eating meat. The barbs were not-so-subtle assaults on Talarico’s manhood, the latest manifestation of the link between meat and masculinity. But there was Talarico on election night, sitting in the house of beef patties, Whatachick’n strips, and bacon-and-egg taquitos.

After a 2019 acquisition by a Chicago-based investment firm, Whataburger has faced allegations of diminishing quality and a nascent rival in Austin’s P. Terry’s Burger Stand. And still, aside from a Dairy Queen or A&W after a high school football game, there may be nowhere in Texas that feels as Texas as a Whataburger when you’re not quite ready to call it a night.

One of the defining features of Whataburger has always been its friendliness to customizing your meal—made to order. Want jalapeños and mustard on your burger, no mayo? Go right ahead, sweetie.

On Tuesday night, as part of national rebuke to President Donald Trump’s party, Texas made its choice clear.

#6565. Croissant Stuffing

Croissant stuffing brings the light, airy texture of French pastry straight to your Thanksgiving table. While most traditional stuffings rely on denser breads, I opted for croissants to create a lighter, fluffier bite, and the result is everything. Trust me, this is the stuffing that has everything—savory, sweet, a little crunch, a bit of freshness—all tossed together with dreamy croissants in your 13" x 9" pan. If you haven’t started planning your Thanksgiving menu (or Friendsgiving contribution), then save this stuffing recipe now.

Recipe tips: I use dry white wine to deglaze the pan and add a touch more flavor to the stuffing, but feel free to use an equal amount of chicken broth in its place if you prefer.

Storage: If you happen to have any stuffing leftover after the big day, simply store it in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days. You can still incorporate it into all of your favorite Thanksgiving leftover ideas (stuffed sweet potatoes, anyone?).

#6563. 12 Years Ago, This Jumbo Jet Vanished Without a Trace. New High-Tech Ocean Robots May Finally Reveal What Happened.

The 2014 disappearance of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 remains one of aviation’s greatest unsolved mysteries. Inside the latest high-stakes search to find the missing Boeing 777.

On January 2, 2018, from the port city of Durban in eastern South Africa, a ship departed at dusk. This was no vessel outfitted for a nighttime pleasure cruise. In fact, it looked downright strange. Its hull was a shade of prison-jumpsuit orange. Its bow was adorned with a large, flat platform resembling a helipad. Antennas, some pointy, some contained in two white domes, covered its superstructure. A crane was mounted on the ship’s stern. Belowdecks sat eight autonomous submersibles, each weighing about 4,000 pounds, or the equivalent of a Ford F-150. This ship was heading east, bound for a section of the southern Indian Ocean about 1,500 miles west of Australia. Its mission? To find the notorious Malaysia Airlines Flight 370.

When MH370 took off from Kuala Lumpur on March 8, 2014, shortly before 1 a.m. local time, there was no indication it wouldn’t be a routine flight. But the Boeing 777-200ER never reached its destination, Beijing. Instead, after 39 minutes in the air, the jetliner disappeared from radar; about seven hours after that, it vanished altogether. Satellite communications analyzed afterward showed that MH370 had turned southward and continued on that course until it presumably exhausted its fuel supply and crashed in the Indian Ocean off the western seaboard of Australia.

An expansive search was quickly mounted, the largest ever for a missing plane. Some 60 ships and 50 aircraft from 26 countries participated, at a cost of more than $150 million. More than 46,000 square miles of Indian Ocean seabed were scanned over a three-year period.

But the plane was never located, and the question of MH370’s whereabouts set off a freneticism rivaled perhaps only by the mystery of Amelia Earhart’s fate on her final flight. In the decade-plus since the plane vanished, numerous and varied hypotheses have surfaced. The aircraft crashed somewhere else, some suggested. Others insisted the plane was shot out of the sky. So vexing was MH370’s disappearance that it even spawned a Netflix docuseries in 2023. Still others contend that, without a doubt, MH370 is on the bottom of the southern Indian Ocean.

Which explains the odd-looking ship that set off on its easterly course in 2018. The craft, a Norwegian-built research vessel named Seabed Constructor, was leased to Ocean Infinity, a deep-sea exploration firm with offices in Europe, Canada, Australia, and the United States. The Malaysian government contracted the company on a no-find, no-fee basis to look for MH370—a mission that promised a reward of up to $70 million. Over several months, Ocean Infinity used its autonomous subs to scan a grid of 9,600 square miles just north of the location where the original underwater search took place. By May of that year, having found nothing, the company suspended its mission.

Bringing the story of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 to a definitive close has been equal parts confounding and elusive. A fool’s errand, one might say. But in spring 2025, the government of Malaysia again contracted the firm—now equipped with new vessels of its own design, as well as advanced underwater robots—to mount a fresh search for MH370. In taking up the search again, in one of the toughest marine environments in the world, Ocean Infinity would be risking money and its reputation in the process. What if, for the second time, it failed to find a debris field of MH370 under the waters of the southern Indian Ocean? What if the black boxes couldn’t be located? What if we never get a definitive answer to how Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 went missing without a trace?

After its 12:42 a.m. takeoff from Kuala Lumpur, with 227 passengers and 10 flight attendants on board, Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 quickly reached its cruising altitude of 35,000 feet and steered toward Beijing. Flying the plane were first officer Fariq Abdul Hamid, 27, and pilot in command Zaharie Ahmad Shah, 53. For Hamid, this was his final training flight before becoming a fully certified pilot. He was in good hands. Zaharie (who was known by his first name) was one of the most senior captains at Malaysia Airlines. He also owned a sophisticated Microsoft flight simulator that he used frequently at home.

At 1:08 a.m., MH370 flew out over the Malaysian coastline, soaring above the South China Sea toward Vietnam. Just 11 minutes later, when the handoff from Kuala Lumpur controllers to Vietnam’s air traffic jurisdiction was about to take place, air traffic control in Kuala Lumpur radioed MH370 one final time.

“Malaysian three-seven-zero, contact Ho Chi Minh one-two-zero-decimal-nine. Good night,” they said.

“Good night. Malaysian three-seven-zero,” came the reply from the cockpit.

Those were the last words ever heard from the plane.

Soon the Vietnamese controllers saw MH370 cross into its airspace. But then something unexpected happened. Air traffic relies on secondary radar, whereby a transponder on an airplane sends a signal that contains information identifying the plane and its cruising altitude. This flight, instead, disappeared entirely from air traffic radar at 1:21 a.m. It wasn’t until four hours later, at around 5:30 a.m., that any sort of emergency response commenced.

The simple fact was that at 6:30 a.m. on March 8, MH370—carrying passengers from China, Malaysia, Indonesia, Taiwan, India, Australia, New Zealand, France, Canada, the U.S., Ukraine, Russia, Iran, and the Netherlands—should have landed in Beijing. It didn’t.

Making sense of how an object as large as a Boeing 777 goes poof in the night is hard to fathom in our modern age. And for the human mind, which craves order and explanation, it is downright maddening—which might explain the bevy of individuals, with no connection to the flight whatsoever, who jumped in eager to provide answers. Over the many years since MH370’s disappearance, a variety of theories emerged about what happened to the plane. One scenario involves MH370 traveling toward Diego Garcia, a small atoll in the Indian Ocean where the U.S. has an army base, before being shot down. Another scenario claims the plane landed in the jungles of Cambodia. Other theories as to what happened to the flight received major airtime in 2023 during Netflix’s three-part docuseries MH370: The Plane That Disappeared. The plane, one person speculated, was hijacked by Russian agents and rerouted to Kazakhstan. Another person claimed the U.S. Air Force shot down MH370 over the South China Sea.

Whether the U.S. Air Force was really responsible was never seriously considered by Malaysia. But officials had suspected that the plane crashed in the South China Sea en route to Beijing. Accident investigators from Europe, Australia, and the U.S. teamed up with the Malaysian government and began searching the sea’s surface for any floating debris. That search was called off in April 2014 when nothing was found.

Yet within a week after MH370 apparently flew off the map, another theory surfaced in the Wall Street Journal. The article contains, to this day, the most plausible and reasonable explanation, one agreed upon by experts in aviation, satellite communications, and government: MH370 continued flying for hours after it disappeared from radar, turned west, away from its expected destination in Beijing, and then southward, ultimately meeting its demise in the waters of the southern Indian Ocean.

After the article was published, the Malaysian government eventually admitted that the account was true—which meant it had carried on a pointless search in the South China Sea for weeks. (In a comprehensive article for The Atlantic written in 2019, the late author and pilot William Langewiesche noted that autocratic bureaucracies with government-owned airlines generally want bad press to go away. It would be better, in other words, not to solve the puzzle, but to make the matter fade into memory as quickly as possible.)

To arrive at such a conclusion, the WSJ relied on an analysis of technical data from Inmarsat, a company that provides satellite services on land, at sea, and in the air. Although MH370 disappeared from air traffic radar screens, a feat easily achieved by whomever was manning the cockpit controls, it continued to link up every so often to a geostationary Inmarsat satellite over the Indian Ocean. Called “handshakes,” these linkups are electronic blips that, while tiny, yielded the most information about what happened to the plane. There were seven handshakes altogether: two that came automatically from the plane, and five others initiated automatically from an Inmarsat ground station in Perth, Australia.

The Inmarsat linkups provided two critical values. The first value is the burst timing offset, or BTO. It’s a measure of the round-trip time it takes for a blip to go from a ground station to a satellite to (in this case) an aircraft, then back up to the satellite and back to the ground station. It’s essentially the distance between the plane and the satellite, and that information gets processed as a series of rings, or arcs, of all possible locations. When it comes to MH370, the most important arc is the last one, the seventh, which the plane crossed at 8:19 a.m. Kuala Lumpur time. What’s important to note is that the seventh arc contains two location possibilities: If MH370 turned north, it may have ended up in Kazakhstan. If it went south, its location is in the southern Indian Ocean.

Determining the direction comes down to the second value: burst frequency offset, or BFO. It shows the difference between the expected frequency from a transmitter and the frequency ultimately received. As Langewiesche explained, the BFO is “a measure of radio-frequency Doppler shifts associated with high-speed movement in relation to satellite position.” Think about it and it makes sense: Neither planes nor satellites are stationary objects, so expected signals won’t match signals that actually get transmitted between the two. (That’s the Doppler effect, that change in frequency of radio waves.) Measuring BFO is a way to determine a plane’s speed and heading. During their investigation into the satellite data, Inmarsat technicians in London picked up on a distortion in the BFO value that suggested MH370 turned south at 2:40 a.m. Further analysis showed that MH370 entered a steep descent, as much as 15,000 feet per minute, just before crossing the seventh arc, which presumably happened after the plane ran out of fuel and both of its engines failed. From there it would have plunged violently into the ocean and shattered into millions of confetti-like pieces, to use Langewiesche’s analogy.

And it’s the satellite data, too, that paints a picture of MH370’s deviated flight path. Once the plane disappeared from secondary radar, it did an about-face over the South China Sea, flew back across Malaysia, over the Strait of Malacca separating Malaysia to the northeast and Indonesia to the southwest, and then, very suddenly, made a sharp turn to the southwest, away from the Andaman Sea to the west of Thailand. Accident investigators later determined that this turn was so tight there was no way the plane was still operating on autopilot. Someone was actively steering it.

What the satellite data doesn’t explain is why this happened—or who might have been flying the plane. Was it a potential hijacker? The available evidence says no: Malaysian and Chinese investigators, aided by American FBI agents, ran background checks on all passengers and flight attendants and cleared them of suspicion.

That left the pilots. Fariq Abdul Hamid was a young man with a fresh career as a prestigious Malaysia Airlines pilot ahead of him. Meanwhile, pilot in command Zaharie Ahmad Shah was portrayed in official reports as “someone beyond reproach.” Just a simple family man. Yet as Langewiesche discovered during his reporting in Malaysia, the official depiction of Zaharie did not align with the man’s private life: His wife had moved out, and he was “often lonely and sad.” He admitted to his own friends that he spent his off-hours “pacing empty rooms waiting for the days between flights to go by.” Among aviation investigators, there was strong suspicion, Langewiesche wrote, that Zaharie was clinically depressed.

And then there’s his flight simulator. Most times, Zaharie let simulated flights play out, from wheels up to wheels down. But a forensic investigation of his simulator showed that Zaharie had done a dry run of a flight profile that eerily mirrored MH370’s final flight path. What’s more, Langewiesche reported, “he advanced the flight manually in multiple stages, repeatedly jumping the flight forward and subtracting the fuel as necessary until it was gone.”

Was it Zaharie? One of the pilot’s lifelong friends, another Boeing 777 captain, told Langewiesche he believed it could have been. It’s not like such an event is without precedent: In 1999, for example, the copilot of EgyptAir Flight 990 intentionally crashed the plane into the ocean just south of Nantucket, Massachusetts. In 2015, the copilot of a Germanwings airliner deliberately crashed that plane into the French Alps. In a report published in 2014, the Federal Aviation Administration cites eight different examples of pilot suicides. And surveys conducted of pilots show that 4 percent have thought about taking their own lives.

As the search pressed on over the years, a group of researchers called the Independent Group emerged, made up of engineers and satellite experts who had found one another online as they simultaneously researched the MH370 crash. One of them, an engineer from Virginia named Victor Iannello, was the person who analyzed Zaharie’s simulated flight, coming to the conclusion that the simulation wasn’t some random event, but rather a potentially pivotal clue as to what happened on MH370’s final flight.

“Until MH370 is found and the reason for its disappearance is known, we will be bombarded with conspiracy theories, false leads, books, and movies which will provide nothing but conjecture,” said Prahlad Shirsath three months after the crash. His wife, Kranti, had been on board. “We need to find the truth,” he continued, “and ensure this never happens again.”

Where is that truth? Perhaps at the bottom of the Indian Ocean, the suspected location of the flight’s data recorder and cockpit voice recorder. Recovering the black boxes might help investigators resolve what happened to MH370. But we have to find them first.

The ocean is vast, and the ocean is scary. The deep ocean especially. Consider, for a moment, the possibility that we know more about Earth’s immediate orbit than we know about its oceans. In space, more than 9,000 satellites roam. On Earth, barely one-quarter of the planet’s oceans are mapped in any coherent way so as to make them discernible for underwater exploration.

In May 2014, the governments of Malaysia and China agreed that the Australians should lead the search for MH370, under the auspices of the Australian Transport Safety Bureau. Fugro, a Dutch firm, was contracted to do the work, with payment coming from Malaysia, China, and Australia. Given the satellite data that suggested splashdown on or about the seventh arc, an area of roughly 11,500 square miles across the arc was selected for exploration. This put the search area between 930 and 1,700 miles away from Australia’s western coast.

“Unforgivable” is perhaps the best word for describing the conditions of the Indian Ocean where search efforts were concentrated. The area saw ripping winds as high as 50 miles an hour, sudden powerful storms marked by 30-foot-high swells, and dense rain and fog. These were the least ideal conditions for sending ships out to sea for long periods of time, far from the closest ports, in a search for the maritime equivalent of a needle in a haystack.

When the underwater search for the remains of MH370 finally kicked off, the depths of the southern Indian Ocean were a mystery. An impressive level of surveying was conducted between May and December of 2014—with further mapping through early 2017—to even understand the topography of the deep ocean floor in this part of the world. It had never been mapped before. Fugro deployed three ships: the Equator, equipped with a hull-mounted echo sounder (to measure depth); the Discovery, with side-scan sonar; and the Supporter, which deployed a single autonomous underwater vehicle with side scanners, sonar, and an echo sounder. In all, close to 275,000 square miles of the deep ocean was surveyed, an area much larger than the search zone but valuable nonetheless for understanding the terrain.

Ridges, peaks, valleys, even underwater volcanoes covered the seabed. Most concerning was a deep underwater canyon that sliced horizontally through the seventh arc, believed by some to be the area where the remains of MH370 would be found. Dubbed Broken Ridge, it was formed by tectonic plate shifts more than 40 million years ago. Its depths reached between 2,000 and 20,000 feet beneath the ocean’s surface; sections of its topography were covered in sediment as thick as 1,000 feet.

“It’s like trying to imagine the Rocky Mountains underwater,” says Mike Exner, another member of the Independent Group. Exner is a retired entrepreneur from Colorado with a background in electrical engineering and satellite communications, having founded several of his own companies. He has also been a licensed pilot for more than 50 years. Exner was the person who studied Inmarsat data and civilian radar—primary radar scans resulting from simple pings about objects in the sky—to conclude that in MH370’s final hours, a flight to the seventh arc would not have been possible if there had been some sort of computer glitch or other systems failure.

“All those turns had to be done manually,” Exner says. “I think we’re about 99 percent sure Zaharie did it.” He adds that he can’t be 100 percent sure but says that once you consider the backgrounds of his copilot, the cabin crew, and the passengers, many of the signs point to him.

For almost three years, Fugro’s ships looked across areas on or near the seventh arc for any signs of the plane. Admittedly, there was a technological element working against them. Autonomous underwater vehicles have been game changers in underwater search and rescue, but they still come with certain drawbacks. Traditional radio waves with meaningful data rates don’t penetrate seawater at even paltry depths of six inches. Communication from ship or shore to a vehicle relies instead on sound waves. But even those become useless once the vehicle is roughly five miles away from its launch point.

“You have more contact with the Mars rover than you do [with] . . . a deep survey vehicle,” says J. Carl Hartsfield, director and senior program manager of the Oceanographic Systems Lab at the nonprofit Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution in Massachusetts.

So we humans have to place a great deal of trust in technology that we can’t control once it gets out into the ocean. What’s more, Fugro had only one autonomous underwater vehicle at its disposal, and its maximum diving depth was 13,000 feet, which meant it wasn’t reaching the seabed most of the time. As the years went on, the search zone was expanded from the original 23,000 square miles to an area surpassing 46,000 square miles. But not a scrap of the plane was found, and on January 17, 2017, the Australian-led search was suspended, pending further evidence of the plane’s location.

Could it be that MH370 really isn’t near the seventh arc? Could it have ended up somewhere else? David Mearns, a marine scientist who has led several deep-ocean explorations, says there are only two ways to explain why any piece of the aircraft wasn’t found underwater.

“One, they haven’t looked in the right place. Or two, they’ve looked in the right place, but they missed it,” he says. “Anybody who comes up with anything else doesn’t know what they’re talking about.”

By the time Ocean Infinity arrived at the scene of the crash in January 2018, much more had been deduced about MH370’s probable location. While the initial underwater search took place, an amateur campaign to search for debris from the missing plane began. At the center of this was Blaine Gibson, a Seattle-based lawyer with a penchant for wearing a fedora. (The connection to Indiana Jones isn’t lost on him. By his own admission, Gibson is fascinated by mysteries and archaeology. According to him, he once went searching for the Ark of the Covenant, the gold-plated chest containing the tablets on which the Ten Commandments were inscribed.)

“I was astonished to learn that there was no organized search of beaches and shorelines,” he says. “It always seemed to me that the first piece of debris from this plane was probably just going to be found washed to shore by someone walking on the beach.”

He was right. In July 2015, a flaperon, an airfoil that attaches to a plane wing next to the flap, was discovered by a beach cleaning crew on the French island of Réunion, more than 3,500 miles west of Australia. A right wing flap was found on Pemba Island off the coast of Tanzania, in East Africa, in June 2016. And about four months earlier that same year, Gibson located a honeycomb object broken off from a plane’s horizontal stabilizer with the words “No Step” written on it, a piece that was confirmed to be “almost certainly from MH370 by matching part number, stencil, paint, and composition,” says Gibson. In all, more than 50 pieces of debris have been found so far, much of it on Africa’s eastern coast. (The currents in the Southern Hemisphere move in a counterclockwise swirl: east to west when they’re close to the equator; the opposite direction farther south.)

The significance of the physical evidence can’t be overstated. It appears to confirm that the plane crashed in the southern Indian Ocean, that it shattered on impact, and that there should still be more debris left on the ocean floor. The discoveries also refined the search area: Drift analysis conducted by the University of Western Australia put the crash site at a latitude somewhere between 28.3 degrees south and 33.2 degrees south.

In other words, the evidence provided Ocean Infinity a tighter target. In 2018, Seabed Constructor started its search grid at about 35 degrees south and some 1,300 miles to the southwest of Australia’s west coast. It was also better equipped this time, having brought eight autonomous free-swimming submersibles called HUGINs. These robot crafts, designed and manufactured by Norway-based Kongsberg Discovery, are able to reach depths of 20,000 feet. Each comes with a lithium-polymer battery pack weighing 660 pounds; that allows for around 60 hours of uninterrupted search time. Each is also equipped with a downward-pointing sonar system as well as side-mounted sonars to send out pings to objects on the ocean floor. Onboard magnetometers on every HUGIN can confirm whether a return ping indicates something metallic in nature.

Back in January 2018, The Economist reported that Seabed Constructor was “the most advanced civilian survey vessel,” and predicted that if it couldn’t find MH370, it was “likely that nothing will, and that the mystery of MH370 will remain unsolved.” In May, Ocean Infinity turned back to port, having found nothing on the ocean floor.

That two underwater searches proved fruitless has led to differing views as to where, exactly, the plane landed in the southern Indian Ocean. Richard Godfrey, a retired British aerospace engineer and a founding member of the Independent Group, believes the plane is farther north on the seventh arc. His conclusion largely rests on an analysis he’s conducted of data from WSPR, or Weak Signal Propagation Reporter. Amateur radio operators constantly send test signals and record the data that comes back. Godfrey says that when an aircraft flies through such a signal, it creates a disruption that can be used to track that craft. His results put MH370 inside an 18-mile circle at 29.128 degrees south latitude, approximately 970 miles west of Perth.

“It will only take one more search of this area,” Godfrey told the BBC in 2024, “and we will find MH370.”

Meanwhile, other research groups think differently. One contends MH370 is farther east of the seventh arc, in a 20,000-foot-deep hole that lies along the longitudinal line of Penang Island just off Malaysia’s western coast. Two separate groups believe that MH370 did not dive into the ocean and shatter; they think MH370 came to a controlled, guided landing, and then sank. Part of their argument rests on anomalies in the BFO data, those radio-frequency Doppler shifts. The predicted BFO came in at a much higher frequency than what was observed, possibly indicating that initial thoughts of where the aircraft came to rest are wrong.

One of those pushing this interpretation is Vincent Lyne, a former researcher at the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies at the University of Tasmania. He laid out his argument in a paper published in December 2024 and called special attention to the two large-scale searches along the seventh arc.

“A significant positive outcome for ocean research was the huge volume of seafloor data collected across [about 46,000 square miles],” he wrote. “It still remains the most intensely mapped seafloor area of our planet. MH370 was simply not there!”

How these interpretations factored into Ocean Infinity’s new search was unclear. The company is tight-lipped and declined an interview for this article, but CEO Oliver Plunkett did acknowledge Godfrey’s WSPR research in a 2022 teleconference with relatives who lost people on Malaysia Airlines Flight 370.

If there’s a new dispute over the fate of MH370, it rests largely on where the plane will be found in the southern Indian Ocean, and not that the plane is somewhere under the seas in that part of the world. Gibson, who discovered part of the plane’s horizontal stabilizer, maintains that there’s no way a controlled landing took place. He cites the more than 50 pieces of debris that have been recovered since MH370 went down. “It’s not intact under water,” he tells me.

Exner, for his part, thinks the WSPR data is no substitute for the Inmarsat satellite communications. “Focus strictly on the seventh arc between 32 and 36 degrees south latitude,” he says. “[MH370 is] probably within 50 miles of that arc. Even though [Ocean Infinity] didn’t find it in the first search, that doesn’t mean it isn’t there.”

When Ocean Infinity ultimately resumed its quest for MH370, it was going back with even newer technology. In the time since its 2018 search, the company had built a fleet of more than 15 ships, ranging from vessels as short as 46 feet and as long as 282 feet. While small crews could climb aboard these ships, all of the vessels were nonetheless designed for remote operation from Ocean Infinity’s control centers at company locations. Ocean Infinity had also developed a line of proprietary underwater autonomous vehicles and acquired additional HUGIN submersibles to aid in its efforts.

The company had also accrued a solid track record of successful searches. Just under six months after Ocean Infinity suspended its search for MH370 in 2018, it discovered the lost Argentine Navy submarine San Juan in the Atlantic Ocean. The following year, it located the remains of the South Korean supertanker Stellar Daisy, which sank in the South Atlantic in 2017. In 2024, Ocean Infinity discovered the wreck of a U.S. World War II destroyer, USS Stewart, that the U.S. Navy had sunk deliberately for target practice in the waters of the Pacific Ocean off San Francisco.

Despite all that, Ocean Infinity trawled the unforgiving waters of the southern Indian Ocean for a few days in March 2025 until rough seas forced it back to port. It resumed searching in late December 2025 and kept at it through January 23, 2026, before departing the search area empty-handed.

“The scale of the challenge both geographically and technologically is almost impossible to comprehend,” said Ocean Infinity’s Plunkett in a March 2026 press release. “If nothing else, we can say with confidence that it isn’t where we looked. That matters—it brings clarity, and it will help those continuing to study the evidence refine their thinking and shape future search strategies.”

Underwater searches, obviously, are not easy or cheap endeavors. When Air France Flight 447 bound for Paris from Rio de Janeiro crashed and sank in the Atlantic Ocean off the northeastern coast of Brazil in 2009, the search team that was dispatched knew where to look for the Airbus jet. And despite it resting at a depth of only about 13,000 feet, the searchers still took almost two years to find it.

Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution’s Hartsfield, whose lab helped facilitate that search, can’t remember the exact figures but estimates that the ships deployed in the search operate at a cost of around $65,000 a day. The Remus 6000 Autonomous Underwater Vehicle used to locate the Airbus cost about another $15,000 a day (in 2026 dollars).

“Although this phase of the search has concluded, our commitment has not,” said Plunkett. “We’re continuing to work with the Malaysian government in the hope of being able to return when circumstances allow.” Ocean Infinity’s current contract runs until June 2026, which means if it hasn’t happened, it’s unlikely that a new search will get underway this year.

But as technology continues to advance, maybe someday an armada of vessels will hit the rough seas near the seventh arc once again—probing the depths, scanning the seabed, sending sonar scans into the darkness—and unearth the newest blips of hope in this maddening unsolved mystery.

Andrew Zaleski, a writer based near Washington, D.C., covers science, technology, and business.

In this simple, elegant salad, the spicy flavor of thinly sliced raw kale is offset by nutty Grana Padano cheese, bright lemon, and sweet-tart dried currants.

To a large serving bowl, add the kale, Grana Padano, currants, oil, lemon juice, 1 teaspoon of salt, and ½ teaspoon of black pepper and toss thoroughly. Set aside to rest for 5–10 minutes, then toss again. Taste and add more cheese, salt, and/or black pepper if desired.

#6561. Cacio E Pepe Mac & Cheese

Stovetop mac and cheese is the equivalent of childhood heaven. While I’ll never turn my head at the classic version, this cacio e pepe mac and cheese delivers the same comforting nostalgia, but with a grown-up upgrade. The best part? You most likely already have all of the ingredients on hand. Trust me—once you try this simple, elevated version, you’ll be putting your Kraft days behind you.

The components:All of the ingredients are relatively budget-friendly; the only item you’ll be spending a bit more on is good Pecorino Romano. To make it, you’ll need to toast the black pepper in some butter, then add the condensed milk and whole milk. Once the liquid comes to a simmer, add the American cheese and stir constantly until melted. Off the heat, add the Pecorino and shells and continue to cook for about a minute, just until the sauce tightens around the pasta. Once it coats every noodle perfectly, you’re ready to dig in.

Storage:It’s hard to believe there will be leftovers, but if you’re meal prepping for lunch, store portions in airtight containers in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the microwave or on the stove with a little extra milk to loosen.

See the new facial reconstruction of a man from Roman-era Scotland who was decapitated after his death and buried near a Roman fort.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Researchers have virtually reconstructed the face of a man who was decapitated after his death almost 2,000 years ago and then buried near a Roman military fort in Scotland.

While it's unclear why the man was beheaded, other burials hundreds of miles away may offer a clue. A chemical analysis of the man's remains suggests that he grew up in southern Britain. Beheading bodies may have been an obscure burial rite for some southern Britons, as other decapitated bodies from about the same time have been found in that region, John H. Reid, an archaeologist at the Trimontium Trust who was not involved in the excavations, told Live Science.

Another mystery is why a southern Briton was on the Roman frontier, but it seems that he was working for the Roman army when he died, researchers at National Museums Scotland said in a statement. However, his skeleton shows the man's right arm had such limited movement that he could not have used a sword, so he was probably not a soldier, they added.

Despite this disability, however, it's possible that the man used weapons in his other hand, or had a job in the Roman army that did not require frontline fighting, such as a clerk.

"He could have been left-handed, or he could have had a 'desk job'," said Reid, who is the author of the book "The Eagle and the Bear: A New History of Roman Scotland" (Birlinn, 2023).

The man was probably about 50 years old when he died between A.D. 142 and 165. His remains were then buried near the Roman fort at Inveresk, on Scotland's east coast just southeast of what's now Edinburgh, according to the statement.

An analysis of the man's skeleton indicated that he had lived an active life. His nose had been broken and healed, and his right elbow showed extensive bone growth, perhaps from arthritis. Reid said the bone growth may have been his body's response to a physical injury.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Researchers at National Museums Scotland and the independent U.K.-based forensic anthropologist Christopher Rynn created the facial construction based on the man's skull.

The facial reconstruction is based on the shape of the man's skull. He is shown here without a beard, which was based on what was common at this time.

The Roman fort at Inveresk was built around A.D. 140 and acted as a command-and-supply center for Roman forts along the Antonine Wall, which ran along the shortest route between Scotland's west coast and east coast — roughly the line between Glasgow and Edinburgh, although neither city existed at the time.

The Romans had hoped to secure all of Scotland under their rule after their invasion of Britain under Emperor Claudius in A.D. 43. They tried to impose control after their victory against a coalition of native Caledonian tribes at the Battle of Mons Graupius (possibly near the Scottish city of Perth) in about 83. But by about 120, the Romans had retreated to the heavily fortified line of Hadrian's Wall, near the modern border of England and Scotland.

The fort at Inveresk was built for a second push that aimed to secure Roman control over southern Scotland by establishing the Antonine Wall. But this failed too, and after A.D. 162, the Romans withdrew again to Hadrian's Wall, until the final collapse of Roman rule in Britain in the early fifth century.

Jess Turner, an osteoarchaeologist at National Museums Scotland, with the skull of the man buried outside the Roman fort at Inveresk.

Reid told Live Science that Scotland's soil seldom preserved human skeletons, making the discovery of a Roman-era burial an uncommon find. Although the man had been decapitated after his death, other aspects of his grave indicated he was buried with dignity. In other words, his burial was unlike those of executed criminals, who were often decapitated in Roman-era Britain, he said.

The remains from six Roman-era burials have been found at Inveresk, and four of the dead had been similarly beheaded, the statement said.

There are several ways non-Romans could have served with the Roman army, Reid told Live Science. They might have been employed as servants or artisans attached to the Roman legions, or they might have been soldiers in Roman auxiliary units or even citizen-based legions, he said. By the time of the Antonine Wall, few members of the Roman army in Scotland would have been from the Italian peninsula, he added.

The chemical analysis looked at the ratios of isotopes, or variations of chemical elements, in the man's remains. This analysis suggested that the man had grown up in southern Britain. Alternatively, he may have been recruited from a nearby region, such as the coast of what's now the Netherlands, that gave the same isotopic profile, Reid said.

Reid and his colleagues have found extensive evidence of the Roman army at the Burnswark site in southern Scotland, including the deadly whistling sling bullets they used against their "barbarian" foes. Archaeological work there is ongoing.

What do you know about the Empire's conquest of the British Isles? Find out with our Roman Britain quiz!

Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

#6558. 31 Thanksgiving Desserts to Cap Your Holiday Feast

There’s Thanksgiving dinner, and then there are Thanksgiving desserts. These are two separate events, and in between, it’s perfectly fine to take a disco nap. (In fact, we recommend it.)

“This is the magnum opus of Thanksgiving dessert recipes,” writes one reader whose 90-year-old grandfather asked for a repeat performance. “You bet your boots I will—it’s the best apple pie, ever.”

A colossal, self-serve mousse is a baller host move—no tidy slicing, no fussy garnishing, no jockeying for oven space. Set out bowls and spoons and let guests help themselves. Vanilla lovers, try our Colossal Crème Brûlée.

Butter-toasted pecans get the glory, but sour cream does the work, balancing both the gooey pecan layer and the pile of whipped cream. Between them? A thick layer of silky brown sugar custard.

A slice of Thanksgiving pie is nice, but how about a slice of pumpkin flan under a veneer of caramel? This one takes a page from Puerto Rican flan de queso, with cream cheese lending richness, tang, and luxurious texture.

Consider this pie a tangy exclamation point to the holiday meal: cranberry-lime curd in a flaky cream cheese crust, crowned with billows of meringue.

Brown sugar takes some of the fuss out of caramel cake’s famously finicky frosting while browned butter adds toasty depth. Spread it over tender yellow cake layers and finish with flaky salt.

Silky filling, flaky crust, a whisper of spice: This is pumpkin pie done right. Sweetened condensed milk gives the custard its richness; maple syrup and vanilla round out the flavor.

Skip the rolling pin: Buttered phyllo encloses an orange-scented custard, with crumpled sheets forming a dramatically ruffled top. Cinnamon sugar adds crunch to this no-roll pie.

This plush pumpkin spice cake wears a thick swoop of tangy cream cheese frosting. Bake the cake a day ahead, then add the frosting in the lull between dinner and dessert.

If most holiday desserts feel a tad too sweet for you, herbal rosemary and fruity olive oil give this cake just enough savory elements to justify a second helping.

Blanketing quartered apples with rough-puff pastry feels rustic enough, but once baked and inverted, this shimmering, blushing tart dominates the holiday table.

Sweet potato, warming spices, and orange zest get a gloss of dark chocolate in this autumnal loaf cake. Bake it up to three days ahead, leaving the ganache for later.

A deeply browned top and cracked sides are the goal here, not a baking mishap. Underneath: a custardy, pumpkin-spiced cheesecake that needs neither a crust nor a water bath.

Pecan pie meets Hawaiian-style butter mochi in this chewy, coconut-milk-rich cake. Miso-and-maple-coated pecans bring salty-sweet crunch, with some sinking into the batter as the cake bakes.

This date cake blanketed in toffee sauce tastes like cozying up by the fireside after a game of football on the lawn. Bake the unsauced cake a day ahead, then rewarm before finishing.

Cinnamon-spiced pumpkin cake rolled around walnut-studded cream cheese filling needs little embellishment. A dusting of powdered sugar is plenty—each slice supplies its own dramatic swirl.

This glamorous layer cake, with jewel-toned swipes of cranberry jam, white chocolate–cream cheese frosting, and sugared cranberries, looks and tastes like winter is coming (in the best possible way).

A no-bake Oreo crust, a rich chocolate filling, and a tower of whipped cream come together in this shut-the-room-up dessert.

Caramel-glazed apple halves crown this nutty upside-down cake, all baked in the same skillet used to brown the fruit. A scoop of vanilla ice cream on top? We wouldn’t say no.

A floral, earthy saffron soak gives this sponge cake a pudding-like texture and its vibrant yellow color, while pistachios add nutty crunch.

Inspired by the flavors of a pumpkin spice latte, this rendition of old-school tiramisu calls for soaking ladyfingers in bourbon-spiked espresso, then enveloping them in plumes of pumpkin-mascarpone cream.

Cranberries with dinner and again for dessert? Absolutely. Tart filling hides between layers of buttery, crumbly walnut crust in this Linzer tart. Prefer individual portions? Try these cranberry hand pies.

Pumpkin crumb cake is like the brownie of Thanksgiving desserts: easy to tote and slice for sharing. Here, sweet rice flour gives the cake a chewy bounce beneath a buttery, crispy-crumbly pecan streusel.
