#6540. Even for Desperate Restaurants, Fake Reviews Just Aren’t Worth It

A new report proves that planting fake Yelp reviews has dire long-term impacts on restaurants

When Yelp was first launched in 2004, it flopped. The company’s initial model of an email-based referral service failed to take off until its creators realized users were taking the platform into their own hands; in lieu of sending one another recommendations via email chain, they began using a “hidden” link at the bottom of the startup’s website to write unsolicited reviews of everything from doctors to restaurants. Yelp 2.0 launched in 2005, and gave those reviews a more visible place to live online — one that emboldened users to feel more authentic stewardship, by way of direct authorship, over hyping up the businesses they enjoyed (or didn’t). The startup bought a whopping 20-million-business database, and amplified a world of reviews outside of the restaurant- critic echo chamber. It was a fresh democratization of information, which was itself one of the more optimistic legacies of the Y2K internet.

It’s been over 20 years since Yelp was founded. At its best, the platform still feels like a place where the voices of hungry, curious diners can share their personal experiences and offer recommendations and tips; at its worst, it feels like a bloated repository for reviews filled with misdirected anger, unreasonable expectations, or else completely fake customer reviews. Initially, unsubstantiated and unreliable reviews were more often written by a person — either someone from the business itself, or paid by the business; now, a fake review can be penned by a paid influencer, a detailed generative AI prompt, or purchased from third-party agencies that will produce fake bot reviews in bulk.

Fake reviews were perhaps inevitable. Bot-driven comments became ubiquitous during an overripe moment in the untamed internet’s lifespan. But how does a restaurant shamed for gamifying its reviews — even if it was, presumably, out of desperation in a tough economic landscape — regain customers’ broken trust?

… The offending restaurant’s foot traffic went down by 8 percent, and dipped even lower around the holidays, a time when would-be diners rely even more on Yelp.

In 2026’s AI-addled digital ecosystem, researchers are starting to understand even more about how paid-for, planted reviews impact the restaurants behind them, and whether trying to gamify platforms to achieve high ratings is worth it at all for businesses. A recently published working paper on the consequences of restaurants flagged by Yelp for fake (planted, incentivized) reviews found that since 2023, more than 4,900 businesses have been flagged with Yelp’s “Consumer Alert” banner, which exists on the penalized business’ page for a 90-day period and lets Yelp users know that the business has been caught peddling fake reviews. In 2020, the fast-casual chain Burgerim was found guilty of planting fake reviews, and received over 200 digital warning banners across its various locations’ Yelp pages.

The impacts of that digital pillory extend far beyond its 90-day duration. Yi Cao is an assistant professor of accounting at George Mason University, and the co-author of the paper; almost immediately, Cao noticed the offending restaurant’s foot traffic went down by 8 percent, and dipped even lower around the holidays, a time when would-be diners rely even more on Yelp. Cao’s team cross-analyzed the business’ performance on Yelp with real-life foot traffic reports (from global location data firm SafeGraph) and credit card transaction data (courtesy of Consumer Edge), and discovered that most of the penalized restaurants struggled to recover to pre-alert traffic even after a year and a half. The stink of chicanery lingered.

While Cao says his team doesn’t know every signal that Yelp uses to identify fake reviews, they do know that it relies “substantially on reports from consumers and business owners,” and that “they also have an algorithm running in the background to screen reviews for AI-generated language — which is a sign of possible review inflation.” At this point, the cost of planting a good review is only getting steeper as the technology capable of detecting it improves. “This is a classical theory of a trade-off between the benefits of manipulating reputation and the risks of getting caught,” Cao explains, “When the risk is relatively low, the business owners decide the incremental benefits are worth the risk.”

Yelp’s real restaurant reviews don’t necessarily need to be etched in stone, but as AI-penned reviews become less detectable and more sophisticated, what diners want now, more than ever, is a human touch and a sense of authenticity.

#6539. Martian Polar Crater Ice Shifts with Seasonal Frost

The planet Mars shares many landforms and weather patterns with the Earth, including changing seasons, volcanoes, canyons, dust storms and dust devils, and water ice. But one feature that Earth and Mars share among the eight planets in our solar system are polar ice caps. Both are one of each planetâs striking features, but the major difference is while Earthâs polar ice caps are both comprised of water, Marsâ north polar ice cap is only comprised of water while its southern polar ice cap is carbon dioxide. The reasons for this are determined by altitude, but Marsâ northern polar ice cap is one of the most studied regions primarily due to its water ice composition. But how does the north polar ice cap water ice change with the seasons compared to Earth, and what can this teach scientists about Marsâ climate history?

Now, an international team of researchers might have shed new light on this conundrum. As discussed in a recent study published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, the researchers challenged our understanding of ice deposits in Marsâ northern polar ice cap region. The primary motivation behind this study was to fill a longstanding knowledge gap regarding the seasonal changes in Martian polar ice deposits, specifically focusing on craters. The researchers note that better understanding seasonal changes in polar ice cap deposits could help gain insights into long-term climate changes on the Red Planet.

For the study, the researchers analyzed images of 36 craters within the northern polar ice cap region of Mars. The images were obtained from NASAâs Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter's High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) camera between 2006 and 2025. This time period is also referred to as Mars Years (MY) 28â38 since one year on Mars is 668 Earth days. The goal of the study was to identify how polar ice deposits on crater floors changed with seasons, specifically whether the deposits increased or decreased in size based on winter or summer months, respectively.

In the end, the researchers found that 32 of the 36 craters exhibited changes in bright deposits, broadly indicating ice deposits are expanding and shrinking with the seasons. Of the remaining four craters, the researchers didnât observe changes in brightness. The researchers note that seasonal frost deposits on the outside of each crater could be responsible for the changes in brightness.

âNot all craters exhibit changes in frost coverage from one Mars year to the next,â the study notes. âFor a given Mars year, only a subset of craters show altered frost conditions relative to previous years, while others maintain similar or nearly identical frost extents. This spatial heterogeneity suggests that seasonal frost cycles and interannual mass balance are localized processes rather than cap-wide phenomena. Local topography, crater geometry, and microclimatic conditions likely modulate energy balance and vapor transport, leading to crater-specific responses to broader climatic forcing.â

Essentially, the researchers found the changes in crater ice deposits are triggered by local climate changes, as opposed to being triggered by larger climate changes. The reason why understanding Marsâ climate changes is important is to help pin down specific triggers, whether itâs seasonal or related to other factors. For example, Mars experiences much larger climate changes on grander scales compared to Earth due to the Red Planetâs planetary tilt having much larger swings than Earth. However, as this study demonstrates, local climates are still capable of delivering their own changes disconnected from the larger climate picture. This study identifies seasonal changes in polar ice deposits while providing motivation for future modeling work that could help expand our understanding of localized climates on Mars.

What new insights into Mars polar crater ice will researchers make in the coming years and decades? Only time will tell, and this is why we science!

#6538. Spinach Artichoke Baked Potatoes

This baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal. Classic twice-baked potatoes require two trips to the oven to deliver a pillowy, gussied-up filling and crispy skins all in one bite. Here, I’ve streamlined the workflow with a microwave. By zapping your spuds to start, you can reduce the overall baking time without sacrificing texture. Pick a large russet (or Idaho) for the best results; their relatively high starch and low moisture content helps them bake up airy and light, not gummy.

The rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks. Cream cheese and mozzarella pack in enough dairy richness for a satisfying cheese pull and mellow out the subtle bitterness of baby spinach and nutty tang of artichoke hearts. (It’s important that your cream cheese is room temperature before you mash it in with the veggies. If it’s still got a chill from the fridge, it won’t fully incorporate.) The Worcestershire sauce is optional, but just a few shakes from the bottle bring instant savory depth to the filling.

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

Preheat oven to 425°. Poke 1 large russet potato (about 12 oz.) all over with a fork; rub with avocado or vegetable oil to coat and sprinkle with kosher salt. Microwave potato on a microwave-proof plate on high 5 minutes. Turn potato over and microwave on high until fork-tender, about 5 minutes more. Let potato sit until just cool enough to handle.

While potato is cooling, microwave 5 oz. baby spinach with 2 Tbsp. water in a medium microwave-proof glass bowl until wilted, about 2 minutes. Carefully press leaves to release as much liquid as possible, then drain off liquid. Coarsely chop spinach.

Mix 2 Tbsp. cream cheese, room temperature, in a medium bowl until smooth. Add spinach, 4 quartered artichoke hearts (from a 14-oz. can), coarsely chopped, 2 Tbsp. finely grated Parmesan, 2 Tbsp. coarsely grated mozzarella, ½ tsp. garlic powder, and ¼ tsp. Worcestershire sauce (if using) and fold to combine; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

Slice potato in half lengthwise and lightly fluff flesh in each half. Set on a small foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Divide spinach mixture between potato halves, piling high (don’t pack too tightly). Sprinkle more Parmesan over. Bake potato halves until very tender when squeezed and skin is wrinkled and crisp, 20–25 minutes. Let cool slightly before eating.

In two new surveys, U.S. adults report lying to their doctors and their children's doctors about symptoms in hopes of being prescribed antibiotics.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nearly 30% of U.S. adults have lied to doctors in an effort to obtain antibiotics, either by exaggerating their actual symptoms or by fabricating symptoms, the results of a new national survey suggest. Additionally, in a second survey, about one-quarter of children's caregivers reported lying about their kids' symptoms to get antibiotics on their behalf.

"As clinicians, we know that patients lie to us sometimes," Dr. Jeffrey Linder, a general internist and primary care clinician-investigator at Northwestern Medicine, wrote in a commentary about the survey findings.

However, the results are still important because the inappropriate use of antibiotics can contribute to the mounting problem of antibiotic resistance, in which bacteria build up a tolerance to the drugs designed to kill them. Recent data released by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) highlight the extent of the problem: In 2023, drug-resistant bacteria and fungi caused about 9.7 million infections in the U.S., up from 2.8 million in 2017. In turn, the estimated number of deaths caused by drug-resistant germs rose from 35,000 to 50,800 between the two years.

A major factor driving resistance among bacteria is the misuse of antibiotics — in other words, using antibiotics for ailments like viral infections, which the drugs do not treat. For individual patients, such prescriptions don't cure their illness and can result in an upset stomach or issues with the gut microbiome, the community of microbes in the intestines. Simultaneously, they place extra pressure on bacteria to evolve resistance, granting the germs opportunities to pick up new strategies for thwarting antibiotics.

Doctors play a big role in ensuring that the antibiotic prescriptions they write are necessary. Part of their decision-making process comes down to what patients say about their symptoms, some of which may be fabricated, the two new surveys suggest.

The new surveys were published Friday (Oct. 30) in the journal JAMA Network Open.

The first survey was completed by nearly 960 adults from across the U.S. in January and February 2026. It asked whether the respondents had ever told a healthcare provider that their symptoms were worse or more long-lasting than they were in order to get antibiotics, as well as whether they'd ever made up symptoms for the same reason. It then inquired about what motivated a given patient to lie — or avoid lying, if they were truthful — as well as posed contextual questions about their demographics, health behaviors and beliefs.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Overall, about 28% of the respondents reported misrepresenting their symptoms, including 26% who exaggerated their existing symptoms and 17% who fabricated symptoms. They most frequently lied about cold-like symptoms, such as fever, cough and sore throat. About two-thirds of these patients were at least moderately confident that their lie would motivate a clinician to prescribe them antibiotics, and 77% said the strategy worked for them at least once.

Often, patients' motivations for lying centered around feeling very sick, holding strong beliefs that antibiotics would help them recover quickly and get back to their responsibilities, and wanting control over the treatments prescribed to them. Compared with people who didn't lie, those who lied were also more likely to feel that clinicians didn't take them seriously or more likely to endorse statements suggesting that antibiotic resistance is a hoax.

"Greater antibiotic knowledge and aversion to taking antibiotics were associated with lower odds of misrepresentation," meaning lying about symptoms, the study authors noted.

Less than 30% of these patients regretted their lies or taking the antibiotics prescribed to them. Those that did express regret noted experiencing side effects, noticing that the treatment didn't help or feeling that the lying itself was morally wrong.

The second survey was much smaller; it included 236 parents and other guardians of children and teens under 18 years old. It posed similar questions but asked whether the caregivers had lied about their children's symptoms and, if so, what motivated them to lie.

About 27% reported lying about a child's symptoms to get antibiotics, with 87% of these caregivers believing that their lying worked at least once. Their reasons for lying were very similar to those expressed by the respondents in the first survey.

"These findings suggest that symptom misrepresentation may contribute to antibiotic overuse in pediatric care," the study authors concluded.

Ideally, antibiotics should be used only when truly needed, to help relieve the pressure on bacteria to gain resistance.

The surveys reached a diverse group of people, including a range of ages, demographics and locations within the United States; however, the respondents were not necessarily representative of the whole U.S. population, the authors noted. The prevalence of lying should therefore be seen as a tentative measure to be checked in future studies, rather than an unbiased, population-level metric, they wrote. It's also possible that not all the respondents who lied disclosed that they did so or remembered that they had done so.

Especially in outpatient settings, which account for most antibiotic use among U.S. patients, it can be difficult for doctors to quickly determine whether a patient needs an antibiotic.

One factor is that there's a lack of fast, surefire diagnostic tests for many bacterial infections. Outpatient appointments are also extremely short, so doctors sometimes worry about overlooking an infection that could then get worse, Julia Szymczak, a medical sociologist at the University of Utah School of Medicine, previously told Live Science. Another major factor is that clinicians can face pressure to prescribe antibiotics from their adult patients or from children's caregivers, as the new surveys reflect.

But in the face of these pressures and patients' occasional lies, Linder argues that it's still up to the clinicians to do the right thing. "While clinicians might interpret patients' symptom maximization and questions as demands for antibiotics, symptoms do not determine the indication, a diagnosis does," he wrote in the commentary.

"It does not track that approximately 80% of respondents who reported misrepresenting their symptoms obtained a prescription," he added, "unless prescribers were being willfully deceived or, more likely, just getting worn down with what they perceive as patient demand, regardless of actual clinical appropriateness."

When it comes to making decisions about individual patients, Linder argued that doctors don't necessarily need to think about the big picture of antibiotic resistance and how their patient's case fits into that global trend. Rather, providers should simply ask whether a given prescription is more likely to help or hurt that patient, he said.

"Clinicians' obligation is to act in patients' best interest," he said, "even if patients are hoping we do something different, even if patients do not like it, or even if patients lie about their symptoms."

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6536. The 9 Best Pop-Up Canopy Tents for Outdoor Activities and Events

Insta-shade and rain coverage for all your backyard barbecues, park outings, and tailgates.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Whether it's a weekend barbecue, a tailgate, or the sidelines of a kid’s soccer game, pop-up canopy tents are the best solution for substantial shade and shelter at outdoor events.

I’ve personally researched, tested, and essentially lived under pop-up canopies over the last few years, doing activities like puzzles and watching movies, and working in what I love to call my second office. If there's one thing I've learned, it's that while pop-up canopy tents may look similar, they’re actually purpose-built, and the details that distinguish one from the next aren’t always obvious to the casual observer.

For example, a tent that's perfect for a tailgate party is lightweight, super fast to set up, and has a relatively compact footprint. The canopy that’s in my backyard took two people to set up and is a larger, more durable structure. A pop-up canopy for the beach is designed to stay in place when a gust of wind rushes on shore.

Below, I walk you through the best pop-up canopy tents for specific activities and include info about why I love it and where it falls short. Following my reviews, I’ve laid out key considerations to take into account when shopping for a pop-up canopy.

This pop-up canopy takes our top spot because of its durable water-resistant canopy, height-adjustable frame, and top-point air ventilation.

The canopy's 300-denier polyester fabric has a water-resistant polyurethane lining and is coated in silver, which helps protect you from UV rays. It’s also rated UPF 50+, so it withstands hot, sunny days and improves the tent’s longevity.

The powder-coated steel frame is height-adjustable and very easy to open, thanks to large push-button brackets. We also appreciate that the canopy is finished at the edges with white trim and that its corners extend midway down the side poles. Plus, the top air vent allows for air and smoke from below to escape instead of accumulate, so you can easily place a controlled campfire underneath it on a rainy day. Similarly, the vent lets wind blow by more easily without toppling over.

The tent comes in a rainbow of colors and three sizes. Stakes, ropes, sandbags, and a wheeled carrying case that doubles as a backpack are all included. The sandbags provided may be too light to hold the canopy down by themselves in heavy winds, so you may need to invest in larger ones.

For something with a little more coverage and durability, we recommend going with a pop-up canopy tent that has sidewalls. We especially like this model from Eurmax because the sidewalls attach with velcro, so they can easily come on or off depending on weather conditions.

The strong, cross-trussed frame has a powder-coated finish and adjusts to three heights, plus the tent is topped with a heavy-duty polyester canopy, which is water-resistant and rated UPF 50+.

The sidewalls are a lighter polyester, and seams throughout are sealed to prevent leaks. Along with the tent, you’ll also get four sandbags to ensure stability. We also appreciate that this comes with a wheeled carrying case too, because this tent weighs just over 60 pounds.

If you’re looking for a budget-friendly pop-up canopy that doesn’t skimp on durability, this model from Phi Villa is tough to beat. In addition to its durability, one-person setup, and three height settings, it comes with something I have never seen included with even high-end canopies: an attachable, hanging, five-pocket organizer that holds essentials like keys, snacks, books, or toys.

The canopy itself is made from durable, flame-retardant Oxford fabric, which is especially useful if you plan to grill under the canopy or nearby. It also comes with multiple ways to keep it grounded in wind and storms, including stakes, tie-down ropes, and sandbags. With purchase, you also get a one-year limited warranty for the frame and six months for fabrics and accessories.

My only gripe with this pop-up canopy is the grommeted vent holes along the sides that allow rain to drip through. If you plan to set it up on a rainy day, I highly recommend finding a way to plug each hole to block the rain from pouring through and soaking you and your things.

If it’s fast, easy shade you need and on a budget, the Ozark Trail slant-leg canopy is worth a look. It’s not as durable as the Eurmax or ABC Canopy options above, but at under $100, it’s a solid choice that delivers exactly what you need: a steel frame, a polyester canopy top, and a snap-button setup that takes one person and just a few minutes to get off the ground.

One thing to note related to the slant-leg construction is that while the dimensions are advertised as 10x10, the actual shaded footprint is closer to 8x8 feet (64 square feet). Still, for casual use on a day where weather is fair and free of rain, like a kid's birthday party at the park or a weekend camping trip, it's a genuinely good value.

For tailgating, you need a canopy that is strong, easy to set up, and doesn’t need to be staked to the ground. The Crown Shade pop-up canopy delivers, and as an added bonus there are loads of colors to choose from.

Its patented locking system uses a central hub that locks all four legs into place with a single push, which means it’s ideal for one-person assembly. I also appreciate the sidewall included for protection from the elements, and to create a more intimate space when lined up in the parking lot with other fans and their canopies.

The 150-denier silver-coated fabric is lighter than some of the heavier-duty options on this list; it does make for a lighter load when lugging to games. Make sure you throw a couple of bricks or rocks in the car to fill the included sandbags for extra protection from gusts of wind.

When it comes to finding a great camping canopy, you need something extra durable that can withstand not only the elements but also being lugged to the campsite with ease, or able to be pitched safely on uneven ground. If you’re looking for something rugged that’s both functional and dependable, this pop-up canopy from Coleman is the best choice.

The Coleman Oasis has a center-hub opening and closing system. The frame pops open with a single push and takedown is just as easy thanks to the pull-strap. The steel frame is built to withstand winds up to 35 mph (when properly staked with the included ropes).

The UPF 50+ fabric handles sun exposure well while the vented canopy lets heat escape. The only gripe I have is that it does not come with sandbags, so if you are expecting bad weather, you may want to pack your own sandbag set up. This canopy comes in two sizes 10 x10 or 13x13, and you can opt for a one side wall design for extra protection from the elements.

Pop-up canopy tents for constant backyard use need to look good, be durable and spacious, and keep bugs out during dinner. The Crown Shades 11x14 gazebo fits the bill on all these points.

It’s roomy enough for a full-length patio table and has strong zip-close mesh screen walls. The pre-assembled, rope-strung netting is far easier to install than traditional hook-by-hook netting I’ve encountered on other models.

The reinforced steel frame with an eight-point center locking system feels more substantial underfoot than most. Also, the double-roof vented design keeps the space noticeably cooler during humid backyard dinners compared to single-layer canopy tops I've used.

While I have set this up by myself, it’s easier and safer as a two-person job. Keep in mind that when the walls are zipped closed, the actual space is 9 by 12 feet, not 11 x 14; the lost ground space is due to the canopy design overhang.

Worrying about a traditional pop-up canopy tent getting swept up on a windy beach day ruins the vibe. That is why I am sending a huge shoutout to the Shibumi Shade. This thing was made for seriously windy beach days.

In fact, it needs just a little wind to work well, which the beach is never short of. Instead of a rigid frame, it uses an arched, wind-powered flowing design that catches the ocean breeze and holds its shape with as little as 3 mph of wind. It weighs under five pounds, fits in a small bag and pitches in about three minutes.

It covers about 150 square feet, enough shade for a group of up to eight people, and the open-air design keeps airflow moving at all times, so I can actually stay cool and protected from the sun all day long.

For the overall and value picks, I looked at frames and fabrics that could reasonably handle every activity on this list. I prioritized peak height, fabric construction and durability, and included accessories like sandbags and tie-down ropes and stakes.

For the budget pick, I looked for a canopy that delivered a stable, easy setup even with less durable materials. I also made notes where the actual shade coverage falls short of the advertised footprint—an important thing to note if you require specific square footage.

For tailgating, I focused on setup speed and the ability to stay in place in a parking lot. For the backyard, I prioritized walls for bug protection, ventilation, and a larger footprint suited to dining or large seating furniture rather than simple folding chairs and plastic tables. For camping, I weighed wind resistance against portability.

And for the beach, I intentionally looked outside the traditional steel-frame category, prioritizing a design that works well with wind and sand, and, of course, ease of transport across dunes and sand.

The two things that determine how long a canopy survives in the elements are the frame material and the fabric denier (a measure of fabric thickness).

I always look for powder-coated steel frames on anything I plan to use regularly, since they resist rust and hold up to repeated ups and downs better than lighter alloy frames. For fabric, anything rated CPAI-84 has passed a flame-resistance standard, and higher denier counts (ideally 300D and up) hold up to UV exposure and light rain without degrading as quickly.

If I'm buying a canopy that'll live outdoors semi-permanently, like my beloved backyard gazebo I write about above, I prioritize a double-roof or vented design, since trapped heat and pooled rainwater are the two things most likely to shorten a canopy's lifespan. It’s worth the extra spend.

Nearly every canopy on this list offers multiple height settings, and I've come to see this as non-negotiable rather than nice-to-have. It can dramatically help in wind and rain: lower settings help in windy conditions by reducing how much the canopy catches the breeze, while higher settings give more headroom and better airflow underneath. I also pay attention to whether sandbags and tie-down ropes are included, since staking out a canopy with ropes at an angle also dramatically improves its wind resistance compared to relying on the legs and sandbags alone.

This is where the mechanism matters as much as the material. Central-hub or "one-push" designs, like the ones on the Crown Shades and Coleman Oasis, let me pop the whole frame solo from the middle rather than pulling each corner out individually, which is both faster and easier for one person. I also look at how the canopy packs away: a bag with a wheeled base and a dedicated pocket for stakes and ropes comes in handy when dragging to and from home.

How much a canopy weighs, and how well it travels, matters differently depending on where I'm taking it and what I need it for. For a canopy that's mostly staying in the backyard, weight barely registers; I’ll take a heavy-duty frame and canopy that weighs more than I can comfortably carry happily. However, for tailgating or camping, where I'm loading and unloading a vehicle full of stuff, I care a lot about whether the carry bag has wheels versus just a shoulder strap that weighs me down. And for the beach, where I'm hauling gear across soft sand, weight becomes the single most important factor, which is exactly why a 4-pound wind-powered shade like the Shibumi Shade beats a 40-pound steel frame every time.

In terms of construction, there are two different types of frames: pyramid (sometimes referred to as “cathedral”) and cross-trussed. Pyramid frames are generally less expensive and offer more headroom by design. The hollow pyramid structure keeps the top space up to the point of the covering. The biggest drawback with pyramid canopy tents is they are less sturdy and more subject to breaking or bending under heavy weight. This is because the poles that hold the point up top are single poles, angled, and not cross-trussed, which means they may bow or bend under pressure.

Your alternative is a canopy tent with cross trusses across the center and one pole that rises to create the same pointed top. This is, as you might have guessed, the cross-trussed model. These have a lower ceiling than pyramid options, but they make up for that with a much sturdier construction. The added cross trusses across the canopy make them more resistant to bending or breaking, though it also makes them more expensive and heavier to carry.

Depending on use, you may want to consider a pop-up canopy tent with sidewalls or a model with add-on walls sold separately to give yourself extra customization. Sidewalls provide some protection from wind, and if you're using a tent at a farmers’ market or fair, they can make your pop-up more inviting. Similarly, even vented sidewalls, which let air pass through, can offer some protection from bees and mosquitoes.

Most pop-up canopy tents come with extras like stakes, sandbags, and tie-down ropes for keeping the tent secure, especially on windy days. They also usually include a wheeled storage bag, along with an optional carrying strap for easy portability.

If you choose a tent that does not come with these items, you may want to consider purchasing them separately. For instance, these sandbags will keep any of our tents in place when stakes aren’t an option and the wind is high. They’re also designed to last with sun protection and thick, waterproof material.

Most pop-up canopy tents are designed for simple setup and can often be assembled by a single person with average strength. Taking the canopy down is typically just as straightforward. That said, it’s important to follow the instructions carefully. The canopy fabric usually needs to be properly positioned and secured on the frame before fully extending the structure. Skipping or rushing this step puts unnecessary strain on the material and may lead to stretching or tearing.

For the most part, pop-up canopies are designed to handle wind gusts up to about 15 mph with ease. That said, I have learned that properly securing your canopy is one of the most important factors in determining if your canopy can withstand higher wind gusts or major storms. Properly secure your canopy to its frame according to the manufacturer's instructions, and place the stakes in the feet of the canopy when possible. I also add sandbags for extra security from high winds. (I actually fill mine with bricks or heavy rocks because who has 50 pounds of sand lying around?) By properly securing the canopy and the frame, you will minimize the danger of the frame shifting and moving, which can tear the canopy.

To date, I haven’t encountered a pop-up canopy that didn’t include some form of anchoring system. These anchor systems typically come in a few different styles, such as stakes that fit through holes drilled into the canopy feet, grommeted loops at each corner for securing ropes or heavy-duty cord to ground spikes, or weighted sandbags that attach around each leg.

Whatever is provided, it’s essential that you use it. That said, if you choose to leave your canopy up for an extended period of time or all year long and a major storm is going to blow through, use your judgment as to whether you should take it down completely or reinforce the anchor system.

#6535. New Research Resolves the Mystery Behind Van Gogh's The Starry Night

Starry Night, the iconic painting by legendary Impressionist Vincent Van Gogh, has inspired debate among art historians and astronomers for decades. Was the painting something that Van Gogh was spontaneously inspired to create in the early morning hours in July 1889, or did it present a realistic depiction of the night sky over Saint-RÃ©my (where he painted it)? According to a recent study conducted jointly by South Korean telescope manufacturer SLLAB and the School of Space Research at Kyung Hee University, it's the latter.

For over a century and a half, scholars focused primarily on religious and symbolic interpretations of the painting. It was not until the mid-1980s that studies were presented that analyzed its astronomical aspects. These were conducted by UCLA art historian Albert Boime (1984) and Harvard astronomer Charles Whitney (1986), who examined celestial correspondences and proposed constellation identifications based on a mid-June date. However, the two reached conflicting conclusions, and no studies since have examined the painting using observational geometry.

The study, presented in Scientific Reports (a Nature journal), instead narrows the dates on which a crescent Moon, Venus, and the Hyades star cluster (which appear closely together in the painting) fell within Van Gogh's field of view. The study's first author, Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, CEO of SLLAB and a Ph.D. candidate at Kyung Hee University's School of Space Research, has spent years building telescopes and observing the night sky and was inspired to weigh in on the debate.

(a)The stars in The Starry Night (1889) overlaid by the real stars after matching for size, orientation, and position; red dashed lines show the residual differences. (b) The stars in CafÃ© Terrace at Night (1888), left, and the stars around the Summer Triangle. Credit: Kim et al., Scientific Reports

"To an observational astronomer, the cluster of stars in The Starry Night is the Hyades in Taurus," he said. "But the moment I read the earlier studies explaining it as Aries, I heard the painting calling to me." The research builds on Kim's previous book (released in 2025) and began with two field trips to France in 2019 to gather additional evidence and add quantitative data. Traditionally, the painting was dated to June 18th, 1889, based on a letter Van Gogh wrote to his brother, Leo.

However, on that date, the Moon was in its waning gibbous phase, which does not match the slender crescent in the painting. On July 22nd, the Moon was a crescent, and the Hyades cluster would have been seen rising in the east alongside Venus (placing it in the Taurus constellation). In the past, that date was thought to be one when Van Gogh experienced one of his seizures, but cross-analysis of the original French and Dutch letters and the details mentioned in both suggests his seizure began in late July.

Using on-site photographs taken in Arles, the team verified Van Gogh's field of view overlooking the RhÃ´ne River. Afterward, they traveled to Saint-RÃ©my, where they located the spot where Van Gogh drew the landscape in preparation for his painting. They then conducted a statistical shape analysis to confirm that the five central stars in the painting corresponded to the Hyades cluster, which matched even more closely in the pen drawing Van Gogh made after he finished the painting.

These results suggest that the sky in the painting was based on actual observation rather than pure impressionist feeling. The methods employed could also be extended to other historical night paintings, leading to collaborative efforts between astronomers and art historians. The team has already used the same method on another of Van Gogh's famous creations that features stars in the sky - CafÃ© Terrace at Night (painted in 1888) - and found a possible match to the Summer Triangle asterism.

"I hope this work prompts a renewed, multidisciplinary look at the sequence and working methods of the Saint-RÃ©my paintings, and at Van Gogh's movements that summer," Kim said. "Our conversation with Van Gogh's other skies is still ongoing. We plan to tell those stories one by one."

#6534. Food-Themed Fashion Is Starting to Feel Gluttonous

﻿The millennial avocado obsession walked so the Loewe tomato clutch could run

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

There was a time, not too long ago, when a purse shaped like a baguette felt like a thrilling — even subversive — novelty. Now, we hardly bat an eye when we see that Moschino has made a trompe l’oeil celery purse, or that Big Bud Press is making a hot-dog-and-pretzel-print jumpsuit in collaboration with a Los Angeles bar. How did we get here? And has it all become a little too much?

Fashion has long found inspiration from the culinary world, but the influx of food-fueled prints, graphics, and trompe l’oeil accessories that picked up steam during the pandemic have now reached a cultural tipping point.

The then-emerging brand made food a central theme of its vision: Its cake-topped aviator caps, Ferrero Rocher heels, and beeswax-sculpted cheese hats — hyperrealistic, absurdist food designs capable of achieving instant social media virality. Prior to working in fashion, Puppets designer Carly Mark was working as an artist whose pieces revolved around candies and snacks. As she told Business of Fashion in 2023, the Puppets universe felt like the ideal pairing given what she considers food and fashion’s motivators: pleasure and money.

During the pandemic, the much-duped “strawberry dress” took over TikTok, and Tombolo Company found a hit on its hands with its vongole shirt, which debuted in 2019, but found peak popularity in 2021. The shirt appeared in Vogue in 2020, and InsideHook called it an “obvious bedfellow to day-drinks, rooftops and weekenders” — in other words, a status symbol. Katie Kimmel’s T-shirts made chicken-parm enthusiasm akin to being a devout sports fan, and in 2022, this very publication called “seafood kitsch” the look of the summer, as items like Rachel Antonoff’s super-popular seafood-tower dress flew off the digital shelves.

Why was food so primed to become a motif in clothing at this point in culture? One could make the argument that it has roots in the millennial optimism years: Earlier in the 2000s and 2010s, the concept of “foodies” was new. Brands printed tongue-in-cheek food- and coffee-related motifs and slogans (a fervent love of avocados comes to mind) on hipster apparel, as the idea that “you are what you eat” developed growing fervor. That period was a key stepping stone in the evolution toward the far more elaborate and pervasive marketability of food-as-identity we see today. Content creator Cole Poska, who is a partner and creative director at Beyond Studios, tells Eater that “food brands have something most brands would kill for: decades of nostalgia, iconic identities, and consumers who are borderline obsessed with them.” Poska’s own Instagram often reimagines restaurant merch just for fun; his designs for Cheesecake Factory apparel went viral, such as a hat that resembles the iconic brown bread. He points out that people will defend their favorite fast-food order like it’s a family member, and with the kind of loyalty that’s hard to manufacture. The same could be said about their martini order, or favorite taco spot; it’s all a way of telling others who we are through what we like.

But the fatigue is undoubtedly here. In 2024, Bon Appétit asked “Why Does Every Dress Have Pasta and Cocktail Shrimp on It?” And as the novelty factor of a shrimp-print dress has worn off, the next question might be: Will there be any true longevity for these food-as-fashion moments? Our feeds overflow with products that are hurriedly designed for flash-in-the-pan viral trends and quickly destined for a landfill; arguably more so if the object in question prioritizes shock value and gimmicks over function and brand identity.

This is undoubtedly all related to the accelerated speed of trend cycles and shortened consumer attention spans. However, as Leah Asmelash wrote last year for CNN, the rising costs of food also casts an increasingly sinister shadow over food-themed fashion. In 2026, a $425 cardigan emblazoned with oysters has waning originality compared to a few years ago; it falls into banality at best and the Hunger Games at worst; its wearer indicating that they’re financially comfortable and, more importantly, well-fed. In that light, beyond its role in identity, food has become more of a status symbol than ever. A sweater touting one’s love of caviar is shorthand for their access to and appreciation of luxury, culinary and otherwise. But sporting the mass-market Temu version? It’s more akin to wearing a faux Gucci belt.

“Food brands have something most brands would kill for: decades of nostalgia, iconic identities, and consumers who are borderline obsessed with them.”

If it’s possible to escape the sense of accelerated-trend-cycle disposability, it may have to be through a more subtle approach than, say, a bag that looks like a giant stick of butter. Sam Salad is the co-founder of Meals, a Los Angeles-based, workwear-inspired apparel company that, by its own description, “bakes ‘food culture’ into apparel, blurring the lines between the clothes we eat and the food we wear.” Utility is at the forefront of Meals, which offers a classic chef pant with a slightly fuller cut, in both basic colors and subdued aesthetic homages to blue cheese and watermelon. When Meals launched in 2019, Salad was selling premium denim along Venice’s Abbot Kinney Boulevard, a hotbed of Instagrammy food culture and trendy restaurants like Gjelina that helped inspire his own brand. “Design today has to translate across languages and platforms,” Salad tells Eater.

Food is hardly a new bedfellow for fashion designers, even if today’s hyper-fast trend cycle has kicked it into overdrive. “Food is totally universal,” Salad says. “Issey Miyake once merchandised their pleats collection as little omakase sets.” He cites that collection among other fashion-meets-food moments that he considers successful, such as the iconic Salvador Dalí- and Elsa Schiaparelli-designed lobster dress. At the time of its 1937 creation, the dress was a scandal: It assumed a conformity-defying sartorial stance and was fittingly worn by Wallace Simpson. Today, its highly devolved spawn are available on Shein for $13.

As it stands, one clear way out of corny, food motif purgatory is for brands — fashion or food — to focus less on quantity and more on storytelling and quality. “We do a few things really well, and that’s enough,” Salad says, “Like In-N-Out [Burger].”

Poska’s philosophy is similar. “I’d rather make one thing people talk about for a year than 20 things people forget about tomorrow,” he says. “The first person to make a candle look like a stick of butter is a genius. The hundredth person is just making a candle.”

#6533. Researchers May Have Solved a Puzzling Contradiction in the Ryugu Sample

The Solar System's asteroids are sometimes referred to as fossils because they preserve evidence of the conditions when the Solar System formed. Asteroids are critically different than their planetary counterparts. On the rocky planets, the rock itself has been subjected to billions of years of change. On Earth, tectonic plates have melted rocks, exposure to water has altered its mineral content, and pressure deep inside the Earth has transformed its crystalline structure. Cosmic and solar radiation has also driven fundamental changes on some worlds, and across Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars, a mixture of these factors have altered the rock.

But asteroids and the parent bodies they came from haven't been subjected to all of these forces. In many ways, they remain unchanged from the early days of the Solar System, 4.5 billion years ago. They haven't remained completely unchanged; that would be next to impossible. But their ancient state and what it can teach us about the Solar System's history is why we've sent missions to collect samples and return them to Earth.

In 2020, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's (JAXA)Hayabusa 2 successfully completed its sampling mission to asteroid Ryugu and returned its precious sample to Earth. Almost six years after its arrival on Earth, the Ryugu sample is still generating valuable scientific results, as researchers examine its mineralogical and chemical composition.

The newest results are in research titled "Pervasive poorly crystalline Mg-rich hydrous silicate material in C-type asteroid matrices." It's published in Nature Communications Earth and Environment, and the lead author is Reon Okumura from the Division of Geosciences and Civil Engineering at Kanazawa University, Japan.

Ryugu and other carbonaceous chondrites present an apparent contradiction. It involves aqueous alteration, where contact with water creates mineralogical and chemical changes in rocks and minerals. Aqueous alteration isn't a rare action that happens only in space environments; it's common on Earth. The best-known example is how clay forms from common silicate rocks in Earth's crust, from exposure to water. It's basically how soil is created.

A JAXA official successfully retrieving the 16 kg capsule that it contained a sample from the asteroid Ryugu. (Courtesy: JAXA)

There's obviously no soil on Ryugu, but there is aqueous alteration. "C-type asteroid-derived samples, including Ryugu and carbonaceous chondrites, consist primarily of fine-grained matrices of magnesium-rich hydrous silicates formed by aqueous alteration," the paper states.

The contradiction stems from the matrix of minerals in the asteroid. There seems to be two components, each altered under a different set of aqueous conditions. That implies that Ryugu's interior matrix is patchy, which is highly improbable. An asteroid can be clumpy on a macroscale, but how can it have two components in the same mineral matrix? That's been a nagging question in cosmochemistry: how can aqueous alteration happen to some of the matrix while leaving some of it more intact?

The authors write that Ryugu's matrix is "commonly interpreted as mixtures of serpentine- and saponite-like phyllosilicates..." Serpentine and saponite are both found on Earth, where they're created when rock is aqueously altered. But despite the fact that they're generally interpreted to be these substances, "their mineralogical characteristics do not fully correspond to these well-crystalline terrestrial layered silicates."

To dig into this apparent contradiction, the researchers used the SPring-8 synchrotron radiation facility and the Photon Factory High Energy Accelerator, both in Japan. Both of these research facilities use powerful x-rays to look deeply into the Ryugu sample.

They found the expected serpentine and saponite, but they also identified something else: poorly crystalline magnesium silicate hydrate (M-S-H).

âWhat makes M-S-H particularly interesting is that it can accommodate a wide range of magnesium-to-silicon ratios,â said study corresponding author Keisuke Fukushi of Kanazawa University. âThis flexibility may be key to understanding how water-rock interactions proceeded without erasing pre-existing chemical differences within their parent asteroids.â

The composition of most materials remains stable when subjected to the same aqueous conditions. But previous research and lab work shows that M-S-H is a bit of an oddball: it can exist in the same aqueous conditions and have different magnesium to silicon ratios. So this work suggests that M-S-H is the initial starting point, and that if it formed into serpentine and saponite phases, the presence of M-S-H can explain the two different outcomes without necessarily requiring a different aqueous alteration for each one.

This illustration helps explain the findings. The previous interpretation on the left shows tighly packed grains of serpentine and saponite, with the parallel lines representing their orderly crystal structure. The alternating blue and green lines in some grains represent interleaves of serpentine and saponite layers in the same crystal. There's almost no empty space between grains. The image on the right shows the new model, with a background of poorly crystalline M-S-H, making up the bulk of the matrix. In this model, serpentine and saponite are a minor part of the matrix, and are poorly-formed intrusions. Image Credit: Keisuke FUKUSHI, Kanazawa University (2026)

The study says something not only about Ryugu, but about carbonaceous chondrites. Much of their matrices could be poorly crystalline M-S-H. If this material precipitated first and then was transformed later, the different compositions of clay-like minerals found in the matrix could have arisen without a separate, distinct water environment for different regions of the parent asteroid.

"Assuming its initial precipitation and subsequent mineralogical transformations, a wide range of compositional variation can be produced without requiring separate aqueous conditions for each local composition," the authors write. "This framework provides a physicochemical basis for explaining the compositional variability and associated phyllosilicate diversity of C-type chondritic matrices within a parent-body alteration scenario."

The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) is developing a reputation for successful sampling missions, one of the most difficult type of missions to complete. The original Hayabusa mission, though plagued with difficulties, still managed to return a small sample from asteroid Itokawa in 2010. Hayabusa 2 was a complete success, as this research shows. And at this moment, JAXA's Martian Moons eXplorer mission is on its way to collect a sample from Phobos, the largest of Mars' two moons.

That sample should be on Earth five years from now. What questions will it answer?

#6532. We’re in the Era of the $200 Cup of Coffee

Can coffee join the ranks of wine when it comes to high-end tastings?

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Starting this week, it’s also home to a $200 cup of coffee.

Bushwick’s Sey Coffee recently announced that it would be touring a rare Panamanian geisha from Finca Sophia, a coffee farm in Panama’s Chiriquí highlands. Sey scooped up the geisha at auction for $44,275, which comes to $6,325 per kilogram, or roughly $200 per cup. The geisha is billed as extraordinarily aromatic, floral, and juicy; Doug Cohen, Sey’s director of brand strategy, advises enjoying it with a clean palate, completely black, and taking your time with it. “As the coffee cools, different aspects of its character become apparent, and that evolution is part of the experience,” he says.

Even among fourth-wave coffee shops where prices continue to climb higher, Sey’s $200 cup is an outlier. “Coffee as a premium product is relatively new,” says Cohen. “For so long, coffee has been treated as a commodity, and its value has been constrained by that perception.” He says that both before and right after COVID, folks were becoming more curious about coffee, and educating themselves on platforms like Youtube, Discord, and online forums about how to appreciate it and “understand just how high the ceiling of quality can be.” The arrival of the $200 cup of coffee from a cafe in a neighborhood at the epicenter of conversations about both culinary innovation and gentrification feels ripe for closer examination.

So, how did this coffee end up at this price? “We have been purchasing coffee from Finca Sophia for several years,” Cohen says. “This release really grew out of that existing relationship.” When Finca’s general manager told Cohen that the farm’s yields were down by approximately 95 percent, Cohen says a bigger question was raised: “What does it mean to be a good partner when the people you have built relationships with are facing a difficult year?” Buying up the geisha beans felt like a way to both support Sey’s producer, and further develop what Cohen calls “elevated coffee experiences.”

In the 2010s, the artisanal coffeehouse wave washed over the country, and especially Brooklyn, with hipster gusto. Sey Coffee was an integral part of that boom. Initially called Lofted Coffee, it operated out of its founders’ Bushwick loft until it rebranded to Sey in 2017, and expanded operations to its present Bushwick location on Grattan Street. That space has become something of a local icon since; Sprudge called its aesthetic “shoebox crossed with an airplane hangar”; the minimal-industrial, cream-hued interiors hit a very Axel Vervoordt-with-a-cyber-sigil-tattoo note (positive). The shop’s cachet has drawn coffee lovers, artists, yuppies, and artist-yuppies; customers have snacked on the gluten-free pastries from L’imprimerie (and now, post-L’imprimerie closure, pastries from Smør), and often post up with their dogs thanks to the semi-indoor-outdoor layout.

Sey is hoping to elevate the coffee shop model to something more premium, with a stated focus on ethics and sustainability. Thus far, it’s earned acclaim for those efforts. Food & Wine named it the best coffee shop in New York and received positive media attention for opting out of tipping, choosing instead to pay its staff up to more than 80 percent above the NYC hourly minimum wage; full-time baristas can make up to $31 per hour in addition to receiving benefits and a share of the cafe’s revenue.

Increasingly, coffee is getting the same treatment as high-end dining and tasting experiences. There’s the omakase-style menu at NYC’s Driftaway Coffee, or San Francisco’s Komakase coffee tasting room, both of which steer coffee away from quick consumption and toward a world of degustation that appears to have more in common with pricier wine and spirit tastings. The expansion of “espresso house” chain Watch House stateside is also an indicator: The London-based specialty roaster expanded to a fourth location in New York City this summer, raising eyebrows for its $32 cup of coffee while also reportedly scouting for more locations in Austin, Chicago, and Miami.

The emerging demand may be just much about luxury as it is about craft. I can’t help but wonder if the $200 cup of coffee is happening in Bushwick because the Girls-era Bushwickian has grown up and wants more exclusive experiences. Is this what happens when, as culture writer Raven Smith said on his new BBC podcast last week, the indie outgrows its sleaze? “For us, this is not about pushing prices higher for the sake of it,” Cohen says. “It is about challenging how we assign value to coffee in the first place. What is an extraordinary coffee actually worth?”

As much as we may lament climbing prices for specialty coffee and espresso, why wouldn’t this happen to the category when so many other aspects of food and beverage — from cocktails to sushi to bread — are following the same trajectory? Higher consumer costs notwithstanding, the marketing of specialty beans does steer U.S. coffee culture away from its productivity-focused consumption and the work-optimized “coffee break.”

“Why do we accept that certain wines can command thousands of dollars, yet question whether coffee can have comparable value?” Cohen asks. It’s a fair question, albeit one that I’d answer with another: Once we acknowledge that coffee should command a higher price, who still gets to drink it?

#6531. The JWST May Have Found Where Heavy Black Hole Seeds Formed

Astrophysicists think that the supermassive black holes (SMBH) we see in the modern Universe are the result of a long drawn-out process. That process is referred to as the hierarchical black hole mergers framework. It explains how some SMBH can reach such staggering masses. Some of the most massive appear to have billions of solar masses.

The idea is that these SMBH start out as seeds, and those seeds are stellar-mass black holes. Two processes create them. One is when massive stars between about 8 and 50 solar masses reach the end of their lives of fusion. They either explode as supernovae, and their cores collapse, forming black holes, or they collapse directly into black holes. The other is when two neutron stars merge.

In between stellar mass black holes and SMBH are intermediate mass black holes (IMBH.) These black holes range in mass from about 100 solar masses to 100,000 solar masses. The observational evidence for IMBHs is still thin, but it's persistent.

A 2024 paper focused on Omega Centauri, a globular cluster on the outskirts of the Milky Way, as the site of an IMBH. A group of fast-moving stars in the center of Omega Centauri can only be explained by the presence of an IMBH with about 8,200 solar masses, according to that work.

Gravitational waves from a black hole merger are also evidence of an IMBH. A 2020 paper presented the only direct evidence of an IMBH when the waves showed that two black holes, with 85 and 66 solar masses, merged to create an IMBH with about 142 solar masses.

But what are the birthplaces of these IMBH? Some must have formed in the early Universe to act as seeds for the SMBH we see today.

Research titled "Massive star clusters detected by JWST as natural birth places to form intermediate-mass black holes" may have the answer. It's published in Astronomy and Astrophysics, and the lead author is Viola Bocchi. Bocchi is from the Sapienza University of Rome.

"The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has revealed a population of dense stellar systems at high redshifts, including the âCosmic Gemsâ arc (zââ¼â10.2) and the âFirefly Sparkleâ (zââ¼â8.3). With masses in the range 105 Mââ107 Mâ and half-mass radii in the range â¼0.4â15 pc, these systems are ideally suited to form intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) via collision-based models," the authors write.

The Cosmic Gems arc is a gravitationally lensed galaxy, and the JWST observed its light when the Universe was only about 460 million years old. The JWST found five dense star clusters there.

The Cosmic Gems was first discovered by the Hubble during its Reionization Lensing Cluster Survey (RELICS) and was identified as a powerful source of radiation during the Epoch of Reionization. In 2024, the JWST took another look and found the five Young Massive Clusters (YMC), the first discovery of such ancient clusters.

The Firefly Sparkle is another gravitationally lensed early galaxies, imaged only about 600 million years after the Big Bang. The JWST found 10 YMCs in the Firefly Sparkle.

This image shows the Firefly Sparkle galaxy, where the JWST found 10 YMCs. It also shows a pair of companion galaxies. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Chris Willott (National Research Council Canada), Lamiya Mowla (Wellesley College), Kartheik Iyer (Columbia University)

This research shows that not only were all these YMCs sources of ionizing radiation, they may have been the birthplaces of IMBH.

Due to the density in these YMCs, n-body simulations weren't viable. Instead, the researchers used a model based on runaway collisions and mass-loss by stellar winds to estimate the resulting IMBH masses. They then validated these results against direct N-body simulations of compact star clusters.

"With masses in the range 105 Mââ107 Mâ and half-mass radii in the range â¼0.4â15 pc, these systems are ideally suited to form intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) via collision-based models," the authors write. "Our estimates yield typical IMBH masses in the range â¼102 Mâ to â¼4âÃâ103 Mâ, implying typical formation efficiencies on the few percent level."

The clusters in the Cosmic Gems yieled the heaviest IMBH, with masses ranging from 1600â2700 Mâ. "The extreme compactness of the Cosmic Gems clusters (Rhââ¼â1 pc) facilitates the formation of black hole seeds with high masses of 1600â2700 Mâ," the authors write. Rh â¼â1 pc is the radius of the sphere that contains half of the clusterâs total mass and measures how compact a cluster is.

"The low metallicity (Zââ²â0.02âZâ) is a critical factor for retaining the seed mass despite stellar winds," the authors write.

These young clusters also have low metallicities because not enough stars have lived and died in them to generate higher metallicity. Their low metallicity played a critical role in forming IMBH. Low metallicity limits mass-loss due to stellar winds, and that let the objects keep growing.

The results from the Firefly Sparkle are different. "In contrast to the Cosmic Gems, these clusters exhibit significantly larger radii (Rhââ¼â4âââ6 pc) for typically lower total masses (105âââ106âMâ)," the authors write. That creates cores that are less massive, limiting the potential for the runaway collision process to create IMBH. The black hole masses in Firefly Sparkle range 1.8âÃâ102âââ8.1âÃâ102âMâ. That's about 180 to 810 Mâ, which represents the lower boundary for IMBH masses.

This artist's illustration shows what the Firefly Sparkle galaxy looked like about 600 million years after the big bang if it wasnât stretched and distorted by gravitational lensing. This illustration is based on images and data from NASAâs James Webb Space Telescope. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, Ralf Crawford (STScI). Science: Lamiya Mowla (Wellesley College), Guillaume Desprez (Saint Mary's University)

Overall, the lower range for IMBH masses in this work (~100 solar mases) is comparable to black holes formed by massive Population III stars, the Universe's hypothetical first stars, which were likely extremely massive. But, "the upper bound extends significantly higher, allowing the most massive clusters to produce objects firmly in the âheavy seedâ regime," the authors write. "Forming such heavy seeds is highly beneficial to form SMBHs at high redshift."

These results aren't observational in the sense that the JWST didn't observe any IMBH. But they do show a plausible environment where IMBH could form and potentially lead to the SMBH we see in the centers of galaxies like ours.

These results could also explain the JWST's Little Red Dots. Their spectra are often interpreted as being powered by SMBH. "Our results suggest that dense massive star clusters could provide possible massive seeds from which the SMBHs in the LRDs may have grown," the researchers write.

The researchers state some caveats, based on some acknowledged weaknesses in their work. Many properties of these clusters are unknown, including their rotation and their internal structure, which could change the outcomes and lower the IMBH masses.

The initial mass function also isn't known, but it could be top-heavy. "This possibility, along with a possible primordial mass segregation, would favor the formation of massive IMBHs, though we did not explore it here in detail," the authors explain.

Researchers will no doubt dig deeper into these young massive clusters and try to fill in some of the blanks that remain. But this research shows that they could be the source of the heavy seed IMBH that eventually form SMBH.

"Our results suggest that these dense, metal-poor clusters are viable factories for heavy seeds that are capable of growing into the supermassive black holes observed in the early Universe," the authors conlude. .

A new study revealed that people who rely on AI for basic tasks become less motivated over time. Live Science polled its readers on whether they have experienced this situation.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

While people use artificial intelligence (AI) tools to help with tasks like learning new skills or answering questions, a new study suggests that these benefits may come with a downside.

The findings, presented at the 2026 Conference on Language Modeling in San Francisco earlier this month, revealed that people who used AI assistance for reading comprehension or math problems were more likely to struggle or give up when the AI assistance was removed. The results suggest that relying too much on AI could lower people's motivations to overcome challenging situations.

In the wake of this study, Live Science recently polled its readers on whether they felt AI was making them less motivated after using it.

More than 140 readers voted in the poll, with 30% of voters picking "No, I don't use AI at all, so this situation doesn't apply to me."

"If AI were only a tool, controlled by those who use it I might give it a try," said one commenter in response. "But it isn't under control at all. It gets into your bank accounts and moves money without authorization. It encourages suicide and self-harm. It is addictive and makes people lazy. I know someone who uses it to answer questions and while it is detailed, it makes her lazier, asking one question and getting the answer without her searching for it. AI Is a danger. It should not be allowed."

Other comments reflected this sentiment, with one reader writing, "Use of all automatic aids decrease[s] attention and retention. I see it in the use of navigation devices where drivers ought to recognize routes after a couple of times. AI helps research and cuts down lengthy searches, but over use of summaries weakens critical faculties."

Other commenters questioned whether AI is the problem, or if people are just inclined to take the easy option, asking "Would you get the same results if the answers to all but a few problems were provided on separate sheet of paper?" and another writing, "I think researchers should also investigate whether shovels decrease motivation to dig holes with one's hands. AI, like a shovel, is only a tool."

Do you agree with these readers? Let us know in the comments!

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry is the Content Manager at Live Science. Formerly, she was the Content Manager at Space.com and before that the Science Communicator at JILA, a physics research institute. Kenna is also a book author, with her upcoming book 'Octopus X' scheduled for release in spring of 2027. Her beats include physics, health, environmental science, technology, AI, animal intelligence, corvids, and cephalopods.

#6527. The Vera Rubin Has Found Two More of the Milky Way's Dim Satellites

Massive galaxies like the Milky Way have a retinue of smaller, dim satellites on their outskirts. They're hard to detect, and while astronomers have found about 65 of the Milky Way's dwarf satellite galaxies, and about 40 globular clusters in its halo, they suspect there are many dwarf satellites and globular clusters yet to be found. Now the Vera Rubin Observatory has found two more.

The Milky Way's satellites are either small dim galaxies or globular clusters, and both are part of the assembly history of the Milky Way through mergers. These two detections by the Rubin, found in its Early Data Preview 2 (EDP2) released in July 2026, are almost certainly the beginning of many more discoveries of Milky Way satellites by the powerful observatory. One is a most likely a dim dwarf galaxy named Aquarius IV, and one is a globular cluster named Rubin-GC1.

This figure shows the locations of both Rubin-GC1 and Aquarius IV. Rubin-GC1's detection was particularly impressive, since it's in the direction of the Milky Way's bulge, a region with a dense stellar population and thick dust. Image Credit: NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA, ESA/Gaia/DPAC, W. Cerny

The discoveries are presented in two new papers.

One is titled "Discovery of the Distant, Ultra-faint Milky Way Satellite Aquarius IV with the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Early Data Preview 2." It's published in Research Notes of the American Astronomical Society, and the lead author is William Cerny, an astronomy student in Yaleâs Graduate School of Arts and Sciences.

"We present the discovery of Aquarius IV (RubinâJ2201â0234)âthe first ultra-faint Milky Way (MW) satellite to be identified using data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory," the authors write. It was confirmed in images from the Dark Energy Camera. The authors say it's a low-luminosity, compact stellar system in the outer Galactic halo.

It's stellar population is ancient and low-metallicity. "These properties closely resemble those of the smallest and faintest confirmed ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (UFDs), though a globular cluster classification is not ruled out," the researchers write.

Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies can have as little as a few hundred stars, which makes them smaller than some globular clusters (GCs). But there's one critical difference between UFDs and GCs: UFDs have dark matter while GCs don't (except for a few possible outliers).

Only a small number of the stars in Aquarius IV have been detected so far, so whether or not it is a UFD for sure will depend on deeper imaging and spectroscopy.

âWhat I find especially exciting is that these discoveries are just the beginning for Rubin,â said first author Cerny. (He is also the second author of the Rubin-GC1 study, which has been accepted by The Astrophysical Journal Letters.)

âIf the observatory can find systems this faint and difficult with only its preview data, its full 10-year survey will undoubtedly provide us with many more Milky Way satellite discoveries,â Cerny said. âThese new satellites will give us new opportunities to test models of galaxy formation, trace the assembly history of the Milky Way, and investigate the nature of dark matter.â

These panels are images centered on Aquarius IV. The star in the lower panel marks a Blue Horizontal Branch star used to determine the distance to Aquarius IV. The stars in the bottom panel are also coloured according to their probability of being members of Aquarius IV. The grey stars are almost certainly not members, while colours ranging from purple through red, orange, and yellow represent increasing probability. Image Credit: William Cerny et al 2026 Res. Notes AAS 10 239

The second paper is "Rubin Observatory Reveals a Dust-Shrouded Halo Globular Cluster in Ophiuchus," and it will be published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. It's currently available at arxiv.org and the lead author is Aashay Pai. Pai is a graduate student in the Department of Physics at the University of Chicago.

"We present the discovery of the Milky Way satellite Rubin-GC1 (Rubin J1628â1735) using data from the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatoryâs Early Data Preview 2," the authors write. The stars in Rubin-GC1 have an intermediate age of about 9.2 billion years, and are moderately rich in metals, meaning it's most likely a very faint GC. "Together, these properties suggest Rubin-GC1 is most likely a star cluster in the faint tail of the luminosity function of globular clusters surrounding the Milky Way," the authors write.

Based on comparisons to the Sagittarius dwarf spheroidal galaxy, Rubin-GC1 is most likely a cluster accreted to the Milky Way, associated with the Sagittarius leading arm. The Sagittarius leading arm is a massive tidal stream of stars from the Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal Galaxy, torn away as that galaxy merges with the Milky Way.

The panel on the left shows the Sagittarius trailing and leading arms. (The DES images are not part of this work.) The image on the right shows roughly where Rubin-GC1 is located, shown with the gold star. The Milky Way's center is shown with the black cross, and the circle with the dot inside is the Sun. Image Credit: Left: By NOIRLab, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=139367207. Right: Aashay Pai et al. 2026.

âFinding new Milky Way satellites in Rubin Observatory data has been an exciting future prospect for most of my career,â said Marla Geha, a professor of astronomy and physics in Yaleâs Faculty of Arts and Sciences, and co-author on both studies. âIt is remarkable this is now a reality.â

Rubin-GC1 was detected in the direction of the galactic bulge, where stellar density is very high and the dust is thick. Finding it in those conditions makes the detection even more impressive. "The discovery of Rubin-GC1 highlights the potential of Rubin to uncover faint, resolved satellites in dust-shrouded regions of the Milky Way, including remnants of the accretion events that have shaped the Galaxyâs hierarchical assembly," the authors write.

The panel on the left is what's called a 'smoothed isochrone filtered stellar density map.' It's a visualization tool in astronomy used to detect and map faint structures like ultra-faint dwarf galaxies by masking out field stars based on a color-magnitude curve. The panel on the right is a more familiar type of image used to show the region itself. Image Credit: Aashay Pai et al. 2026.

âThese discoveries are incredibly promising,â Geha said. âContinued discoveries will allow us to complete the census of satellite galaxies around the Milky Way, which is a key to understanding how the faintest galaxies form.â

The Vera Rubin Observatory is mostly known as a transient-detecting observatory, and as the maker of a ten-year long movie of the sky in its Legacy Survey of Space and Time. But it's more than that. As it images the sky repeatedly, dim objects will become clearer. "The sensitivity of Rubin LSST will steadily increase, and systems similar to Aquarius IV are ultimately expected to be detectable with >85% efficiency using the same search algorithm applied here," the authors of the first paper write.

Not only that, but its observations will work with observations from other observatories, like the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, to detect even more objects. "The identification of Rubin-GC1 heralds an exciting era of discovery as Rubin, Euclid, and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope pierce the shroud of Galactic dust to reveal faint satellites that were hitherto hidden by our Galaxy," the authors of the second paper write.

Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies and globular clusters are puzzle pieces in the history of the Milky Way's growth through mergers. The mergers are ongoing, as interactions between the Magellanic Clouds and the Milky Way show.

By finding more of the Milky Way satellites, a picture of all of these mergers, and the role dark matter plays, will become clearer. By mapping out these objects and the streams they're sometimes a part of, astronomers can detect where dark matter also concentrates in clumps. These dark matter sub-halos will show how our galaxy grew larger by consuming smaller galaxies with their own dark matter halos.
