#6437. Scientists Discover Crows Make Decisions Twice As Fast as Humans

Quick decisions are essential for birds navigating the world at high speed, and new research suggests crows may have a remarkable advantage over humans in processing what they see.

A crow can make a visual decision in less than a quarter of a second, about twice as fast as a human or monkey. Researchers at the University of Tübingen discovered this remarkable speed by asking two carrion crows to identify the direction of moving dots on a screen. The birds made their choices in an average of just 235 milliseconds while maintaining a high degree of accuracy.

During the experiment, the crows watched patterns of moving dots on a touchscreen and had to determine whether most were traveling to the left or right. They indicated their answer by pecking a target on the corresponding side of the screen. Some patterns made the direction easy to identify, while others were much harder to interpret.

“Even when the patterns of motion were hard to recognize, the crows’ decisions were still better than random choices,” Philipp Schmidbauer reports, “and with clear signals, they achieved an accuracy of nearly 100 percent.”

Schmidbauer and Professor Andreas Nieder, both from the University of Tübingen’s Institute of Neurobiology, investigated how the birds’ brains could process visual information so quickly. Their study, published in the journal Science, examined the activity of individual nerve cells, or neurons, in a brain region called the nidopallium caudolaterale. This area helps birds process information and make decisions, performing a role comparable to that of the prefrontal cortex in humans.

The recordings revealed that the crows’ brains began distinguishing between the two possible directions just 70 milliseconds after the moving dots appeared. As the birds processed what they were seeing, neural activity gradually increased until it reached a threshold associated with making a decision. These signals reflected both how clearly the dots indicated a particular direction and which direction the crow ultimately chose.

“These findings show that neuronal dynamics in the avian brain are consistent with established models of decision-making in humans and non-human primates,” says Andreas Nieder.

Unlike humans and other primates, birds do not have a layered cerebral cortex. Despite this structural difference, the findings suggest that their brains use similar fundamental principles to make decisions. The remarkable difference is how quickly the crows appear to carry out this process.

Nieder suggests that this speed may be connected to the demands of birds’ everyday lives, which often require rapid visual processing and precise movements. “Birds rely on their vision to carry out precise, rapid maneuvers during flight and to guide their beaks towards objects when foraging,” he says.

Although these demands could help explain the crows’ speed, researchers still need to determine exactly which mechanisms allow birds to make visual decisions so much faster than primates.

Reference: “Ultrarapid decision-making in an avian brain” by Philipp Schmidbauer and Andreas Nieder, 22 October 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.aed6459

#6436. The 8 Best RV Generators Give You Go-Anywhere Power

Having the juice to power your appliances and electronics makes a mobile home feel truly homey.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Driving an RV lets you bring the comforts of home along on your road trip, but having a portable generator is essential. It powers your electric appliances and charges electronics, like your phone and laptop. If your RV doesn’t come equipped with a built-in generator, then you’ll need to bring one along.

To be clear: There are no official, task-specific “RV generators,” but some portable generators are better-suited to the task than others. For starters, most RVs have a 30-amp (A) outlet that lets you provide power to your entire RV, charging its batteries while running everything from lights to the air conditioner. The best RV generators need to be fairly beefy–powerful enough to keep multiple appliances running with juice to spare–but also portable enough to pack and, often, move in and out of the RV door.

An RV generator is a big investment, but an important one. We’ll help you find the right option for your setup and walk you through the shopping process and recommend the best models we’ve found and tested. With our picks, you can keep the power flowing wherever you roam.

Looking for more backup power solutions? Here are our reviews of the best portable generators, the best solar generators, and the best home generators.

This rock-solid block of generator excellence from Champion is as perfect for RVing as it gets. Its 4,500-watt output is more than enough to run your entire RV, including the air conditioner. At the same time, it’s surprisingly quiet, clocking in at just 61 decibels—the same volume as a dishwasher.

While it’s heavy at just over 100 pounds, it's fairly compact—the size of a couple of car batteries—and an integrated handle and wheels make it fairly easy to move around. It offers up to 14 hours of runtime on a single tank of gas (2.25 gallons), and you can expand the power capabilities by pairing it with a compatible generator using an optional parallel kit.

Champion has a whole line of inverter generators, but we recommend this one because it features a remote starter with a range of up to 80 feet, which we appreciate when we don’t feel like messing around with a generator in the cold or dark.

The Wen DF360iX offers quite a bit of utility for an affordable price. For starters, there is the option to run the generator on gasoline or propane at up to 3,600 or 3,500 starting watts, respectively, and either 900 or 2,600 running watts. (Propane generates slightly less power than gas.) That’s enough electricity for small to mid-size RVs.

At 49 pounds, this generator's relatively lightweight, but it doesn’t cut back on ports to keep the price low. It has a 30-amp port for direct connection to an RV, two three-prong AC ports, a 12-volt DC receptacle, and two USB-A ports. It also has an auto-shutoff feature if the fuel runs too low and a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor that detects if dangerous levels are present. Like most inverter generators, it produces less noise. This model is rated at around 65 decibels of noise, which is quiet enough that it shouldn’t be too noisy for public areas like a campground.

There are some drawbacks to a generator at this price range, however. The size of the gas tank may be a concern. If you’re using gas and need it to run overnight, you’ll need a generator with a larger tank. At just 1.5 gallons, you only get up to five hours of usage with a half-load runtime (though using a 20-pound propane tank as your fuel can get that up to 14 hours). But if all you need is something basic, this gives you what you need at a good price.

Previously, we recommended the Pro version of this power station—mainly because it was highly portable with wheels and a telescoping handle—but Jackery has since discontinued it. Its replacement, the HomePower 3000, isn't quite as easy to move around, but it makes up for it with more power: It can generate up to 3,600 watts for 3,072 watt-hours of power capacity, and uses a LiFePO4 battery, which is more efficient and longer-lasting than the previous model.

While the HomePower 3000 no longer has wheels, it does have handles and weighs just under 60 pounds. There are larger portable power stations out there, but many are even more cumbersome than this one, making them exponentially more painful to lug in and out of your RV’s storage area.

More importantly, when paired with a pair of 200-watt SolarSaga panels, you can recharge the station in around 9 hours under sunny conditions. Of course, it can also be pre-charged much faster using an AC outlet, but when using solar, you can take yourself off-grid for longer periods.

It’s got all the connections you’ll need to power your RV, including a 30-amp outlet, plus four AC outlets, a 12-volt receptacle, and four USB ports should you need them. Other nice features include an app that allows you to monitor its power levels and output from your phone, and a battery management system that protects the station from power surges, overcurrent, and even extreme temperature conditions.

Dual-fuel generators are very nice to have on an RV, because the two types of fuel work well in different scenarios: gasoline is easy to obtain just about everywhere you go, so it's great for long, isolated trips or living off-grid, but makes a lot of noise. Propane isn’t quite as accessible, but it allows your generator to run more quietly.

We like the GD400BN specifically because it's powerful, quiet, and portable. With its 4,000-watt output, it’s more than capable of powering your entire rig, with the air conditioner, but it’s built solid and weighs less than 50 pounds. Another plug or two would’ve been nice–its single AC outlet limits things a bit if you have any reason to plug in power tools or equipment. For all intents and purposes, this is a very nice dual-fuel generator and comes at a decent price to boot.

At this point, the Honda EU2200i is nothing short of a campsite icon. You see them all the time at campsites, and with good reason: They are renowned for doing pretty much everything right.

Weighing in at just over 46 pounds and not much larger than a couple of stacked shoeboxes, this is about as portable as RV-capable generators get. It’s also one of the quietest options in its class, purring along at 47-58 decibels, or about the same volume as a normal conversation. Test Editor Brad Ford found the same thing in his testing, calling the EU2200i “remarkably quiet.”

“The EU2200i is ideal for camping and other outdoor events where generator noise might be frowned on,” he wrote in our guide to the best portable generators.

And its durability is outright famous: I have personally spent years on end bumping and bashing one all over the place, and it just won’t break.

The primary downside is its 2,200-watt outage, which makes sense for its size but is relatively small if you’re powering an RV. Still, given how often you see it around, RVers are clearly okay working around its limitations.

I can report firsthand that the EcoFlow Delta Pro Ultra is an absolute performance monster, with massive output (7,500 watts) and enormous capacity (6,500 watt-hours), which you can expand further by adding extra 6,000-watt-hour batteries.

I recently had one along for a cloudy camping trip where solar panels would have been useless, but it didn’t matter because its charge lasted a solid three days (though it was cool weather and I wasn’t using my a/c—for that you’ll need solar). It also charges very quickly: I charged mine via a wall outlet in about 2 hours. I could easily use this generator to back up my entire house, so needless to say, it can store and produce enough energy to handily power an a/c and everything else you may need in your RV—particularly with a good solar setup.

The downside to carrying a generator like this around, of course, is the weight. At just over 180 pounds, it’s way too heavy to move in or out of an RV solo. It’s more portable than you might think, though: You can remove the batteries from the generator, then carry it out in more manageable parts. Plus, the power station has wheels to help you move it around. Ultimately, the Delta Pro Ultra is probably overkill for most RVers, but it pushes the boundaries on what you can expect from an RV-compatible generator.

When we tested the Bluetti Elite 300, we were impressed that this compact station boasted an impressive battery capacity of just over 3,000 watt-hours and 2,400 watts of output. Plus, it includes a 120-volt 30-amp port, which is handy for connecting it to a small RV or pop-up camper. It’s not quite enough power to run a heating or cooling system for a significant amount of time, but for lights, small appliances, and other items that need power, this station will deliver.

We were also pleased with its solar recharging capability. The Elite 300 can accept up to 1,200 watts of input, which is a high amount for a station this size. It worked well when we paired it with a 250-watt portable panel.

The only thing we didn’t like was the inability to add an expansion battery to increase your capacity. That’s not a huge detractor, but it’s something we’ve seen in stations even smaller than this one. But at the end of the day, the Bluetti Elite 300 delivers a lot of power and runtime, but is still very portable and easy to store in an RV.

Full Bluetti Elite 300 Solar Generator Review

If you want to be a good neighbor at your campsite, this generator from Westinghouse keeps the rumble to a minimum. Thanks to a special throttling system that only produces as much power as needed, it spins down when you aren’t drawing much rather than constantly roaring at full speed. That keeps the volume down, dropping to a decibel level akin to generators half its size at low usage. I’ve used older versions of what were essentially the same model; they were very quiet then, and reviews indicate the volume has gone down even more.

Its hefty 4,500-watt output is substantial, considering the lack of racket, and capable of powering an entire RV without issue. It also has a remote starter, which allows me to fire it up from the comfort of indoors.

This Westinghouse is fairly heavy, though a retractable handle, wheels, and lifting handles make it easier to move around. And its relatively compact shape passes through an RV door without too much trouble. All in all, it provides ample power while keeping the noise to a minimum.

We’ve used RV generators in all shapes and sizes for decades, and regularly test new models from both top manufacturers and up-and-coming startups. Our current selections are the result of all that experience. To supplement that experience, we compared our findings against a variety of expert reviews and those from real-world buyers at retailers like Amazon.

The recommendations below span a range of price points, portability, and operating specs, and situational needs, and after much testing and consideration, we are confident that these are truly some of the best RV generators you can buy right now.

Size matters–in watts (W), that is. Though power needs of RVs can vary widely, we generally suggest that most RVs need at least 2,000 watts at any given time—enough to power an air conditioner, fridge, lights, and a few devices. However, with just 2,000 watts, you’ll have to be careful about running the a/c along with other appliances, or you might run out of power quickly. If you’re spending a fair amount of time inside and plan to use your a/c often, look for a larger generator that can put out upwards of 3,500 watts.

If you’re using a solar generator (i.e., a power station connected to solar panels), you also need to consider your generator’s capacity, or its ability to store energy that’s been harnessed by a solar panel. To power an RV, you should look for a power station that can store at least 3,000 watt-hours (Wh), which is enough to power a fridge, lights, devices, and small appliances for a couple of days. And it needs to have an output of at least 2,000 watts, which allows it to power said essentials simultaneously.

Keep in mind that solar generators generally cannot generate as much juice as gas or a direct electrical hookup. Unless you have an extraordinary solar panel array and perfect sun to keep the power flowing, you probably won’t be able to power a full suite of appliances on solar alone.

Many RV generators run on gasoline, but there are also dual-fuel generators that allow you to use gas or propane. The advantage of propane is that it can run for longer when using, for example, a 20-pound tank (sometimes twice a long as the gas tank). It will also allow the generator to run more quietly. The disadvantage of propane is that it will deliver slightly less wattage.

A solar generator, a battery-based power station that you can recharge using a set of solar panels, is an increasingly popular and attractive option as well. You’ll need both to harness the power of the sun. While it takes time to fully charge a power station via solar panels, they’re more sustainable and work well if you’re camping off-grid. Plus, if you need to charge it in a hurry, all power stations can recharge by plugging them into a wall outlet.

Remember: It is never safe to run a gas or propane generator inside your RV. They emit carbon monoxide, which is deadly when allowed to build up indoors. Power stations, however, are safe to use indoors.

In addition to the standard 30-amp/120-volt outlet that you want to properly hook up your RV, the best RV generators will have a variety of plugs that will allow you to power or charge other devices directly. We usually look for standard AC outlets, like you’d find at home, which come in handy for plugging in power tools, outdoor appliances, or whatever else. Many generators also come with USB-A and USB-C ports to charge laptops, phones, and other tech.

If you plan on running everything off your RV, port variety may not be as important. But it’s a very nice value add if you plan to use the generator away from your RV.

Since any RV enthusiast is bound to find themselves in a campground or RV park during their travels. The locations often have rules around noise levels and won’t allow noisy generators to bother other guests. The National Park Service, for example, prohibits “operating motorized equipment or machinery that exceeds a noise level of 60 decibels.” This is based on a range of 50 feet. That gives you a little wiggle room, but we recommend 65 decibels or lower.

Traditional, fuel-based generators are often louder than this, so for RV use, we recommend using inverter generators. Not only do these run much quieter, but they provide more stable current, which is important if you are powering sensitive devices such as TVs, laptops, and microwaves. Meanwhile, power stations run virtually silently, so noise level is never an issue for them.

There’s no “set it and forget it” RV generator: You will need to move it around often, so it needs to be light enough for one to two people to carry in and out. In general, lighter is better, but we’d generally look for one around 40-50 pounds for a 2,000-watt generator, or 50-100 pounds for 3,000-4,000 watts. Some generators feature built-in wheels and handles, which makes life easier when moving them around.

All this moving also means the generator needs to be durable enough to take a few bumps here and there. Plus, you want it to last as long as possible without needing repairs. It’s hard to gauge durability on spec, but certain brands have reputations for strong build quality and sturdy construction. Even then, it always pays to look at user reviews and find out if your pick has a reputation for holding up over time.

Portable gas generators run anywhere from 6 to 18 hours, depending on their fuel capacity. When properly well-maintained, you should be able to run it until the tank runs dry, fill it back up, then start over. Never attempt to refill the gas tank while the generator is running, which can lead to fires.

Power stations, sometimes referred to as solar generators, can run for several hours to several days, depending on the capacity of the battery and how much power you are using. Once depleted, the battery can take 1-2.5 hours to recharge using AC power, or 9 or more hours using solar panels.

Various experts recommend that fuel-based (gas and propane) generators be placed anywhere from 5-25 feet away from the RV or home, but we’ve found that 5-10 feet is about right. Just make sure the generator is clear of doors and windows. You don’t want to run the risk of carbon monoxide blowing into the RV. Also, it shouldn’t push up against a wall or other gear–you’re your generator well-ventilated on all sides.

Because they don’t emit any exhaust fumes, power stations can be set up wherever you like; however, if you are pairing them with solar panels, you’ll need them to be within cable distance of the panels, and your panels will need to be positioned to capture sunlight.

You can, but you shouldn’t. Electricity and water don’t mix, and running a generator in the rain can have unpredictable results. At best, it may fry the generator or your RV electrical system. At worst, it could cause a fire or electrocute someone.

#6435. NASA’s Swift telescope faced a fiery demise after a failed rescue

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

During more than 22 years, the Swift Observatory made itself indispensable

This artist’s rendition shows NASA’s Swift Observatory in orbit around Earth.

NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

For two decades, when the high-energy universe called, NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has answered. But now, the spacecraft’s tenure has ended, just when its skills might be more valuable than ever. On November 4, Swift reentered Earth’s atmosphere, where it was expected to burn up. This fiery end capped an uncontrollable fall from space.

The telescope launched in 2004, tailored to reveal the secrets of gamma-ray bursts. These outbursts are the most powerful kind scientists have ever seen, but they often faded before earlier telescopes could respond. Swift took its name from its ability to jump to work when a flash went off. That talent both illuminated these elusive bursts and made the observatory a cornerstone of modern astronomy for far longer than scientists ever dreamed.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“This was designed to be a two-year mission,” says astrophysicist Brad Cenko of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md. “We’re coming up on year 22. We are so fortunate to have had the opportunity to do all the things that we have.”

Over the decades, the spacecraft has lost about half its original altitude as it constantly slammed into molecules in the atmosphere. Those minuscule impacts infinitesimally slowed the observatory, pushing it closer to Earth. The sun’s relatively high activity in recent years has accelerated the process, leaving the spacecraft unable to continue into the 2030s as engineers hoped. A spacecraft commissioned by NASA to loft Swift out of danger launched in early July, but by late August, technical issues made a boost attempt impossible.

Swift was doomed — with nothing lined up to replace its unique capabilities.

When scientists dreamed up the Swift mission, the massive energy and elusive nature of gamma-ray bursts made them one of the most tantalizing phenomena out there. Astronomers desperately wanted to understand how they worked.

Swift was equipped with three instruments. Its Burst Alert Telescope gave scientists eyes on gamma-ray emissions from up to half the visible sky, with the resolution to pinpoint where light is coming from. The agile spacecraft could then swing itself and its other instruments — one tuned to X-rays and the other to visible and ultraviolet light — to quickly give scientists a view of a patch of sky across a swath of types of light. It was a combination unlike any observatory before or since.

“It’s such a unique telescope,” says astrophysicist Wen-fai Fong of Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill., who is not part of the mission team. “It has all these views of the universe, all in one observatory, which by itself is rare, but it can also rapidly point any of these instruments.”

Swift’s roster of accomplishments speaks to the power of that recipe. “Almost immediately after launch, Swift started discovering things,” says astrophysicist Lynn Cominsky of Sonoma State University in Rohnert Park, Calif. That’s not an exaggeration: One record-breaking observation, taken just the month after launch, revealed that stellar corpses with powerful magnetic fields undergo outbursts that create a distinct kind of gamma-ray signature.

Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab/NASA

That observation pushed back against scientists’ existing categorization of gamma-ray bursts. Before Swift, the bursts fell into two buckets. Long gamma-ray bursts lasted as long as minutes, and scientists believed they stemmed from exploding stars triggering supernovae. Short gamma-ray bursts, in contrast, lasted less than two seconds and were believed to originate in merging neutron stars, the superdense remains of a star large enough to explode but too small to create a black hole.

Swift confirmed this basic sketch, but also complicated it by finding bursts that didn’t cleanly fit into this binary. “The more data you get, the more confused you get,” Cominsky says. Other notable bursts the telescope observed included the brightest (gamma-ray burst) of all time, nicknamed BOAT, the highest-energy photons from such a burst, and multiple claimants to the title of most distant burst.

Notably, all of Swift’s data was public right away, even as team scientists were still working to understand what the telescope had seen. “That was very new,” Fong says, crediting the mission with inspiring other observatory teams to follow suit.

As other astronomers heard about Swift’s work, they realized how powerful the observatory might be for their own interests as well. As Swift’s tenure unfolded, astronomers started asking to borrow the nimble observatory to study a whole range of objects changing on the sky.

“With scientists, if you give them a tool to do something, they will other find other things that you can do with that tool,” says astrophysicist Phil Evans of the University of Leicester in England. In its later years, Swift observed between five and 10 “targets of opportunity” most days, tallying hundreds or even thousands in a year.

Perhaps its most ground-breaking collaborations were partnerships with observatories hunting for ghostly neutrinos that travel nearly as quickly as light but don’t interact often, and for gravitational waves, the ripples in spacetime triggered by massive objects. In 2017, Swift participated in back-to-back discoveries: the unique explosion caused by two neutron stars merging, then the first neutrino traced back to its origin.

Since then, all efforts to observe light affiliated with a neutrino or gravitational-wave signal have come up empty. “We had these two really close together and then nothing since,” Evans says. “Which is frustrating, but also kind of fun.”

A range of current and future observatories will be able to take over some of Swift’s work, but not all of it. Even during the six months this year when Swift paused operations to prepare for the boost attempt, scientists felt its loss, says astrophysicist Judith Racusin of NASA Goddard. Racusin worked with Swift during its early years before turning her focus to NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, which launched in 2008 but boasts different strengths than its colleague. “We’re going to miss out,” she says of Swift’s loss. “Not just on the common events we have thousands of, but the really rare, unusual ones, which are often the ones we learn the most from.”

Mission personnel had Swift cram in as much science as possible as its demise approached. After the boost attempt was called off, the team turned Swift’s instruments back on for a scientific swan song. That included technical observations to ensure the utility of all its recent data, as well as indirect observations of Earth’s atmosphere at lower altitudes than many spacecraft are able to withstand. Swift even caught glimpses of a comet in its final weeks.

And, of course, there were gamma-ray bursts. One particularly intriguing burst came in late September and was rather far away but remarkably energetic.

“It feels a little bit like a last hurrah of Swift,” Racusin says of the event. “It’s a burst that we’ll be studying for some time, so I’m really glad we got Swift data on it while we could.”

#6434. Scientists Spent 7 Years Studying Moth Wings and Discovered Something Unexpected

A search to change the patterns on moth wings uncovered something unexpected: wider tails, suggesting that evolution may reshape insects’ defenses by modifying features they already possess.

A luna moth’s leaf-like wings help it escape the notice of predators that hunt by sight. Other giant silk moths display prominent eyespots that can make them look threatening. A new study suggests that moving between those appearances can require only a small change in the signals that guide wing development.

Over seven years, Andrei Sourakov hand-reared more than 700 luna (Actias luna) and polyphemus (Antheraea polyphemus) moths from egg to adulthood. Sourakov is the collection coordinator of Lepidoptera at the Florida Museum of Natural History and an affiliate associate professor of entomology at the University of Florida. His findings, recently published in Evolution & Development, reveal how treatments during development can alter both the patterns and shapes of moth wings.

Sourakov treated developing moths with small amounts of heparin and dextran sulfate. Both are sulfated polysaccharides, molecules made of linked sugars with attached sulfate groups. They increase the activity of a group of proteins called Wnt, which help direct development.

He administered tiny quantities of heparin shortly before and after pupation, when caterpillars enter the pupal stage and undergo their final transformation into adults. Wing patterns are determined during this period. For two years, the treatments failed to produce the changes he was seeking, so he continued adjusting the concentration and timing of the doses.

“I kept trying, and eventually, I achieved a single transformation. But it wasn’t of the wing pattern. It was the wing shape. This single specimen was so different that I couldn’t ignore it,” he said.

That specimen was a luna moth whose hindwing tails had grown wider than those of any moth he had previously reared. Scientists think luna moths evolved their long tails to deflect bat attacks away from the main part of their bodies.

“I thought, this is very bizarre. Maybe the genes that are normally responsible for wing patterns are here responsible for wing shape, because that’s seemingly the only thing that was transformed.”

Further adjustments to the timing of heparin treatment eventually produced changes in both wing shape and eyespots, overturning that initial explanation.

In polyphemus moths, the yellow borders around the two lemon-shaped eyespots on the forewings thickened. Brown scales surrounding those markings, which normally matched the rest of the wings, became whiter. On the hindwings, the black borders around the eyespots expanded. Together, these changes made the markings more conspicuous.

Luna moths underwent a similarly striking transformation. Their round hindwing eyespots took on a squinting appearance and developed thick, dark borders resembling mascara, turning subtle markings into a more noticeable display. Both heparin and dextran sulfate also changed the shape of luna moth wings, something not previously achieved experimentally in Lepidoptera, the group that includes all moths and butterflies.

“Some giant silk moths have eyespots that make them appear threatening to would-be predators. Others look like leaves, with translucent eyespots resembling holes to make it more convincing. What’s amazing to me, and what I learned from this study, is how easy it is for these features to go from one state to another. They do this without big inventions by simply expanding or contracting existing elements to the point where eyespots look completely different. All they need is a slight increase in the amount of certain compounds at the right moment,” Sourakov said.

Moth and butterfly eyespots occupy different parts of the wings, a clue that they evolved independently. Sourakov’s original goal was to investigate whether the two groups used the same genes to create these markings or had independently arrived at similar designs.

He tested the responses of several giant silk moth species to sulfated polysaccharides, reasoning that similar responses in different species could indicate homologous eyespots, meaning markings with a shared evolutionary origin. Further experiments would be needed to confirm that relationship.

In nymphalids, the largest family of butterflies, eyespots sit along the wing margins. Giving these butterflies heparin early in development can eliminate their eyespots entirely. Yet in Sourakov’s earlier experiments with two giant silk moth species, their eyespots grew larger. He interpreted those opposite responses as a clear indication that the moth and butterfly markings evolved separately. After his initial giant silk moth studies were published in 2020, he expanded the work to include luna moths, better known for their long tails than their faint eyespots.

The changes in wing shape remain harder to explain, particularly because they have not been observed in butterflies treated this way. One possibility involves how moth and butterfly wings acquire their outlines.

Earlier in development, before those marginal cells die, another signaling protein called Wingless helps control the size of individual wing sections between veins. Wingless does respond to the two compounds. However, the wingless gene is mostly inactive by the time eyespots begin forming, which is when Sourakov starts his treatments. That timing helps explain why experiments focused on eyespots seldom change the size of those wing sections.

The gene can also be activated when damaged wing cells need repair, allowing new cells to grow in wounded areas. In pipevine swallowtail butterflies, it has another role in the development of their tiny wing tails. A landmark study published in 2010 showed that both cut and wingless are active during tail formation in these butterflies.

Sourakov suspects that the same genes may help form luna moth tails. If so, natural selection would have independently recruited wingless for the evolution of wing tails in moths and butterflies. Those tails serve different purposes. The small tails of pipevine swallowtails help visually distract birds by contributing to a false head effect, drawing attention away from the insect’s actual head. Luna moth tails are much longer, and their shape also affects how the moths fly.

“This is just my deduction, but I think it is very plausible and would explain why in butterflies or other moths we don’t see much change to the wing shape in response to heparin– wingless is not turning on at that stage of wing development in most species,” Sourakov said.

The ease of altering wing markings also suggests a possible route for rapid adaptation to a changing environment. If a luna moth’s leaflike disguise stopped protecting it, mutations that made its eyespots more visible could be favored under pressure from hunting birds. In principle, that could shift its appearance within just a few generations.

“If you are a smaller bird or a squirrel, you will think twice before attacking something in the darkness of the forest that looks like the eyes of an owl. Butterflies and moths are masters of such deceptions,” Sourakov said.

Reference: “Wing Shape and Color Pattern Modifications in Giant Silk Moths Using Sulfated Polysaccharides: Understanding Morphogenic Signals in Pupal Wings of Lepidoptera” by Andrei Sourakov, 21 August 2026, Evolution & Development. DOI: 10.1111/ede.70058

Chemical signatures found in a Brazilian dinosaur bone may be preserved red blood cells, a new study suggests, but not all experts agree.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Red blood cells found in a 115 million-year-old dinosaur fossil from Brazil are the oldest chemical evidence of blood-related material in a dinosaur fossil, a new study claims.

However, not everyone agrees with the research team's conclusions, with some experts saying the shape doesn't match those of reptilian red blood cells.

In the new research, published Monday (Nov. 2) in the journal PNAS, the scientists said they identified microscopic structures resembling red blood cells alongside chemical signatures of heme, the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin.

The new findings come from limb bones of a roughly 10-foot-long (3 meters) dinosaur called Aratasaurus museunacionali. While previous research has detected blood in dinosaur fossils, this is the first study to use chemical processes to identify heme-based signatures in dinosaur bones.

"Traditionally, fossils give us information through bones, teeth, shells and morphology. But exceptionally preserved fossils may contain another archive of information: microscopic structures and molecular traces of the original organism," study co-author Kliti Grice, a professor in the School of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Curtin University in Australia, told Live Science via email. "That opens the possibility of asking questions about ancient biology that skeletal anatomy alone cannot answer."

The team was not originally looking for traces of dinosaur blood, Grice said. Her research was driven by a broader question: How much of an ancient organism's original biology can survive fossilization?

To investigate, Grice and her team studied the limb bones of A. museunacionali, an extinct species of small theropod that lived during the Early Cretaceous period in Brazil. Theropods were a group of mostly meat-eating dinosaurs that walked on two legs. They included famous predators such as Tyrannosaurus rex and Velociraptor.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Using microscopic and chemical analysis on the theropod's limb bones, the researchers found numerous microscopic structures within vascular canals, channels that once carried blood vessels through the bone. Their shape, size and location were consistent with red blood cells, the team said.

"We combined microscopy, mineralogical analyses and molecular geochemistry," Grice said. "Critically, we investigated the chemistry in situ [in the bone itself], so we could relate the chemical signals to the microscopic structures in their physical context within the fossil. That is much stronger than simply extracting molecules from a piece of fossil and assuming where they originated."

The team's chemical analyses detected preserved heme-related compounds associated with these structures, providing more chemical evidence to support the idea that the finding could be traces of dinosaur blood, as heme is the iron-containing, ring-shaped molecule that forms a key part of the molecule hemoglobin in red blood cells.

Grice and the team think the conditions the theropod dinosaur was buried in could have helped preserve the vascular structures and the red blood cells within them. They suggested that the animal was rapidly covered by sediment in a low-oxygen environment containing microbial mats ‪—‬ thin biofilms made of microorganisms. These conditions may have altered the normal process of decomposition, helping to preserve the microscopic structures and associated chemical signatures.

An illustration of a microbial mat covering A. museunacionali's bones after it died.

"The red-blood-cell-like structures were mineralised with hausmannite, a manganese oxide mineral (Mn₃O₄)," Grice said. "We think early mineralisation helped stabilise or replicate microscopic biological structures before they were completely destroyed, while aspects of the associated chemistry also survived in altered form."

The fossil also contained preserved amino acids associated with collagen, the structural protein found in bone.

While blood has been found in dinosaur fossils before, not everyone agrees that these latest findings are truly red blood cells.

"I very much appreciate this team bringing rigor to the study of deep time fossils," said Mary Schweitzer, a molecular paleontologist at North Carolina State University who was not involved in the study but has previously studied soft tissues from the dinosaur age. "I am in agreement that endogenous [produced within the body] molecules can persist over geological time in some form, and that there is much these can teach us. However, I am not convinced that the images they figure are remnant RBCs [red blood cells] for several reasons."

For one, the structures do not convincingly match the expected appearance of red blood cells in nonmammalian animals, Schweitzer said. Unlike mammalian red blood cells, which lose their nuclei during development, those of birds and reptiles retain their nuclei. This typically produces a characteristic nuclear bulge in the shape of the cell.

According to Schweitzer, the latest findings show the microstructures having more of a concave shape with no nuclear bulge. The structures also were smaller than most non-mammalian red blood cells, "so morphological similarity is not met," Schweitzer said.

"I appreciate these authors bringing technological innovations to the study of dinosaur fossils," she said. "I am excited to see that this team and others are moving forward with a molecular approach to ancient fossil remains."

Editor's Note: This article was updated at 5:44 p.m. E.D.T. to remove an outside comment that suggested the study did not include resonance Raman spectroscopy. The team did perform that analysis.

#6432. A New Era of Bionic Vision? AI Helps Scientists Unlock the Brain’s Visual Cortex

Researchers have used artificial intelligence to improve how a brain implant stimulates the visual cortex of a blind person, potentially advancing the development of bionic eyes.

Artificial intelligence could make future bionic eyes more precise and responsive by improving how electrical signals communicate with the brain. In a study published in Neuron, researchers used deep learning to control brain stimulation in a blind man, producing more accurate neural responses with less electrical current.

The findings could advance visual prostheses that bypass damaged eyes and optic nerves, stimulating the visual cortex directly to generate perceptions of light.

Researchers from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU) tested the approach in a 27-year-old man who lost his sight following a traumatic brain injury. At a hospital in Spain, a temporary implant containing 96 electrodes stimulated his visual cortex, producing phosphenes, perceived as flashes or shapes of light.

Led in part by UCSB professor Michael Beyeler, the team trained a deep neural network to predict brain responses to different stimulation patterns. The AI model also incorporated measurements of resting brain activity, allowing it to account for changes in the brain’s condition before each test.

The AI-designed stimulation patterns produced targeted neural responses more accurately and required less electrical current than comparison approaches. Researchers also found that recorded brain activity predicted the participant’s visual perceptions better than the electrical settings alone.

“Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image,” Beyeler said. “But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation.”

The implant could both stimulate neurons and record their responses, enabling the AI to learn from actual brain activity. The participant also described perceived flashes, including their brightness, size, shape, and color.

The technology could eventually help people who lose their sight through injuries or neurological and inherited conditions. Beyeler emphasized those “who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision,” adding, “For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back.”

Describing the international research effort as “a true collaboration,” Beyeler said the study demonstrated how computational models could influence experiments involving human participants.

“Building a model in the abstract is one thing,” he said. “Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab.”

Although the research remains an early proof of concept, it suggests that future visual prostheses may work better by continuously adjusting stimulation to an individual’s neural responses.

“A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe,” Beyeler said. “It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around.”

Reference: “Deep learning-based control of electrically evoked activity in human visual cortex” by Pehuén Moure, Jacob Granley, Fabrizio Grani, Leili Soo, Antonio Lozano, Rocío López-Peco, Adrián Villamarín-Ortiz, Cristina Soto-Sánchez, Shih-Chii Liu, Michael Beyeler and Eduardo Fernández, 7 August 2026, Neuron. DOI: 10.1016/j.neuron.2026.07.006

#6431. The 7 Best Standing Desk Chairs to Keep You Comfortable All Day Long

Take a break from your standing marathon with one of these stylish and functional seats.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Standing desks have become a go-to upgrade for anyone who works from home. Swapping your desk chair for a standing desk seems like an easy fix for a day spent slouched over a laptop, but standing still and upright for hours isn’t much healthier than sitting all day.

A 2024 study from the University of Sydney found that standing more didn’t lower the risk of heart disease, stroke, or heart failure, and it was linked to a higher risk of circulatory problems like varicose veins and deep vein thrombosis. To get the most out of your standing setup, you also need to sit for parts of the day.

If you work at a bar countertop or have a standing desk that can’t be lowered, a standard desk chair won’t work. The solution is an adjustable desk chair made for higher surfaces. It’s there when you need a break, and it’s easy to roll or slide out of the way when you’re ready to stand again.

For more great additions to your home office, check out our picks for the best WiFi mesh systems, best paper shredders, and our home innovation awards.

Most standing desk chairs are labeled as drafting chairs or task chairs, so we researched both for the best options. We consulted consumer reviews for insight into the types of chairs people enjoy, and scoured online retailers for high-quality options that will last. We prioritized decent adjustability, comfortable seats, and ergonomic shapes that suit a standing desk workspace.

If you’re looking for a standing desk chair that doesn't sacrifice style, then this drafting chair could be the perfect fit. It comes in seven colors to match any interior design scheme and adjusts up to 33 inches in height to fit any standing desk setup.

Both the seat cushion and back are padded for all-day comfort, and the armrests offer extra support when you need it. The attached footrest is also a great place to cool your heels when you want to kick back, relax, and unwind from standing at your desk all day.

If you’re looking for a chair for your standing desk but don’t want to break the bank, this is a great option. For just over $80, you’ll get an ergonomic and comfortable chair that can be adjusted up to 33 inches to reach the highest desks. The back height and seat depth are great for extended sitting, and the adjustable footrest provides extra support.

When you're not using it, you can lower it and store it under your standing desk.

Our pick for the best mesh standing desk chair is this Hylone model. What makes it so great is that every part is adjustable: the height, foot ring, and arms can all be customized to suit your comfort and needs.

This swivel drafting chair raises up to 31.2 inches to reach some of the highest desks, and its footrest adjusts to relieve pressure on your legs after hours of standing. The padded armrests add extra comfort if you need to sit back, relax, and unwind after a long day.

If you catch yourself leaning back in this chair, the breathable mesh keeps you from overheating while you take a break.

While searching for the best chair for your standing desk, you can't go wrong with a classic like this one from Modway. This model is sleek, adjustable, and ergonomic, and will give you some much-needed relief after working and standing all day. With the pull of a lever, the chair can be quickly raised from 21.5 inches to 29.5 inches.

The breathable mesh back, paired with lower-back lumbar support, is a must-have for anyone who needs extra comfort when they sit down. Better yet, despite this chair's long list of standout features, it will set you back just over $160 as of this writing.

Steelcase is known for its ergonomic gaming and office chairs, and interior designers praise its level of customizability. Its Series 2 Stool is a worthy investment if you’re looking for long-term office use, since you can replace each part by ordering directly from Steelcase’s website. If you’re looking for a design that’s best for you, you can customize the Series 2 Stool's frame and seat colors, plus add an optional headrest, adjustable lumbar and arms, and carpet-compatible wheels.

The Series 2 Stool has a highly flexible seat that supports posture changes instantly. The brand recommends this stool for counter and bar-height tables, while its height adjustment and weight capacity are the most generous on this list. Steelcase also has an impressive 12-year warranty that covers part repairs and replacements.

If you're looking for a standing desk chair that's as attractive as it is comfortable, look no further than this padded faux-leather drafting chair from Markece. It is ergonomically designed with a padded backrest and seat cushion for ideal lumbar support, so your back will feel relieved after hours of standing at your desk.

And, if you have an extra-high desk, the seat on this chair can be raised nearly 36 inches above the chair's base.

Modernists and minimalists alike will love this chair. It’s the perfect balance of style and function, and it can fit well in any space. If your perfectly curated standing desk setup needs a chair, this one raises up to 34 inches. And if you want it out of sight when you're not using it, you can lower it and store it under the desk.

What’s even better is that this chair has lumbar support, so it can improve your posture—and keep you comfortable—if you sit in it for a while after standing.

To rest your legs and feet, you need a chair that reaches the right height, supports your feet when you’re seated, and gets out of the way when it’s time to stand.

Measure from the floor to the top of your desk at your usual standing height, then subtract 10 to 12 inches. That’s roughly the seat height you want, leaving room for your thighs under the desk. For a 42-inch desk, look for a seat that reaches 30 to 32 inches. Product listings usually give the seat height at its lowest and highest settings, and our picks top out anywhere from 29.5 inches to 35.8 inches.

At drafting height, your feet won’t reach the floor. Without something to rest them on, your legs dangle, and pressure builds up behind your thighs, which defeats the purpose of sitting down. Look for a foot ring or footrest, ideally one that adjusts, so your knees sit at a comfortable angle.

A backless stool keeps your core engaged and tucks under the desk when you aren't using it, so it's a good choice for small spaces. A chair with a backrest and lumbar support lets you fully rest, which matters more if you plan to sit for longer stretches. Armrests add comfort but can bump the edge of a high desk, so flip-up or removable arms are the most flexible.

Faux leather and vinyl are easy to wipe clean and usually cost less. Mesh breathes better if you run warm, and molded polypropylene or plastic seats are the lightest and easiest to move around. Check the weight capacity too. Our picks range from 250 to 400 pounds. And because you'll be moving the chair aside every time you stand, a lighter frame or smooth-rolling casters make the switch easier.

Researchers identified a 5,300-year-old kidney stone in the burial of a Bronze Age cattle herder in Russia.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A Bronze Age man buried in a monumental tomb near the Black Sea may have died from complications of a urinary tract infection (UTI) more than five millennia ago, according to a new study. Archaeologists identified a grape-size object consistent with a kidney or bladder stone in the man's burial.

"He lived with a chronic urogenital infection," study lead author Natalia Berezina, an anthropologist at Lomonosov Moscow State University in Russia, told Live Science in an email.

"It was not a brief episode," she said. "His last years were probably marked by considerable and more or less constant pain."

Berezina and colleagues investigated a small, stone-like object found in an Early Bronze Age burial in the Stavropol Upland region of southwestern Russia. They published their findings Sept. 30 in the journal Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences.

The burial was part of a kurgan cemetery, an ancient steppe funeral tradition that involved constructing a large mound of dirt over a grave. Archaeologists discovered a catacomb when they excavated the mound, and inside was the skeleton of a man who was in his 40s when he died around 5,300 years ago. The researchers found a flint arrowhead near the man's pelvis.

But during a laboratory analysis after the skeleton was excavated, researchers noticed an odd stone-like object in the collection of hand bones. The brownish object was round with several protrusions and measured about 0.8 inches (2.1 centimeters) in diameter, or roughly the size of a grape. A small crack in the object showed a crystal-like structure inside.

To learn more, the researchers used several analytical methods to determine what the tiny object was made of. First, X-ray fluorescence analysis revealed that the main components of the object were calcium and phosphorus. Then, they used X-ray powder diffraction analysis to identify the crystal structures.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In addition to common minerals, the researchers discovered the presence of whitlockite, a rare calcium salt that is known to occur in kidney, bladder and prostate stones. These "stones," collectively called calculi, are hard masses of minerals, such as calcium-containing salts. They differ in terms of the organ they form within, the exact mechanism of how they form, and their chemical makeup, although kidney and bladder stones tend to contain very similar compounds.

Whitlockite is strongly associated with bacterial infections in the human body, which suggests that the Bronze Age man had a chronic infection that resulted in the stone, the scientists concluded.

"On the balance of the available evidence, we regard a renal [kidney] stone secondary to chronic upper urinary tract infection as the most probable origin," the researchers wrote. That is, the man dealt with chronic or recurrent UTIs, which led to the formation of the stone and likely caused him considerable discomfort. UTIs can contribute to the formation of kidney stones by altering the acidity of urine and making minerals more likely to accumulate.

The researchers aren't sure why the man had urinary tract issues or whether it contributed to his death.

Notably, kidney stones can sometimes travel to the bladder, so it's unclear exactly where the stone was in the man's body when he died. If the stone had obstructed the man's ureter ‪—‬ one of the two long tubes that connect the kidneys to the bladder ‪—‬ it may have caused kidney swelling, a secondary infection or sepsis. These conditions were frequently fatal prior to the invention of antibiotics.

Other possibilities for what caused the stone include a bacterial infection of the man's prostate gland or even a sexually transmitted infection.

The man was likely on the move frequently within this Early Bronze Age steppe society, and other injuries to his skeleton suggested he had a physically demanding life, the researchers wrote. His bones showed that he was well muscled but was also dealing with degenerative joint disease in his spine, shoulders, hips, hands and feet. He had a series of healed fractures in his right shoulder, ribs and forearm.

"These were people who worked with cattle and heavy wagons on the open steppe," Berezina said, "and the injuries that follow from that are the injuries we find." In a previous study at a nearby cemetery, Berezina and colleagues found the skeleton of a man who was injured when a wagon ran over him, several years before his death. "Against that background, four healed fractures in our man look unremarkable," she said.

But the urinary tract stone would have made the man's life difficult, the researchers noted. "This individual suffered from a painful and debilitating chronic urogenital infection, a condition that would have significantly impacted his quality of life," they wrote.

Urolithiasis in the Early Bronze Age of the North Caucasus: A paleopathological case study and insights into ancient lifeways. #6429. ‘Exhumed’ recounts the true story of America’s first vampire

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A historian digs deep to show how fear shapes culture

Science, history and fear intersect in a new book from award-winning podcast creator Aaron Mahnke.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

October is my favorite month. I love when the leaves change colors and the air gets brisk. My hunger for media that sends a shiver down my spine is at an all-time high. This spooky season, I found satiation in Exhumed, a new book by historian Aaron Mahnke.

Mahnke draws on rich science-based history and folklore to show how fear of the unknown has shaped culture throughout history, even into the present day. He cites Taylor Swift, Twilight and other pop culture phenomena in his analysis — a choice that injects fresh air into the otherwise miasmic atmosphere. And thanks to Mahnke’s gripping prose, I felt like I was in the middle of the action. It was hard to lay the book down.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Exhumed kicks off with the true story of America’s first “vampire.”

Walk with me for a moment back in time to Exeter, Rhode Island in 1892. Rampant tuberculosis is killing scores of people, including three members of the Brown family: matriarch Mary and her daughters, Mary O. and Mercy L. Then a son, Edwin, falls ill with the same symptoms — sparking concern that one of the women is an undead vampire who is sucking his life away. The town exhumes the bodies.

Mercy is surprisingly well-preserved. Her hair and nails appear longer and blood dribbles from her skin when it is pierced, “evidence” that confirms everyone’s worst fear: Mercy is indeed a vampire. (Nevermind that she perished in the dead of winter, when temperatures were probably cold enough to substantially slow decomposition.) The town burns Mercy’s heart, though it doesn’t save poor Edwin. These events helped inspire Bram Stoker’s Dracula, which was published five years later.

Interestingly, the cause of tuberculosis — a bacterium — was discovered a full decade before Mercy’s story unfolded. But news doesn’t always travel fast and entrenched beliefs can be difficult to change, even in the face of hard evidence. Exhumed explores this idea far beyond Mercy’s tragic tale.

Fear has led people to do some extremely odd things by today’s standards: burning hearts to kill “vampires,” setting boobie-traps in graves to prevent the dead from rising or drinking the blood of freshly hanged men to “cure” epilepsy.​ Without modern science to explain the unexplained, people often filled in the blanks with stories, Mahnke explains.

He implores readers to withhold judgement. After all, storytelling is one of the main ways that humans make sense of the world. “All of us, both then and now, are simply making the best of what we have, trying to find a way to improve our lives,” Mahnke writes.

Perhaps this practice continues today in different shades.

At one point, eating mummies, or “mumia,” was considered cure-all for most ailments —headaches, stomach troubles and general sickness. Is it too far from the expectations some people have of buying a “health shot” from Whole Foods? Not really!

More than a century after Mercy Brown’s heart was incinerated, we’re still clinging to stories and rituals that offer us a sense of control over the thing we fear most: death. Exhumed makes it clear that we haven’t outrun this instinct, we’ve just given it different packaging.

#6428. The Mystery of Life’s Origin on Earth Just Got More Mysterious

Hydrogen cyanide was crucial for early Earth chemistry. A new study says comets almost certainly didn’t deliver it like we’d previously thought.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Since time immemorial, humanity’s greatest thinkers have wrestled with what is arguably the most burning question of our inquisitive species: Why are we here? Over the millennia, the proposed answers have meandered from the divine to the demonstrable. Then, in 1953, the famous Miller-Urey experiment made it seem increasingly plausible that life emerged from the complex chemistry of early Earth.

However, exactly where life’s building blocks came from remains an open question. Some scientists favor “panspermia,” the idea that life didn't begin on Earth at all. In this view, hardy microbes rode here aboard comets, asteroids, or rocky debris blasted off other worlds, survived the trip through space, and seeded our planet. A softer version of the idea says space rocks delivered life’s raw ingredients rather than life itself, in the form of organic molecules made in the protoplanetary disk around our young sun. Still others argue that Earth needed no outside help and produced everything life required on its own.

But just as important as pinpointing this much sought-after answer is ruling out a few choices. To that end, a new study led by scientists at the University of Cambridge and published in the journal Scientific Reports models the possibility that comets ferried chemicals, specifically hydrogen cyanide (HCN), to the planet’s surface during its infancy more than four billion years ago. A 2022 study found that cyanide on early Earth likely served as a critical reductant (an electron donor in a chemical reaction), and the cyanide also served as a vital intermediate in Stanley Miller and Harold Urey’s famous experiments by producing amino acids when exposed to electricity (possibly from volcanic lightning).

Cometary bombardment is one of the leading theories of how HCN arrived on Earth (though other studies explore whether Earth's own chemistry could have produced the molecule). So the Cambridge team, led by Richard Anslow, modeled whether comets could have delivered it. They found the opposite of what the theory predicts: The chances of comets delivering HCN intact to the surface are vanishingly small, bordering on impossible.

“Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon- and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a ‘get-out-of-jail-free card’ that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life,” Anslow said in a press statement. “It’s kind of a romantic idea, but our results suggest it’s highly unlikely.”

The theory that comets provided the chemical substrate of life runs head first into two major problems. Anslow’s previous work showed that “bouncing comets”—comets whose speeds are impacted by the gravitational influence of multiple planets—could arrive gently enough to deliver their fragile cargo intact. But these new models suggest that such a billiard-ball effect likely didn’t occur in Earth’s neighborhood. Using advances in comet-impact simulations and a better understanding of comet-atmosphere interactions, the researchers concluded that comets usually traveled too fast and at too sharp an angle. On the off chance that HCN did survive the journey, the concentrations would often be too low to be useful, and prebiotic chemistry would need to occur quickly upon arrival. Together, these two requirements push the comet-delivery theory from plausible to a “one-in-a-million” occurrence, Anslow says.

“We can’t rule out for certain that it happened that way,” Anslow said in a press statement. “But it seems to be a really rare occurrence—at best, a one-off fluke.”

Strangely, Earth’s planetary neighbor Mars would’ve had an easier go of it because it’s smaller and its atmosphere is less thick. This would’ve increased the likelihood of comets actually reaching its surface in higher numbers, but the dissolution of the Red Planet’s magnetic field roughly four billion years ago doomed the world to a lifeless existence (as far as complex life goes, that is).

Neither Anslow’s previous work nor this new study rules out the possibility that comets helped deliver life’s ingredients elsewhere in the Milky Way or beyond. But when it comes to the age-old question of why we’re here, these icy wanderers are likely not the answer.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

Rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what Mars-bound astronauts might face showed higher levels of scar tissue in their hearts, indicating they were more vulnerable to heart failure.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Exposure to space radiation may increase astronauts' risk of a dangerous heart condition, a new study in rats hints.

The research, published Sept. 30 in the journal PLOS One, found that rats exposed to levels of radiation similar to what an astronaut might experience on a long-term trip to Mars developed more scar tissue around the small blood vessels of their hearts than rats that were not exposed to this radiation. This scar tissue is indicative of a condition known as cardiac fibrosis, which is known to increase the risk of heart failure.

This scar tissue was observed nearly a year after the rats were first exposed to the radiation.

But since this study was in rats, it cannot definitively say whether this effect will play out in humans. For example, given that humans have a longer life expectancy than rats (80 years versus 2 to 4 years), the effects seen in rats may take around 30 years to show up in humans. However, the study authors say the research highlights the importance of following astronauts' health long after they return to Earth.

"The message that we try to convey … is that the follow-up time is really important," study co-author John Baker, a professor of surgery in the Radiation Bioscience Laboratory at the Medical College of Wisconsin, told Live Science. "When astronauts come back to the Earth, they expect ‪—‬ and we expect ‪—‬ that they're going to live for a long time. I think we have to be wary that they could well develop at least some type of cardiac disease."

The link between exposure to radiation and cardiac issues has been well documented. However, "no astronaut has ever been exposed to galactic cosmic radiation for long periods of time," Baker said, which makes it difficult to determine exactly how space radiation affects the heart.

Although Baker and his team previously pinpointed cardiac issues among rats exposed to radiation, this new study utilized NASA's Simulated Galactic Cosmic Ray Simulation (SimGCRSim). This new simulator provides a more precise comparison of the levels of space radiation an astronaut might experience while exploring deep space for more than a year.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

During the study, the researchers exposed rats to several minutes of radiation proportionate to their size, similar to what they might experience on a trip to Mars and back (a roughly 18-month round trip, with current technology). Some of the rats' hind legs were suspended, to "simulate conditions of weightlessness," Baker said.

After 360 days, the rats that were exposed to cosmic radiation developed twice as much scar tissue around the heart's small blood vessels than unexposed rats. This buildup of scar tissue means "the heart can't relax to the point when it needs to," thereby increasing the risk of heart failure, Baker said.

This effect was not seen in the rats who were exposed only to simulated weightlessness, confirming "it was only the radiation that produced the damaging effect on the heart," Baker said. However, long-term testing revealed that this group of rats had lower levels of key immune cells, suggesting that microgravity also may affect aspects of long-term health. (Numerous studies have shown various short-term health impacts related to microgravity.)

This study "is a very valuable contribution to space biology," Rupak Pathak, an associate professor of pharmaceutical science at the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences who was not involved in the study but holds a doctorate in radiation biology, told Live Science. While rats and humans have clear differences, "they share more than 90% of genetic information," he said, as well as very similar cardiac systems.

Given that the study authors were able to expose the rats to radiation only once, Pathak would like to see further experiments exploring whether chronic radiation exposure affects the function of the heart and other vital organs.

Baker and his colleagues hope that future experiments can be used to help NASA implement safeguards for astronauts on long-term missions, such as providing astronauts heart medications or improving shielding for the spacecraft.

"The more we know before we start, then the better NASA is going to be at working out what types of countermeasures can be developed," said Baker.

#6426. This Halloween, amateur astronomers may be in for a dwarf planet treat

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Astronomers also have their eyes on objects near Neptune that may be solar system building blocks

This 3-D view of the solar system shows the orbit of the dwarf planet candidate 2026 ED138 in the location it held on May 8, 2026. It is among the largest and brightest objects discovered beyond Pluto, but had gone unnoticed until now.

NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA/R. Proctor

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The outer solar system is yielding its secrets to the Vera C. Rubin Observatory.

Less than five months into the observatory’s decade-long survey of the sky, a potential new dwarf planet has already popped up in its data, astronomers reported this week at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society’s Division of Planetary Sciences in Spokane, Wash.

Another team reported a handful of new Neptune Trojans, icy objects that share an orbit with Neptune, at the meeting and in the Astrophysical Journal Letters. The findings are filling in astronomers’ picture of the Kuiper Belt at the solar system’s frigid fringes.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“It feels a little bit like we’re replicating the 1800s and early 1900s, discovering what the solar system even looks like in general,” says Sam Deen, an amateur astronomer based in Simi Valley, Calif. “We’re finding out what there even is in the first place that makes up most of the Kuiper Belt.”

Perched on a mountaintop in Chile, the Vera Rubin Observatory is on a mission to map the entire southern sky every couple of nights, searching for faint and fast-moving cosmic objects. The observatory took its first images in June 2025 and officially began a decade-long survey in June 2026.

Even before the official survey started, Rubin had detected the motion of an object orbiting billions of kilometers beyond Pluto. Rubin observed the object 30 times on 20 nights from March 4 to July 11. But no one knew it was there until October 13, when astrophysicist Matt Holman of the Smithsonian Astronomical Observatory in Cambridge, Mass., ran a search for moving dots of light in the data.

The object, called 2026 ED138, appeared to be about 47 times as far from Earth as Earth is from the sun. Its brightness suggests it’s between 600 and 1,500 kilometers wide, potentially as large as other dwarf planets like Ceres and Makemake. That’s probably big enough to be spherical, making it a dwarf planet.

“It’s really big. It’s damn huge,” Deen says. “No matter what you call it, it’s still the biggest thing we’ve found in the entire solar system in 19 years.”

When Holman realized what he had found, he was thrilled but doubtful. “It’s quite an exciting thing,” Holman said in a news briefing at the meeting on October 27. “But one of the things that you need to do when you discover something potentially of this size is to try to verify that it’s true.”

Holman and colleagues were able to find observations of the same object in archived data from the Dark Energy Camera, located on an adjacent mountaintop in Chile, taken in 2016.

Deen was able to trace it back even farther, to photographic plates taken as part of a sky survey at Palomar Observatory in California in 1954. Other amateur astronomers independently found the same sightings.

“They took an image from Palomar in 1954, and another about half an hour after the first one, that both by pure chance happen to point at where ED138 is,” Deen says. “And it’s really obvious. If you know it’s supposed to be there, it’s not particularly faint.”

So why didn’t anybody notice it until now? It’s partly because ED138 practically crawls across the sky, orbiting the sun once every 280 years. It was also moving against a dense background of Milky Way stars, where it blended in.

By combining observations spanning decades, astronomers can calculate the object’s orbit with more precision.

Deen is hoping to observe the potential new dwarf planet pass in front of a distant star on Halloween. That sort of observation, called an occultation, can help reveal more details of the putative dwarf planet’s size and shape, and even whether it has moons or rings. Usually, it takes years to understand an object’s orbit well enough to predict an occultation, Deen says. “Getting to do it immediately is like being a kid in a candy shop, really.”

Caltech, Space Telescope Science Institute

Caltech, Space Telescope Science Institute

A crop of newly spotted Neptune Trojans were masked by the Milky Way, too. These asteroids gather in the same orbit as Neptune, but offset from the planet at 60 degrees. Astronomers think they were some of the original building blocks of the solar system and contain an ancient record of planetary formation and evolution.

Other planets have Trojans, too. Jupiter has thousands. Astronomers think Neptune has many more, but so far they have seen only 30 in the cluster of space objects that orbit ahead of Neptune, and just two in the cluster behind it.

“We would expect these [groups of Trojans] to be symmetric in numbers, so you have to get more than two,” planetary scientist Meg Schwamb said in a news conference at the meeting on October 28.

The trailing cloud happened to have been moving in front of the Milky Way from the perspective of Earth for the last 15 years. Spotting individual Trojans against that crowded background was “like finding a needle in a sequined dress,” said Schwamb, of Queens University Belfast in Northern Ireland.

Schwamb and colleagues examined Vera Rubin data taken from the commissioning phase — the period when engineers were testing the telescope. In this early data haul, the team found two more trailing Trojans, plus one candidate. They seem to be similar in composition to the leading ones, which matches theories of how the solar system formed.

“It just kind of got lucky,” Schwamb said. “These objects photobombed the commissioning survey.”

“This is really the appetizer for what Rubin Observatory is going to do in its mission for the next ten years,” she added. “There’s hundreds more of these objects likely to be found.”

Some of the excitement about these discoveries is dampened by fears of losing observations to bright satellites crisscrossing the telescope’s field of view, says astronomer Sam Lawler of the University of Regina in Canada.

“I have to put in the constant downer of how the increasing numbers of satellites will make these discoveries harder,” Lawler says. “There are one hundred new satellites launching every week, and they keep getting bigger and brighter. These discoveries will be hindered by that.”

But even with the satellites, Lawler anticipates many more cool discoveries from Rubin.

“Just finding a dwarf planet so quickly, maybe we’ll find something even bigger,” she says. “There could be something the size of Mars out there. And then we’d have the whole planet debate all over again. It would be fun.”
