#6425. The Real Ark of the Covenant May Be Hiding in Ethiopia—and Only One Man Alive Is Allowed to See It

According to an ancient Ethiopian epic, the biblical relic was stolen in a 3,000-year-old temple heist—and now sits in a tiny chapel guarded by a single monk for life.

Next to the Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion in the ancient city of Axum, Ethiopia, stands a small, fenced-off sanctuary called the Chapel of the Tablet. Entry is forbidden to everyone on Earth except one man: a lone monk appointed for life to watch over its contents.

According to believers, he’s guarding one of history’s most sacred and sought-after relics: the Ark of the Covenant.

In the Hebrew Bible, the Ark is described in precise detail: a rectangular chest of acacia wood overlaid inside and out with gold, measuring roughly four feet long by two feet wide and high, and crowned with two golden cherubim with outstretched wings. Forged at Mount Sinai to house the Ten Commandments and serve as God’s literal throne on Earth, the Ark guided the Israelites through the wilderness, toppled enemy armies, and eventually became the sacred centerpiece of King Solomon’s Temple in Jerusalem. Then, during the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem in 586 B.C.E., this ultimate seat of divine power vanished from the biblical record without a trace.

For millennia, its disappearance has fueled endless archaeological quests, conspiracy theories, and pop-culture touchstones like 1981’s Raiders of the Lost Ark. Yet according to the Kebra Nagast (“The Glory of the Kings”), a revered 14th-century Ethiopian national epic, the Ark was never lost at all. Instead, it was smuggled out of Jerusalem nearly 3,000 years ago by Menelik I, the son of King Solomon and Makeda—better known outside Ethiopia as the Queen of Sheba.

According to the epic, Menelik grew up in Ethiopia before traveling to Jerusalem in his early twenties to meet his father, carrying a royal ring Solomon had left with his mother as proof of his lineage. Solomon recognized the young man immediately—he was the spitting image of his grandfather, King David—and begged his favored son to stay and inherit the throne of Israel.

Menelik insisted on returning home to rule his mother’s kingdom. Reluctantly, Solomon agreed, but on one condition. The firstborn sons of Jerusalem’s highest-ranking nobles, priests, and military commanders were ordered to accompany Menelik as his new royal court to establish a “second Israel” in Ethiopia.

That decree sealed the Ark’s fate. Devastated at the thought of leaving the presence of God behind, the young elites conspired to pull off an ancient inside job. The heist was masterminded by Azariah, son of the High Priest Zadok. Prompted by an angel in a vision, Azariah commissioned an exact wooden replica of the Ark. Under cover of night, he and his co-conspirators slipped into the Temple, swapped the genuine Ark for the decoy, and hid the real relic in their luggage.

When Menelik’s caravan departed the next day, the Kebra Nagast claims the Ark’s power lifted their wagons and animals off the ground, propelling them toward Ethiopia at supernatural speed. By the time Zadok discovered the counterfeit and Solomon’s army gave frantic chase, the Ethiopians were long gone.

Christianity was still centuries away, so as tradition has it, the relic was first kept on Tana Qirqos, a remote island on Ethiopia’s Lake Tana, where priests guarded it for 800 years. Then around 340 C.E., when King Ezana of the Aksumite Empire converted to Christianity, the Ark was ceremoniously moved to the newly built Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion in Axum, permanently linking the ancient Israelite covenant with Ethiopian Christianity.

Over the centuries, whenever invaders threatened Axum—including Queen Gudit’s forces in the 10th century and the devastating Adal War in the 16th century—monks spirited the Ark away to mountain strongholds and island refuges until the cathedral could be rebuilt. In the 1960s, Empress Menen Asfaw, wife of Emperor Haile Selassie, funded the dedicated Chapel of the Tablet next door. According to local monastic lore, the move was necessary because a divine “heat” radiating from the Ark was cracking the ancient stone walls of its previous sanctum.

Because the Ethiopian Orthodox Church forbids anyone—including scholars, archaeologists, and even the church’s own patriarch—from laying eyes on the relic, its authenticity remains impossible to verify scientifically. Only one outsider in modern history has claimed to get a look. In 1941, British army officer Edward Ullendorff—later a prominent professor of Ethiopian studies—allegedly used his military clout and fluency in classical Ge’ez to talk his way inside the sanctuary. In a 1992 interview, Ullendorff claimed the chest he saw was merely a “middle- to late-medieval construction.”

However, Ethiopian officials and historians quickly pointed out a flaw in Ullendorff’s scoop: every church in Ethiopia keeps a replica of the Ark, known as a tabot, for ceremonial use. If Ullendorff saw a medieval wooden box, believers argue, he was simply fooled by a decoy—the exact same trick Azariah used on King Solomon 3,000 years ago.

And so, while treasure hunters continue to scour subterranean tunnels in Jerusalem and desert caves across the Middle East, millions of Ethiopians believe the search is already over. The world’s most famous lost treasure isn’t buried in a secret vault—it’s sitting right on a street corner in Axum, hiding in plain sight.

Shawn Gorman is Deputy Editor of News for Popular Mechanics. Before joining Pop Mech, he specialized in academic reading for educational testing. His diverse academic background also includes time spent as a lecturer and librarian at institutions such as the University of Kentucky, SUNY, and Harvard University. Shawn holds a Ph.D. in Modern Foreign Languages and Literatures from Boston University, an M.A. from The Ohio State University, and a B.A. in History from the University of Oregon. His favorite subjects to explore include computer science, physics, math, and biology. He lives on a medium-sized cat ranch in Easton, Pennsylvania, with his wife and two daughters.

#6424. NASA is searching for a way to protect future astronauts from inhaling Martian dust

NASA’s Perseverance rover found ultrafine Mars dust clinging to spacesuit samples for years, a challenge for protecting future astronauts.

Dust is usually something you can brush off. The finest dust on Mars, however, isn’t like that. On small squares of spacesuit fabric carried by NASA’s Perseverance rover, dust fine enough to reach deep into human lungs has stayed attached through years of driving and drilling.

Perseverance measured that dust over 1,645 Martian days, more than four years on an Earth calendar. Its readings came from PIXL, an X-ray instrument on the end of the rover’s robotic arm.

Scott VanBommel, a Perseverance scientist at Washington University in St. Louis, is the paper’s lead author.

“The existence of Mars dust at these ultrafine sizes has been predicted for a long time, and PIXL gave us the chance to measure it directly on Mars,” he said.

None of this fabric is part of a suit. Five swatches of spacesuit material, each three-quarters of an inch (20 millimeters) square, are mounted on a small panel.

The rover uses that panel to check the settings of another instrument, called SHERLOC. NASA sent the swatches to see how spacesuit materials hold up on the Martian surface.

PIXL has its own test panel, with one sample of Teflon and one of glass made from basalt, a dark volcanic rock. Teflon contains no elements PIXL can detect directly. So any signal the instrument picked up from that sample had to come from dust resting on it.

On SHERLOC’s panel, the team also checked swatches of Teflon and Vectran, two materials used in spacesuits.

Earlier missions had measured Mars dust particles down to about 3 micrometers across. PIXL picked up two groups of even smaller ones.

Fine particles were less than 2.5 micrometers wide, and ultrafine particles were around 100 nanometers. A human hair is about 70 micrometers wide, so the ultrafine grains are roughly 700 times thinner than a hair.

Grain sizes varied from one surface to the next. Dust on PIXL’s Teflon and on SHERLOC’s Vectran swatch averaged about 2 micrometers.

On the basalt glass and SHERLOC’s Teflon swatch, some grains were as small as about 100 to 300 nanometers.

“The larger clumps, the Martian dust bunnies, get shaken off over time. But the smallest particles stay behind, and those are the ones that pose the greatest challenge for human support systems,” VanBommel said.

Static electricity appears to explain which grains cling to which surface. Dust grains become charged as they collide in the air, and different materials on the test panels attracted grains of different sizes.

Plastics like Teflon are common in the outer layers of spacesuits, and the results show they readily collect fine dust.

Some materials held less dust than others, which could guide the choice of materials and protective coatings for future suits and habitats.

Chemically, the dust matched what earlier missions had measured: rich in iron and sulfur. PIXL also found extra phosphorus and signs of calcium sulfate.

During NASA’s Apollo missions, lunar dust scratched visors, degraded the outer layers of spacesuits, and damaged their seals. Some crew members reported symptoms similar to hay fever.

Mars dust is different. Wind keeps knocking the grains into each other, which rounds them off, so they’re less abrasive than grains on the Moon.

They carry more sulfur, chlorine, iron and silica than lunar dust does. Regional and global dust storms can keep them circulating through the atmosphere.

On Earth, airborne particles smaller than 2.5 micrometers are tied to a range of health problems, because they can get deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream.

Studies have shown that ultrafine particles, those no larger than 100 nanometers, can travel from the nose to the brain along the nerve that carries smell.

Martian dust is mostly silicate minerals, and it carries reactive chemicals. Those include perchlorates, which can disrupt the thyroid, and reactive iron, which damages cells. Scientists think the health risk depends on how much dust a person takes in and for how long.

Perseverance measured dust stuck to small samples, not dust floating in the air of a crew’s living space. Researchers still don’t know how much of that dust would get indoors, or how much a person would breathe there.

NASA can use the results as it refines indoor dust limits for astronauts and works out ways to clean gear.

Some designs could keep dust out. A suitport lets an astronaut climb into a suit attached to the outside of a habitat. Airlocks with two chambers could also cut how much dust reaches living quarters.

NASA is already testing some fixes on the Moon. In March 2025, an Electrodynamic Dust Shield developed at Kennedy Space Center in Florida landed on the Moon aboard Firefly Aerospace’s Blue Ghost Mission 1. It used electric fields to clear lunar soil from glass and radiator surfaces.

At Johnson Space Center in Houston, engineers use vacuum chambers and imitation Moon soil to test spacesuit parts and a handheld dust-removal tool ahead of Artemis missions.

Those lunar tests are the proving ground for gear that future crews will eventually need on Mars.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6423. Scientists poured dye into a sinkhole at the bottom of a Florida lake, and it surfaced 35 days later at a famous spring 19 miles away

A pink dye test revealed an underground connection between Florida's Lake Jackson and five natural springs.

On September 19, 2017, scientists poured a pink tracer dye called Rhodamine WT into a sinkhole in the bed of Lake Jackson, about 5 miles (8 kilometers) north of Tallahassee, Florida.

Thirty-five days later, the main peaks of that dye turned up at Wakulla Spring, about 19 miles (30.6 kilometers) to the south.

Traces of the dye reached five separate natural springs in all. The results show a connection between the lake and those springs through underground channels in the limestone.

Only a small amount of dye seems to have made the full trip, and the scientists suspect most of it spread into the porous rock along the way.

Lake Jackson sits in a closed basin of 27,000 acres (10,900 hectares), or 42 square miles (109 square kilometers). Several large sinkholes open in its bed, including Lime Sink in the north and Porter Hole Sink in the south.

The lake’s original name, Okeeheepkee, means “disappearing waters.” Every so often it drains away through the bottom, in events known as dry-downs.

Major or partial dry-downs have been recorded in 1907, 1909, 1932, 1935, 1936, 1957 and 1982, and several times since 1999. In the final stages, the lake appears to drain rapidly, as though someone pulled the plug from a bathtub.

A dry-down can follow a combination of below-average rainfall, low groundwater levels and high evapotranspiration. Heavy storms can refill the lake quickly.

Water that leaves through the lakebed eventually enters the upper Floridan aquifer, according to the Florida Department of Environmental Protection.

Researchers think some of that water may travel to Wakulla Spring, though the agency notes that the timing and flow path still need investigation.

Seán E. McGlynn, technical director of McGlynn Laboratories Inc., carried out the study with co-author Alan W. Niedoroda.

They used fluorescent dye tracing to test whether a subterranean flow between Lake Jackson and Wakulla Spring could be positively demonstrated.

They injected the dye into the lake-bottom sinkhole for six and a half minutes.

Water-quality sondes at Wakulla Spring and nearby Sally Ward Spring recorded the main peaks after 35 days.

Charcoal packs, which absorb dye from passing water, were placed at those two springs and three others nearby. They also picked up dye within time windows that matched the peaks recorded by the sondes.

Each breakthrough event was brief, lasting from one minute to 100 minutes.

In slides for a Florida State University karst symposium, McGlynn put the peak travel time at 35.21 days over 19.1 miles (30.7 kilometers), or 2,864 feet (873 meters) a day.

The results point to a conduit-like system in the aquifer dominated by advection, meaning the dye was carried along by the moving water. On average, it traveled about half a mile (0.8 kilometers) a day.

Because dye showed up at five well-separated springs, the authors conclude that the conduit system is both braided and branching.

The paper describes a leaky conduit, in which much of the dye moving through the channels dispersed into the surrounding limestone matrix.

The study was exploratory, and its authors caution that it allows only conjectural statements about how much of the dye ended up where.

The study’s authors call Wakulla Spring a renowned first-magnitude spring. Its limestone holds many interconnected holes that feed a network of conduits, and it discharges about 300 million gallons (1.1 billion liters) a day, according to Florida State Parks.

Its cave system is the longest mapped underwater cave system in the United States, with conduits extending both north and south of the spring. More than 22 miles (35 kilometers) of passage lie deeper than 190 feet (58 meters).

Earlier dye traces in the Wakulla Spring watershed had already shown that water entering four major swallets later flows out at the spring.

The area’s many sinkholes are developed in the St. Marks Formation, a fossil-rich sandy limestone 20 to 23 million years old.

The 2024 study points to a leaky-conduit flow able to carry nutrients and pollutants rapidly over long distances. The same weakness leaves cave groundwater vulnerable to pollution in other karst regions.

In August 2021, the Florida Geological Survey announced a second trace at Porter Hole Sink, using green fluorescein dye, to confirm the earlier connection.

The dye release was timed to low water and the approach of Tropical Storm Fred, whose rain was expected to push the dye toward 23 monitoring sites. The agency said results could take weeks or months.

“Confirming this connection will help resource managers develop more informed strategies for managing our water resources,” said Guy Means, then acting director of the survey and Florida’s state geologist.

The upper Floridan aquifer supplies drinking water to Leon and Wakulla counties and feeds Wakulla Spring.

The study was published in the journal Journal of Cave and Karst Studies.

#6422. A 1,600-Year-Old Artistic Marvel Seemed Physically Impossible to Recreate. Until One Scientist Did.

It took the better part of two millennia to figure out the science behind how this ancient glass cup could change colors.

Roughly 1,600 years ago, ancient Romans crafted one of the most pristine—and scientifically advanced—works of glass art, a cup that shifts colors between jade green and ruby red. We’ve never adequately replicated the creation, but that’s all changing thanks to the scientific process used in a University of Sheffield project aimed at mimicking the Romans.

“Although if the Romans could have seen me experimenting,” said Lisa Hollands, a team leader at the university’s School of Chemical, Materials, and Biological Engineering, in a statement, “they’d probably laugh and ask: ‘Why does she not know how to make this?’”

Roman color-changing glass first appeared in the fourth century C.E., and the Lycurgus Cup offers the most glamorous example of it. Now on display at the British Museum, it’s one of 40 surviving glass cage cups. Its exterior depicts the mythical Thracian king Lycurgus ensnared in vines. The cup appears green in reflected light and red when light shines through it.

It’s a spectacular museum piece, but it’s long puzzled glassmakers and historians. How did the Romans create this color-shifting trick, now known as the dichroic effect? And why has every modern attempt to reproduce it failed? The leading explanation is that Roman artisans embedded trace amounts of gold and silver in the glass, forming nanoparticles thousands of times smaller than a grain of sand. Because these particles are smaller than the wavelengths of light, they don’t just let light pass through. They absorb and scatter certain colors depending on their size and shape, so the glass looks different depending on how light hits it.

“I knew that making a glass of this type was likely to be a complex task, as it is not just a case of adding nanoparticles to glass,” Hollands said. “I’ve studied and worked with glass for over 25 years, so I used the knowledge and experience I’ve gained, coupled with a modern scientific understanding of what I was trying to achieve.”

Hollands partnered with Caroline Jackson, a leading Roman glass expert, to learn about Roman-era glassmaking and to understand the materials they might have used. “Then came the more difficult part of trying to get small amounts of gold and silver into the glass in the right form,” she said.

Hollands experimented with different furnace types, starting materials with varying oxygen levels, and even sugar. Eventually she hit on a recipe that works: Her glass looks opaque green in reflected light and glows red when light shines through.

This magical effect occurs because when gold and silver join the molten glass mixture, nanocrystals grow. Because the nanoparticles are smaller than the wavelengths of light, Hollands told The Guardian, the electrons in their atoms can block certain colors under the right conditions. “So, for this glass, if light is shone through it, the gold and silver particles block blue and green light, only allowing reds and oranges to pass through,” she said. “If light is reflected off the surface, the particles have the effect of scattering the light, giving the opaque green color we see.”

With the recipe finally cracked, the team asked Elliot Walker to use it in a contemporary sculpture. Walker is one of the UK's foremost glass artists and won season two of Netflix’s Blown Away. “It is a very rare thing to have the opportunity to work with glass developed from ancient mixtures and recipes, and it is always a very exciting one,” Walker said. “You can really get an idea of how the glass makers of the past would have adapted to this sort of glass. It’s like shaking their hands.”

Walker gave the sculpture a classical form to echo the Lycurgus Cup, and he included a blown-glass element to show off its color-shifting effect. “The piece is a blend of the Lycurgus story and the Farnese Atlas sculpture,” he said, “with the globe replaced by a cup.”

The new creation goes on display at the university’s Festival of the Mind on November 6 before shifting permanently into the school’s Turner Museum of Glass.

The Sheffield team said that although the recipe is mainly meant for decorative glass, the science behind it could lead to new photonic materials, which control light, and to advanced glasses for storing radioactive waste. Already, the project has contributed to research on immobilizing complex nuclear waste in glass and understanding the conditions that cause crystals to form, which helps maximize how much waste can be safely locked away.

“What Lisa and Elliot have managed to achieve has surpassed all our expectations,” said Christina Metcalfe, the school’s Molecular Photonic Breadboards project manager. “The incredible historic narrative rally captures people’s imaginations, and I like to think we’ve created something that people will marvel at for years to come.”

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

#6421. Darwin’s finches face a deadly threat hiding in their nests

A DNA study traces how vampire flies spread across the Galápagos, offering clues to protecting Darwin’s finches from the deadly parasites.

A fly’s larvae can kill every chick in a Darwin’s finch nest by feeding on their blood and tissue.

That fly, the avian vampire fly, is now considered the greatest threat to land birds in the Galápagos Islands.

The finches evolved far from any continent, but the fly came from the mainland.

A new DNA study suggests it most likely got in through San Cristóbal, the island closest to mainland Ecuador and historically the first stop for cargo ships.

From there, the flies appear to have spread west. Knowing that route gives conservation teams a clearer idea of where to focus their efforts.

Abbie Hay, a PhD student, and Rachael Dudaniec, an associate professor, led the study at Macquarie University’s School of Natural Sciences in Australia.

They worked with scientists from the Charles Darwin Foundation and other groups to compare island flies with flies from mainland Ecuador, where the species is native.

Scientists know the vampire fly as Philornis downsi. It probably reached the islands with human help sometime before 1964, but it wasn’t identified in finch nests until 1997.

The fly’s larvae feed on growing chicks and sometimes on their mothers.

The fly has been found on 15 of the 17 Galápagos islands where scientists have checked, and it attacks at least 11 species of Darwin’s finches.

Island species can be especially vulnerable to new parasites. Species that evolved in isolation often lack defenses against these newcomers, the authors wrote.

Sonia Kleindorfer, now at the University of Vienna, has led more than two decades of research on the fly and the finches, and this study builds on that work.

The researchers collected flies during the 2024 bird breeding season, from January to April, on five islands: Santa Cruz, Isabela, Floreana, San Cristóbal and Santiago. Santiago is the only one of the five without a human settlement.

Some adult flies were caught in traps. Others were collected from nests as pupae, the stage between larva and adult, after the birds had finished nesting.

In all, the team gathered 235 island flies and 39 mainland flies.

After removing poor-quality samples and close relatives, they compared 169 island flies at more than 33,000 points in their DNA where a single letter varied.

The DNA differences let the team work out which groups had been mixing, without following individual flies between islands.

Groups that mix tend to become genetically similar, while groups that stay apart gradually become more different.

The island flies had much less genetic variety than the mainland flies, and the two formed separate genetic groups.

That fits a genetic bottleneck, where a population starts with just a few founders and carries only part of the original group’s variety.

San Cristóbal stood apart from the other islands. Its flies were the most genetically different from the rest, yet they also had the most genetic variety.

Isabela showed the opposite pattern. Even though it’s by far the largest island in the study, its flies had the least genetic variety.

Three neighboring islands, Isabela, Santa Cruz and Santiago, are just 10 to 17 miles (16 to 27 kilometers) apart, and their flies mixed a lot.

Santa Cruz and Santiago seemed to exchange the most flies, both with each other and with nearby islands.

When the team estimated which way fly genes were moving between islands, only San Cristóbal showed a clear one-way pattern. More of its genes moved out toward the other islands than came back in.

Westward is also the way the wind blows. The southeast trade winds carry air from South America northwest across the islands, which puts San Cristóbal upwind of the others.

Cargo has traveled the same way. Ships from the port of Guayaquil historically stopped at San Cristóbal first, and the cargo then went to Santa Cruz and on to Isabela and Floreana.

Adult flies feed on fruit and vegetables, so shipments of fresh produce could carry them between islands.

“Our results suggest that the fly may be traveling from the mainland to San Cristóbal with human assistance, and from there to other islands through a combination of human activity and natural dispersal,” Dudaniec said.

Adult vampire flies have been found riding on tourist boats between islands. A related species, the stable fly, has been reported to travel up to 140 miles (225 kilometers) on the wind.

That’s farther than San Cristóbal is from any of the other four islands, but how far the vampire fly itself can fly between islands hasn’t been documented.

Right now, conservation workers fight the fly by applying insecticide by hand and by using self-fumigating nesting material.

A wasp called Conura annulifera, which attacks only this fly, looks promising as a natural enemy that could be released to keep it in check.

Choosing where to start matters. Pests with more genetic variety are more likely to evolve resistance to a control agent, the authors wrote, which makes isolated islands that receive fewer new flies better starting points.

“By identifying which populations are genetically connected, we can better understand where flies may be coming from and where control efforts could have the greatest impact,” Dudaniec said.

San Cristóbal presents a challenge. Its flies are the most genetically distinct, but they also have the most genetic variety, and new ones may still be arriving from the mainland.

The island may need several control methods at once, plus tighter checks on what arrives.

Floreana may be an easier place to begin. The team suggested that the island, home to just 111 people, could be a more efficient site for a control trial.

San Cristóbal had the smallest sample in the study, just 21 flies, mostly from nests in one small area. With so few flies, the researchers may have underestimated the island’s genetic variety.

The one-way movement out of San Cristóbal also has two possible explanations.

Flies may still be arriving there and spreading out today, or the DNA may reflect the route of the first flies to settle on the island.

None of the flies collected on other islands looked like a recent arrival from San Cristóbal.

Telling the two explanations apart will take a separate study of the population’s history, the authors wrote.

The mainland source is a mystery, too. Flies from all three mainland sites differed genetically from the island flies, so none of them looks like the population that started the invasion.

One of those sites was a forest about 9 miles (15 kilometers) from the port of Guayaquil. Flies may be reaching the port from somewhere else before they board ships.

The authors wrote that testing flies from places that ship fresh produce to Guayaquil could help trace the invasion back to its source.

The full study was published in the journal Molecular Ecology.

An American astronaut on board the ISS recently snapped a spectacular "fireball" streaking across the nighttime sky over West Africa. The striking "light show" shows a Russian rocket being vaporized as it reenters the upper atmosphere.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What's in the photos? Space debris from a Russian rocket burning up upon reentry

Who took the photos? NASA astronaut Chris Williams

Earlier this year, an astronaut on board the International Space Station (ISS) snapped some striking photos, and an eerily beautiful video, of a "fireball" streaking over Earth as chunks of space debris burned up in the nighttime sky.

NASA's Chris Williams, who lived and worked on the ISS between November 2025 and July 2026, captured the eye-catching images from the station's cupola — a large, roughly dome-shaped series of windows that constantly points down at our planet — and later shared them on the social media platform X.

"Just as we were passing over West Africa, I saw a bright object directly below us, streaking through the upper atmosphere," Williams wrote in the post. "I saw its tail grow and then split apart into a shower of smaller pieces," he added. "It was quite a light show!"

Williams initially peered down at Earth to catch a glimpse of the Russian cargo spacecraft Progress 95, which successfully delivered essential supplies and additional equipment to the ISS later the same day. Instead, he saw what he believed was "some piece of orbital debris or a satellite breaking up as it entered the atmosphere."

Live Science's sister site Space.com later revealed that Williams had actually witnessed the burning remains of the Russian Soyuz rocket that had carried Progress 95 into space, after it lifted off from a recently repaired launchpad at the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.

The Soyuz rocket launched the cargo spacecraft Progress 95, which later docked with the ISS. (This photo shows the Progress 46 mission docking with the station in 2011.)

Shortly after deploying the resupply shuttle into low Earth orbit, the rocket's fairings and booster fell back toward our planet as expected, breaking apart into smaller pieces that were superheated and later vaporized by intense friction as they hit the upper atmosphere, according to Space.com. A very similar fireball was seen above Australia in August 2023, when another Soyuz rocket reentered the atmosphere.

Russia's prior resupply mission, Progress 94, also made headlines earlier this year when one of its antennae failed to deploy after separation from its Soyuz rocket, forcing cosmonauts (Russian astronauts) to use a remote control "backup system" to dock the spacecraft to the ISS.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Historically, the only fireballs visible in Earth's skies have been those caused by meteors, which can similarly break apart in flames. We were recently reminded of this when fireballs were spotted above the U.S. this spring, including one space rock that exploded with a massive sonic boom over Ohio and another that crashed through the roof of a house in Houston. (A NASA statement said the fireball Williams witnessed also may have been caused by meteor activity but was more likely to be the Soyuz rocket.)

However, fireballs from human-made objects are becoming more common. The number of spacecraft orbiting Earth has skyrocketed (pun intended) in recent decades, and "what goes up must come down."

Williams' photographs show how the remains of the Soyuz rocket exploded in a bright flash before stretching out into a train of flaming debris.

Most spacecraft and large pieces of space junk burn up around 50 miles (80 kilometers) above Earth's surface — just below the imaginary boundary with space, known as the Kármán line. While this may lead to visually stunning spectacles like the one Williams captured, scientists are starting to realize that these fireballs may be having a bigger impact on the upper atmosphere than they previously expected.

In recent years, researchers have detected a sharp increase in atmospheric metal pollution from vaporized spacecraft. And while they are still trying to figure out what effect this may have, some scientists have proposed that it could affect the ozone layer or potentially alter Earth's magnetic field.

Additionally, as the number of falling spacecraft rises, the chances that debris may fall to Earth's surface — after failing to properly burn up upon reentry — also increase. This came to the fore in March 2024, when the remains of a 3-ton battery pack that was discarded from the ISS crashed into a family home in Florida.

This 2011 astronaut photo captured one of NASA's iconic space shuttles passing between Earth and the International Space Station for the very last time.

During the Sept. 11 attacks, NASA astronaut Frank Culbertson — the only American not on Earth at the time — snapped a "sobering" shot of smoke pouring across New York City as the second tower fell.

A 2016 satellite photo shows Hurricane Madeline and Hurricane Lester heading straight toward Hawaii. When viewed from above, the twin cyclones and the surrounding clouds look eerily like a giant smiley face.

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. #6419. Why do some autumn leaves change color early? Weather alone can’t explain it

A new study suggests the balance of nutrients inside leaves helps explain why some forests lose their summer green earlier than others.

Shorter days, cooler temperatures, and rainfall all help determine when autumn leaves turn. But weather doesn’t explain all of it, and a new study suggests part of the answer is inside the leaves themselves.

In most of the forests the researchers studied, from Alaska to Hawaii, leaves that held a lot of nitrogen compared with phosphorus lost their summer green earlier in the fall.

A leaf’s chemistry, in other words, seems to carry clues about autumn timing that the weather alone misses.

The study was led by Tong Qiu, an assistant professor of ecology at Duke University’s Nicholas School of the Environment, with Ph.D. candidate Hanshi Chen as first author.

The team worked entirely from airplane and satellite measurements, so the results show a consistent pattern, not proof that nutrients cause the change.

Leaves need nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium to do their job.

These nutrients help build proteins and chlorophyll, the green pigment in leaves, and they help a leaf make and use sugar.

Together, these processes help leaves keep producing food late into the growing season.

The balance between these nutrients has been changing. For decades, farms and industry have released extra nitrogen into the environment.

A 2013 analysis by Josep Peñuelas and colleagues linked human-caused imbalances between nitrogen and phosphorus to changes in natural and farmed ecosystems worldwide.

Peñuelas is also an author of the new study, which notes that rising nitrogen levels are leaving many ecosystems relatively short on phosphorus. What that means for autumn hasn’t been clear.

Checking leaf nutrients across a whole continent is also slow and expensive.

“Usually, measuring nutrients requires people to collect leaves and go back to the lab and do an experiment to quantify their concentrations,” Qiu said.

Instead of collecting leaves, the team used data from the National Ecological Observatory Network, a group of U.S. research sites funded by the National Science Foundation.

A plane flies over each site carrying an imaging spectrometer. This kind of camera records sunlight bouncing off the trees in 426 narrow bands, most of them invisible to the human eye.

Leaves with different amounts of nutrients reflect light a little differently.

Scientists had already matched these readings to about 300 leaf samples from sunlit treetops, and the method was most accurate for nitrogen.

Qiu’s team used this approach to map nutrients across 25 forest sites.

They ranged from Alaska and the mountains of the West to a Texas woodland and a wet mountain forest on volcanic soil in Hawaii.

To track autumn, the team used satellite images sharp enough to show areas about 10 feet (3 meters) across.

For each spot, they identified the fall day when greenness fell near its seasonal minimum, reaching the bottom 15% of its annual range.

The researchers then compared spots within the same forest. They divided each forest site into squares about 100 feet (30 meters) wide, analyzing roughly 4,600 to 62,000 squares per site.

In 20 of the 25 forests, spots where leaves held more nitrogen relative to phosphorus lost their green earlier.

That held even after the team accounted for weather, elevation, tree species, and canopy height.

“There seems to be a sweet spot where nitrogen and phosphorus are in balance,” Qiu said. “If that gets crossed, trees will start changing color earlier.”

The likely reason, the authors wrote, has to do with phosphorus, which cells need to carry energy.

When phosphorus runs low, energy transfer within cells could slow, potentially causing leaves to lose their green earlier.

As leaves shut down for the season, trees break down their chlorophyll and move phosphorus out of the leaves into parts that live through the winter.

Not every forest followed this pattern. In two mountain evergreen forests in the West and at the Hawaiian site, leaves with more nitrogen relative to phosphorus stayed green longer.

In places like these, the authors suggested, extra nitrogen may ease a nitrogen shortage instead of signaling a lack of phosphorus.

With potassium, the pattern flipped. In 19 of the 25 forests, leaves with more nitrogen relative to potassium stayed green longer.

Potassium helps a leaf open and close the tiny pores that let in carbon dioxide, and it helps send sugar to the rest of the tree.

The researchers proposed that when a tree has plenty of potassium, extra nitrogen may help its leaves keep their chlorophyll and keep making food longer.

Two eastern forests, where potassium seemed to be in short supply, showed the reverse. There, leaves with more nitrogen relative to potassium lost their green sooner.

Weather still played a role. In 15 of the 25 forests, spots that got more rain during the growing season tended to stay green longer.

When the team added nutrient information to a model based on weather alone, the model did a better job explaining autumn timing in 22 of the 25 forests.

The authors wrote that forecasts of how long forests stay green could improve if they included nutrients.

That matters for more than fall scenery. Leaves that shut down early stop taking in carbon dioxide early, which gives a forest less time each year to store carbon.

Qiu said an imbalance between nitrogen and phosphorus “is bad for vegetation.”

According to Qiu, the findings could also matter for farm businesses such as orchards, since a productive growing season generally goes with later leaf drop.

Nitrogen released by human activity will likely keep rising, he said, so growers “might need to apply phosphorus to balance out the nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio.”

Orchards weren’t part of the study, though, which looked only at forests and didn’t test adding phosphorus.

The nutrient maps are estimates based on reflected light, not lab tests of individual trees. The authors describe their explanations as plausible, not proven.

Each forest was also mapped during just one summer, when the trees were at their greenest. So the study compares spots within a forest but can’t yet show what happens to the same trees from year to year.

Continued nitrogen pollution, the authors expect, will leave more forests short on phosphorus, a shift that could be linked to earlier autumns and shorter growing seasons.

To find out, they suggest mapping the same forests again and again, across seasons and years. That would show whether leaves start losing their green earlier as a forest’s nutrient balance changes.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

#6418. Melting permafrost has birthed a new type of large landslide

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Wildfires and water underneath the ground could dislodge large chunks of frozen earth

In 2018, an immense landslide in Canada’s Mackenzie Valley dammed the Redstone River (shown) and created a 3.5-kilometer-long lake. Researchers say the event was a new type of large landslide called a permafrost detachment slide.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In 2018, a strange and enormous landslide occurred in Canada’s Northwest Territories. A slab of earth roughly equivalent in volume to seven Great Pyramids of Giza suddenly began sliding downhill, leaving behind a barren scar in the forested landscape. But what puzzled scientists was that the slide had initiated in frozen ground that had been glued in place for years.

An analysis of the event reveals that it represents a new class of catastrophic landslides called permafrost detachment slides, researchers report in the Sept. 28 Geophysical Research Letters. The slides may be set in motion by wildfires that occurred decades earlier, destabilizing the ground and opening cracks through which water infiltrated deep underground. Over time, that water may have thawed the frozen layer from below, eventually unleashing the entire frozen layer in a catastrophic slide.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Large landslides don’t normally mobilize so much still-frozen material, and when they do begin in thawing layers they usually move slowly, says Dmitry Nicolsky, a geophysicist studying permafrost at the University of Alaska Fairbanks who was not involved in the study. But he says this new research suggests scientists need to better study what’s occurring beneath the surface in permafrost regions, because “we don’t know how [the ground] will move — it might go slowly or it might go catastrophically.”

The inspiration for the research manifested in 2019, when permafrost geologist Joseph Young, based at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, Canada, at the time, was helicoptering to a field site in the Northwest Territories to assist a colleague’s research. In some of the valleys out there, the slopes were “just collapsing with landslides everywhere,” says Young, who is now at an engineering firm in Edmonton. That was surprising because they were in an area where the permafrost — ground that has been frozen for at least two consecutive years — shouldn’t have been thawing much.

Once on the ground, more puzzling details emerged. “Traditionally with permafrost, it melts from the top down, and that releases this slurry of muddy material,” Young says. But at some of the landslide sites, large blocks of still-frozen ground seemed to have been moved hundreds of meters, he says.

Young and his colleagues studied two of the largest slides in the region that had moved big chunks of permafrost. These were the 2018 slide, which mobilized 18 million cubic meters of earth and dammed the Redstone River, and another event in 2017 that moved 4.5 million cubic meters of material.

Field observations revealed that both events had initiated along flat sliding surfaces roughly 20 meters underground, where the permafrost layer’s base was identified. Meanwhile, satellite observations showed that the ground at both sites had been gradually moving meters each year for decades.

Young and his colleagues hypothesized that climate warming and wildfire had somehow played a role in causing the slides. They set up instruments nearby that tracked ground temperature from 2020 to 2022, focusing on spots either with undisturbed forest or where wildfire had burned about 25 years earlier.

They then plugged that data into computer simulations to estimate how the ground would have evolved in the decades after a fire. Based on the results, the researchers concluded that wildfire and extreme summer temperatures can warm and weaken the frozen ground surface, causing it to start creeping and form tension cracks. As these cracks grow, water can penetrate deeper into the frozen ground and eventually reach beneath the permafrost layer, causing it to thaw from below and eventually detach.

More than 150 other slides in the region, identified via satellite observations, may also have been permafrost detachment slides, Young says. This could occur wherever there’s a relatively thin and warm permafrost layer and a rapid warming event to set things in motion, he says.

Permafrost is thawing in cold regions around the world, and these huge slides are very visual manifestations of that, Young says. “This is a direct reality of a changing climate.”

#6417. Forget the Novelty Gifts—These Mini EDC Tools Are Compact, Affordable, and Useful

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

EDC, short for everyday carry, is a collection of compact, useful tools you can, well, carry with you every day. This can range from the seemingly innocuous ballpoint pen to the more extravagant multitool, with plenty in between. And while your standard essentials are already condensed, miniaturized versions can take EDC to the next level—and they make a great stocking stuffer, too.

While the term “mini EDC” might sound redundant, it is indeed a thing. Not only are they significantly smaller than your typical pocket knife or multitool, but they’re a little more budget-friendly, making them an ideal stocking stuffer. I was gifted a multitool as a groomsmen’s gift, and I’ve been using it almost every day since.

We’ve rounded up some of the perfect stocking-stuffer-ready EDC essentials ahead of the holiday season, with price and size top of mind. There's something for everybody here, and some are even smaller than pocket-sized.

A closed length of 3.5 inches and a 1.72-inch blade, the Dually screams mighty but mini. Its handle is just long enough to give you the grip and leverage you need while staying compact. It features both a pocket clip and lanyard loop for customized carry.

Olight makes some of the best EDC flashlights we’ve tested—reliable, feature-rich, and cleverly designed—and its Oclip may be its most versatile. Clip it to your cap while drilling, or stand it up on your workbench for a better angle. It lasts up to 144 hours on a single charge and only needs a USB-C cable.

I love a keychain EDC accessory because they’re incredibly hard to lose. The Gerber Shard opens boxes and bottles and can even drive a small screw in a pinch. It covers the bare necessities in the most compact way.

This mobile tripod is about the size of a credit card and holds your phone in either portrait or landscape mode. Made from machined aluminum, it’s extremely lightweight yet durable. Whether you’re watching a show on a flight, taking a Zoom call, or capturing a time-lapse video—Peak Design’s tripod keeps you hands-free.

Leatherman makes some of the best multitools in the business (I love my Wave Plus), and it’s always trying to raise the bar when it comes to EDC. One of the best, if not the best, gift-giving options on the site is the Micra, which, as its name suggests, is a “micro” version of its classic multitool.

While it doesn't have the same bells and whistles as some of its other full-sized options, the Micra still includes 10 tools. This includes a 420HC stainless steel knife, spring-action scissors, four screwdrivers, and a bottle opener. And for just under $50, it’s a killer deal, too.

A Swiss Army knife is essentially the OG multitool, and the Victorinox SD is a certified classic. At just 2.28 x 0.71 x 0.35 inches, it’s objectively one of the smallest EDC essentials on the market, and its timeless design makes it a gift worth giving.

It covers the basics and includes a small blade, scissors, a nail file, a screwdriver, a key ring, a toothpick, and tweezers.

Benchmade makes some of our favorite EDC pocket knives, and the Mini Bugout is a lightweight, condensed version of its most popular EDC blade—the Bugout.

Despite its miniature size, it packs a punch, featuring dense CPM-S30V steel and top-of-the-line edge retention. Even with such a strong and precise blade, the foldable knife is remarkably light and ideal for any adventure.

For a little more bang for your buck, the Sod Buster Jr is a scaled-down, super-compact option that’s just 2.8 inches long but operates like some of its much larger counterparts. Smaller than Case’s marquee Sod Buster, the Jr is constructed with Case’s Tru-Sharp Stainless Steel, a special high-carbon steel that offers exceptional edge retention. It’s also corrosion-resistant, super durable, and about as lightweight a blade as you’ll find at an under-$100 price point.

Believe it or not, you can get even smaller here. So much so, in fact, that we can shrink it down to keychain size. With a 2.5-inch handle, the Elko Slip Joint Keychain Knife is the most compact on the list, but it’s another stocky option that packs a punch. With a rugged black-finished Sandvik 12C27 steel blade and an anodized aluminum handle, this knife is a beast from top to bottom. It also attaches seamlessly to your keys, making it the perfect gift for the forgetful type.

Pens are an underrated component of EDC, and finding the right one is pretty crucial. The right pen, in this case, might just be the smallest one, or at least the most convenient. This compact mini-bolt pen is perfect for EDC, with a lightweight, pocket-friendly design and a pressurized ink cartridge that writes through liquid. If you’re ever in a pinch and need a pen in even the worst conditions, this is a solid emergency option—not to mention a great stocking stuffer.

NASA's Swift Observatory is about to make a fiery reentry through Earth's atmosphere after a private mission to save it failed. Most of the spacecraft will burn up in orbit.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Editor's note: As of 11:15 a.m. EST on Wednesday (Nov. 4), NASA and the Aerospace Corporation both predict that the Swift observatory could have reentered Earth's atmosphere by now. However, no new details on reentry have been provided. Stay tuned for more updates about where and when the telescope will fall.NASA's decades-old Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is rapidly falling out of orbit and could tumble back to Earth any moment now, the space agency says.

According to NASA's latest estimates, shared Monday (Nov. 2), the roughly 3,200-pound (1,450 kilograms) spacecraft was likely to reenter Earth's atmosphere around 3:30 a.m. EST Wednesday (Nov. 4), with an uncertainty of plus or minus 11 hours — meaning the defunct observatory could have plunged down as early as Tuesday evening, and as late as Wednesday afternoon.

An independent analysis from the private nonprofit Aerospace Corporation, which tracks thousands of objects in orbit, similarly estimates that the telescope should have reentered the atmosphere at 6:56 a.m. EST Wednesday, give or take three hours. Both estimates suggest the Swift spacecraft could have already met its demise as of Wednesday morning, though no official confirmation has been shared.

As with all spacecraft reentries, the risk to humans is minimal. Most of the Swift telescope is expected to burn up in the atmosphere, according to NASA. Any surviving fragments will likely fall somewhere between 20.6 degrees south latitude and 20.6 degrees north latitude — a range that includes parts of Mexico, the Caribbean, Central and South America, the Arabian Peninsula, India, Africa and Oceania, but also a lot of ocean.

NASA predicts that the chances of Swift debris falling over a populated area are approximately 1 in 2,100. For comparison, the odds of a person being struck by lightning in their lifetime are 1 in 15,300, according to the National Weather Service.

NASA will continue to update their predictions as the reentry window draws closer.

Swift has detected thousands of deep-space explosions, including sudden flares from neutron stars (illustrated here).

The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is a multiwavelength optical, ultraviolet and X-ray telescope that launched in November 2004 on a mission to study the most powerful explosions in space. Initially designed for a two-year primary mission, the telescope ultimately spent more than 10 times that duration hunting for supernovas, gamma-ray bursts and black-hole-induced eruptions around the universe.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Swift has been rapidly losing altitude for more than a year, after rampant solar activity increased the drag on the aging spacecraft. This past August, a costly mission to boost Swift's orbit with a private spacecraft failed shortly after launch, hammering the final nail in Swift's coffin.

Engineers on the Swift team officially shut down the observatory's science operations on Oct. 20, after the spacecraft fell too low in orbit to continue taking steady observations of the sky.

As Swift goes out with a fiery bang, it leaves behind a trove of scientific data, including contributions to more than 7,000 scientific papers so far, according to NASA. This number will only increase as Swift's final observations are processed.

#6415. Why are ultra-processed foods linked to heart disease? New clues found in the bloodstream

Blood patterns offer new clues to why ultra-processed foods are linked to heart disease, beyond their sugar, salt and saturated fat content.

Sugar, salt and saturated fat might seem to explain why many ultra-processed foods are linked to heart disease.

But a recent study suggests the connection may involve more than those familiar ingredients.

The research followed British civil servants over many years.

A pattern in their blood offered a stronger clue, accounting for about half the link between ultra-processed food and cardiovascular disease.

The finding raises another possibility: how a food is made may matter alongside what goes into it. For now, that’s a possibility, not a proven cause.

Eunice Wang conducted the research while studying for her PhD at University College London, working with colleagues at UCL and Imperial College London.

“We know there is a link between ultra-processed food and disease, but there is uncertainty over what is driving this connection – whether it is due to higher levels of sugar, salt and saturated fat, as well as dense calorie content, or whether the risks also come from food processing,” Wang said.

The team followed people’s health rather than assigning them different diets. That means the researchers could look for links, but couldn’t show that processing caused anyone’s illness.

“Our findings hint that processing itself may play a role, although more research is needed to support this,” Wang said.

These weren’t people recruited for a new diet experiment. They were 6,010 members of Whitehall II, a study that started in 1985 with civil servants working in London government offices.

By the late 1990s, when they gave the blood samples used here, none had heart disease or diabetes.

They had completed questionnaires covering 127 foods twice during that decade.

Two researchers went through the list and used a system called Nova to decide where each food belonged.

Nova groups foods according to their processing. To qualify as ultra-processed, a product consists mostly of substances taken out of foods and combined with additives. Little or none of the whole food remains.

At the other end are minimally processed foods: fruit and vegetables, whole grains and beans, fish and meat. Water and unsweetened tea and coffee belong there too.

For this study, the team counted food and drink by weight. Calories weren’t the yardstick. That allowed them to include drinks that contain no calories.

On that basis, about 18% of what a typical person consumed each day was ultra-processed. The share for minimally processed food was much larger, at about 62%.

Next came the blood samples. The team examined 233 measures, from sugars and amino acids to fats and the particles that carry them.

From these, they picked out 34 measures closely linked to ultra-processed diets and 50 linked to minimally processed diets.

Together, those measures formed two blood patterns, or “signatures.” Each participant received two scores showing how closely their blood measurements matched each pattern.

One difference concerned omega-3 fats, including DHA. Their levels were lower in the blood of people who ate more ultra-processed food.

HDL particles, the carriers of so-called good cholesterol, were lower too. Particles associated with fatty deposits in arteries were more plentiful.

The pattern looked different among people who ate more minimally processed food. They had more omega-3 and other polyunsaturated fats in their blood. Saturated fat accounted for a smaller proportion.

Of the foods examined, fish stood out for its connection with omega-3.

Ultra-processed meats, sweets and ready-to-eat meals stood out among ultra-processed foods, with the strongest and most consistent links to less healthy blood readings.

The team also had years of health records to work with. Across a typical 20-year follow-up, those records showed 1,094 cases of cardiovascular disease, meaning disease of the heart or blood vessels.

For type 2 diabetes, the typical follow-up was about 18 years. There were 853 cases.

To compare diets, the team put people into thirds according to their ultra-processed food intake.

Those in the highest third had a 23% higher cardiovascular disease risk and an 18% higher diabetes risk than those in the lowest third.

These figures took account of age, smoking, exercise and body weight, as well as sugar, salt, fat and fiber in people’s diets.

The same comparison for minimally processed food went in the other direction.

People in the highest third had an 18% lower risk of cardiovascular disease and a 15% lower risk of diabetes than those in the lowest third.

Blood scores were also linked to later disease. People whose blood most closely matched the minimally processed pattern had a 40% lower risk of type 2 diabetes than those whose blood matched it least.

A closer match to the ultra-processed pattern went with about a 20% higher risk of both diseases.

Accounting for people’s reported diets weakened these connections slightly, but didn’t remove them. Blood measurements may therefore capture details that people miss when describing what they eat.

The team estimated that the ultra-processed blood pattern accounted for 51% of the diet’s link with cardiovascular disease and 43% of its link with diabetes.

For the minimally processed pattern, the figures were 47% and 48%.

Salt and saturated fat explained no detectable part of any link in these calculations.

Sugar didn’t explain either diet’s connection with cardiovascular disease, although it accounted for about 27% of the ultra-processed food link with diabetes.

The blood patterns left roughly half of the associations unexplained.

The authors suggested that gut bacteria, inflammation and changes in appetite or fullness might also play a role.

Processing can alter a food’s physical structure and produce new compounds.

Additives and chemicals that pass from packaging into food might also matter, but the study didn’t establish their roles.

Nor did every ultra-processed food show the same association.

Ultra-processed drinks and meats were linked to higher risks of both diseases, while ultra-processed breads were linked to a lower diabetes risk.

Senior author Clare Llewellyn works in UCL’s department of Behavioural Science and Health.

“Current UK dietary guidance does not consider processing itself as a risk but recommends a reduced intake of foods high in ingredients such as sugar, salt and saturated fat,” Llewellyn said.

Llewellyn said the findings could help discussions about whether dietary guidance should consider processing alongside nutrition.

The Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition, an independent adviser to the UK government, is reviewing the evidence on ultra-processed food and health.

There are gaps in this study, too. People had to remember what they ate, and the questionnaires didn’t cover all the details needed to sort foods by processing.

Nor could the blood tests pick up additives, chemicals from packaging or changes in gut bacteria.

Another catch: the same people supplied the data used to build the blood patterns and to test them. A pattern that looks convincing in that group might be less useful in another.

The calculations used to explain parts of each link also depended on assumptions the study couldn’t check.

Most participants were white male civil servants in midlife, and their food records dated from the 1990s.

Since ultra-processed foods have become more common, the authors suggested their estimates may understate today’s links.

Earlier research has found similar blood patterns. Feeding trials have also found differences in blood and urine between diets with and without ultra-processed foods.

What remains uncertain is why roughly half of these links went unexplained, and whether processing itself causes harm. The authors want the work repeated in more varied groups, using other blood-testing methods.

The study is published in the journal BMC Medicine.

#6414. Mount Kilimanjaro reveals a surprising temperature divide as the climate changes

Mount Kilimanjaro’s summit is warming while parts of its middle slopes cool, with expanding vegetation offering a possible explanation.

The summit of Mount Kilimanjaro is warming, while parts of its middle slopes are cooling.

Expanding vegetation may help explain why temperatures are moving in opposite directions on the same mountain.

A temperature analysis spanning almost 5,000 meters of elevation reveals that Africa’s tallest mountain isn’t warming uniformly.

The study was led by PhD student Yaping Mo and professor Nick Pepin at the University of Portsmouth, with collaborators from Nanjing University.

Kilimanjaro is practically designed for this kind of work. It’s a freestanding stratovolcano – an isolated giant punching straight up from the East African plains at around 800 meters to nearly 5,900 meters.

No surrounding mountain ranges to confuse things. Just one massive cone cycling through every ecosystem imaginable.

Coffee and banana plantations at the base, where over a million people farm the well-watered lower slopes. Then tropical rainforest. Then a heathland belt, alpine desert, and finally the shrinking ice cap at the summit.

Each zone is a distinct climate experiment stacked on top of the last.

The team drew on readings from 22 temperature loggers scattered along two transects – the southwestern Machame route, instrumented since 2004, and the northeastern Rongai route, added in 2012.

Stations sit in everything from the savanna near the town of Moshi (991 meters) to the ice field at 5,799 meters.

That’s among the largest continuous elevation monitoring networks on any tropical mountain in the world.

But ground sensors alone can’t cover the whole mountain. So the researchers merged those readings with satellite data from NASA’s MODIS sensors, which pass over Kilimanjaro four times daily.

They then trained a machine learning model (XGBoost) to predict air temperatures across the entire mountain at one-kilometer resolution.

The model performed remarkably well, explaining 94% of daytime and 95% of nighttime temperature variation, with errors averaging less than 1.8°C.

The trend analysis, covering 2004 to 2019, revealed contrasting temperature changes at different elevations.

Near the summit, daytime temperatures rose by 0.05 to 0.10°C per decade. But between 3,000 and 3,500 meters  – the heathland belt – daytime temperatures actually fell by 0.13 to 0.14°C per decade.

At night, the pattern flipped again. Most elevations experienced slight warming of 0.04 to 0.15°C per decade, while the summit barely budged.

“Climate change does not affect every part of a mountain in the same way,” Pepin said.

“Long-term observations across different elevations help us see these local differences and build a more accurate picture of how mountain environments are changing.”

The cooling on the mid-slopes appears tied to biology as much as physics. Heathland vegetation has been expanding upslope, and denser plant cover changes how the surface handles solar energy.

More leaves mean more evapotranspiration, which diverts the sun’s energy into evaporating water rather than heating the air. More canopy means more shade, less bare ground cooking in the equatorial sun.

“The cooling on the middle slopes coincides with the upslope expansion of the heathland zone,” Mo said.

“This signals that changes in vegetation and land cover may be influencing local temperatures, although other factors are also likely to contribute.”

The paper documents 32 wildfire incidents between 2017 and 2021 around the treeline zone, adding another layer of disturbance.

Fire resets the vegetation clock, strips away canopy, and can produce abrupt changes in local temperature signals.

One of the most striking findings involves the gap between what satellites see and what the air actually feels like.

At the ice field, satellite-measured land surface temperature exceeded air temperature by nearly 17°C during the day.

In the desert zone just below, the difference hit almost 16°C. Meanwhile, in the rainforest, that gap shrank to just 2°C.

The explanation comes down to raw physics. Bare rock and exposed surfaces at high altitude absorb intense equatorial solar radiation and heat up dramatically.

These sunlit surfaces can become much warmer than the air above them.

There’s also a complication. The summit contains both ice and dark rock, and those surfaces behave completely differently under sunlight. Ice stays near freezing while bare rock roasts.

Further down, the news was more encouraging. The rainforest zone showed remarkably little daytime warming over the study period.

Conservation and reforestation may have contributed to this stability, but the researchers say that relationship needs further investigation.

“Our research shows that warming is not necessarily uniform across a mountain, even over relatively short distances,” said study co-author Harold Lovell.

“Combining long-term ground measurements with satellite data helps us identify these differences and could provide a way to study temperature changes in other mountainous regions where weather stations are limited.”

Most evidence for elevation-dependent warming comes from mid-latitude mountains – the Tibetan Plateau, the Alps, the Rockies. There, seasonal snow and big swings in solar radiation drive the patterns.

Tropical mountains play by different rules: persistently intense sunlight, weak temperature seasonality, and energy-balance processes that may produce entirely different warming signatures.

Kilimanjaro could provide a model for studying temperature changes on tropical mountains where long-term weather records remain scarce.

The study is published in the journal npj Climate and Atmospheric Sciences.

#6413. The Past, Present, and Future Exist All at Once, Some Physicists Say. Does It Mean Your Fate Is Fixed?

This controversial idea about the universe could solve some of the biggest puzzles in quantum physics, like whether time travel could exist.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

What came first, the chicken or the egg? Normally we’d expect the explanation to run one way—the chicken laid the first egg, or the egg hatched the first chicken. But what if a future chicken could influence the egg before it hatched? That nonintuitive idea has weight when you consider a concept that some physicists are mulling over: that all of time exists all at once.

Welcome to the “block universe,” where the future influences the past, everything that will happen already has, and the nature of free will is debatable.

The way we perceive the cosmos normally is that time flows forward. We get older, our planet revolves around the sun, the universe moves inextricably forward from the Big Bang. But in the block universe interpretation of reality, we don’t actually need to invoke time in this way to explain how things work.

“There’s no flow of time in the block universe,” says Emily Adlam, PhD, an assistant professor of the philosophy of quantum mechanics at Chapman University. “Time is just another dimension, like all the dimensions of space.” It’s akin to the directions “left” and “right” we’re all familiar with, and which both exist simultaneously. Time’s directions—the past and the future—likewise both exist simultaneously, she explains.

Imagine looking into our solar system and first seeing Earth on one side of the sun, then on the other. Would that be proof that time has passed, or would it simply show that our planet’s orbit was carving a path through spacetime? The block universe argues the latter, and there’s a reason for that.

“Our understanding of the flow of time is flawed,” says Rod Sutherland, PhD, a theoretical physicist at the University of Sydney’s Centre for Time. “If you slowed time down to a half, or a quarter, or an eighth, it would be unobservable. It starts to throw doubt on what it means by the flow of time.”

The idea of a block universe dates back more than a century, but in recent years scientists have increasingly explored how a version of it might resolve some of the deepest puzzles of quantum physics.

In particular, Adlam and others have been studying a concept called retrocausality, where events in the future can influence events in the past. It turns out that this is a surprisingly good way to explain some of the peculiarities of the quantum world, which we still don’t understand. “There’s a number of paradoxical aspects of quantum mechanics that become a lot more understandable if you bring this in,” says Sutherland.

For example, in the quantum world two particles can be entangled and seem to share some properties across great distances of space. When they are both measured, they seem to have impossible correlations, implying that there must be some sort of “spooky action at a distance” between them, a term coined by Albert Einstein.

But how does this actually work? One possibility might be retrocausality, where the effect of something can precede the cause. “When you prove there must be spooky action at a distance, you assume the future can’t possibly affect the past,” says Ken Wharton, PhD, a professor of physics and astronomy at San José State University. “If the future could affect the hidden past, those theorems fail.”

Take an example where Alice and Bob are measuring two entangled particles, in two different locations. Under retrocausality, Alice can “cause some past variable, back where the particles were first entangled, and that variable would have also been sent to Bob,” says Wharton. “Some people call it zigzag causality. Then you don’t need spooky action at a distance. It’s just spooky retrocausal action.”

Wharton has also been theoretically exploring retrocausal models of quantum circuits (these are models for quantum computation where information flows along a timeline). That way, he can treat simpler cases as arbitrarily complicated systems. And it matters for us all, he says, in understanding exactly what our place in the universe is.

“It would be weird to have our choices affect the hidden past,” he says. “That would blow our minds. You get all of these weird consequences.” But it just so happens that these weird consequences “look a lot like quantum physics,” he says. “You could say that’s why quantum physics seems so counterintuitive, because retrocausality is so counterintuitive.”

There are two main conceptual ways to perceive retrocausality, says Adlam. One is the two-arrow case, “where you have two distinct and independent arrows of causation going in opposite directions,” she says. “The other scenario is a sort of all-at-once style of retrocausality, where we think of the laws of nature applying all together to the whole of history.”

While retrocausality is intertwined with the block universe idea, the latter could exist without the former being true. Adlam says the block universe interpretation focuses more on time than on the other laws of the universe. She compares the all-at-once idea of retrocausality to a game of Sudoku. “The rules of Sudoku apply to the whole grid, and just tell you whether a solution is valid or invalid,” she says. “The laws of nature could work like that. They could constrain all of spacetime.”

That does raise the question, though, of why we perceive a present—a here and now—in both the block universe and retrocausality concepts. Adlam says that might merely be a matter of perspective. In the same way that looking at the universe from another planet might look different, so too is looking at the universe from our given place in time.

“I am viewing the universe from a location here in California, and you are viewing the universe from some other location elsewhere in space,” she says. “Likewise, there’s a version of me viewing the universe from the 27th of October, and then tomorrow there’ll be another version of me viewing the universe from the 28th of October. They’re different perspectives on this big temporal block.”

It’s worth noting that the design of retrocausality does not allow for time travel. That’s because, if it were possible to send a signal into the past, it would result in a causal paradox where someone could prevent the action and its subsequent effect from taking place at all, says Adlam. That means that any possible retrocausation must be restricted to the hidden past, making it hard to measure.

Retrocausality and the block universe are understandably somewhat controversial ideas, and not everyone is convinced that they really exist. Not only do they bring up some potentially paradoxical scenarios but they also raise questions about whether the future is already fixed, and what that means for free will.

“One of the longstanding philosophical worries about the block universe is that everything is kind of fated and there’s no free will,” says Adlam. “In some sense it’s true,” she adds, but it “doesn’t necessarily mean that we don’t have free will. You have to think more carefully about what you would understand free will to be.”

For example, an idea called compatibilism says that we do have free will “as long as our desires and goals are the causes of our actions,” says Adlam. “It doesn’t matter if all of that was predetermined by physics. As long as I am the cause of my actions, I am acting freely.”

Perhaps future research will tell us more about whether we really live in a block universe, or if an effect can precede a cause. Or maybe that research has already been completed in another part of spacetime, in a cosmos where everything has happened—and is yet to happen, too.
