#6412. Crowds leave a hidden seismic signature beneath a city

Seismic recordings reveal how crowd size and coordinated movements shape ground vibrations, offering clues that could help monitor large gatherings.

Every time you take a step, you shake the ground. Not by much – a fraction of a micron – but seismometers don’t care about “much.” They care about patterns.

And when 11,000 people march through the streets of Troy, New York, or 100,000 pilgrims gather at a hilltop shrine in northern Israel, those tiny individual tremors add up to something a seismologist can read like sheet music.

Asaf Inbal from Tel Aviv University has done exactly that. He analyzed seismic recordings from Tokyo schoolyards, American protest marches, and an Israeli pilgrimage.

That helped him build the first large-scale framework connecting crowd size and behavior to the vibrations they leave in the ground.

The strongest crowd-generated seismic energy lands in the 1–2 hertz band, which lines up neatly with the natural rhythm of human walking.

That’s been suspected for a while, but Inbal nailed it down with data from roughly 300 accelerometers belonging to Tokyo’s Metropolitan Seismic Observation Network (MeSO-Net).

Most of those sensors sit in schoolyards – an accident of infrastructure planning that turned out to be a gift for studying how feet translate into waveforms.

The Tokyo data revealed something unexpectedly precise.

Seismic amplitudes spiked every weekday morning around 8 a.m. when school started. They then dipped at exactly 10:00 for morning break, again at noon for lunch, and once more at 3 p.m. for afternoon tea.

The network was essentially reading the school bell schedule through the ground. Even the pre-dawn hours told a story. A mysterious 5 a.m. amplitude peak turned out to match early morning truck traffic routes through the Chiba Prefecture, confirmed by independent freight data.

The real surprise came when Inbal plotted crowd size against seismic signal strength across five orders of magnitude. The size varied from a handful of schoolchildren to a hundred thousand pilgrims.

Two completely different scaling relationships emerged.

For Tokyo schools, the correlation between crowd size and ground shaking was essentially flat. A school with 1,200 students barely registered more than one with 400.

The correlation coefficient was just 0.08, indicating almost no relationship.

But for outdoor gatherings – protests, rallies, marches, pilgrimages – the relationship was steep and tight, with a correlation coefficient of 0.77 and a scaling slope of 0.81.

The difference isn’t just about numbers. It’s about coordination.

“We found that crowds engaged in coordinated activity tend to generate stronger seismic signals than similarly sized crowds engaged in uncoordinated activity,” Inbal explained.

“More surprisingly, the seismic amplitudes associated with coordinated activity increase more rapidly with crowd size.”

“This suggests that seismic excitation does not depend simply on the number of people. The type of activity also matters, and its influence becomes increasingly significant for larger crowds.”

Children on a playground move in different directions and at different rhythms, producing footfalls that overlap irregularly.

Marching, rhythmic chanting, jumping, and dancing can produce more coordinated ground vibrations.

That coordination may help explain why some gatherings generate stronger seismic signals than others of similar size.

Inbal analyzed two landmark events in detail. The 2020 Black Lives Matter march in Troy, New York, drew approximately 11,000 people.

Its strongest seismic amplifications showed up between 1.5 and 2 Hz, with short-term bursts lasting minutes to hours rather than a clean onset and stop.

The 2021 annual pilgrimage at Meron, Israel – attended by roughly 100,000 people – hit even harder, with amplifications between 1.5 and 2.5 Hz and an additional peak between 3 and 4.5 Hz, likely from rhythmic jumping and dancing.

That Meron pilgrimage ended in catastrophe: a crowd crush killed 45 people. A subsequent state commission of inquiry concluded that the disaster could have been avoided if crowd sizes had been known in real time.

Inbal borrowed a concept from earthquake science to formalize his findings. Just as seismologists use magnitude scales to characterize earthquakes, he developed ground-motion scaling relationships for human crowds.

“Because the seismic signals depend not only on the number of people but also on how they move, I sometimes call these scaling relationships the ‘People’s Magnitude,’” he said.

The approach required some seismological housekeeping. Surface waves generated by stomping feet decay proportionally to one over the square root of distance.

So Inbal corrected all his amplification factors for geometrical spreading before comparing events recorded at different ranges.

He also set strict quality filters. Events had to produce amplification factors above 1.5 for at least 900 consecutive seconds. They also had to fall within specific distance thresholds of the nearest seismometer.

Of the 385 outdoor gatherings that met the distance criteria, 100 passed the amplitude and duration tests.

What drew Inbal down this path was a collision between two of his interests. His earlier work on urban microseismicity – understanding how city noise interferes with earthquake detection – led him to MeSO-Net data.

And as he puts it, this in turn “led me to consider whether seismic data could be used to characterize ground motion generated by human crowds more broadly.”

Along the way, he studied the physics of collective crowd behavior and found “intriguing parallels” with his own work.

“Both studies suggest that interactions among people can have measurable collective consequences,” he noted.

“I’m used to thinking about how interactions between faults manifest themselves in seismic signals, so I found the idea that interactions among people could also leave a measurable seismic signature particularly appealing.”

The practical implications circle back to Meron.

If crowd-generated seismic signals scale predictably with both size and behavioral state, then existing seismic networks could, in theory, monitor large gatherings in real time.

“Ultimately, I’d like to understand whether changes in a crowd’s seismic signature could reveal transitions in its collective behavior, potentially even before those changes become apparent through conventional monitoring,” Inbal concluded.

The study is published in the journal Seismological Research Letters.

A crewed mission to Mars could be one of humanity's greatest achievements, but getting there may come with serious health risks. Beyond the challenges of surviving in space for months at a time, astronauts would face prolonged exposure to cosmic radiation ‪—‬ high-energy particles in space that can penetrate the human body and potentially damage vital organs.

A new study suggested that cosmic radiation could pose a particular threat to heart health. Researchers found evidence that rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what human astronauts might encounter during a mission to Mars and back developed more scar tissue around the small vessels in their hearts compared with rats that weren't exposed to space radiation.

Although the findings haven't been confirmed in humans yet, they add to the growing concerns about the long-term health effects of sending astronauts on long-duration space missions.

NASA and other space agencies are working on ways to eventually send humans to Mars and beyond. Given these latest findings, would you travel to Mars? Vote in the poll below, and let us know your thoughts in the comments.

#6410. Newborn survival improves when families receive financial support

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Rx Kids, a cash transfer program, boosted infants’ health in Flint, Michigan

Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield announces Rx Kids' Detroit debut in 2025. The program began in Flint, Mich., in 2024. “We know how to deliver this support efficiently and with dignity," pediatrician and Rx Kids director Mona Hanna told Science News.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Extra financial support during pregnancy and after birth can help more babies thrive in their earliest days.

The Rx Kids program in Flint, Mich., launched in January 2024, provides extra cash to pregnant residents and their infants, unconditionally. Researchers compared neonatal deaths — those in the first four weeks of life — in 2025 with those in 2021 through 2024 in Flint. The city’s neonatal mortality rate dropped from 10 deaths per 1,000 live births to 5 deaths per 1,000 live births, researchers report November 2 in JAMA Pediatrics. The early neonatal mortality rate, covering deaths in the first week of life, fell from 8 per 1,000 to 2. For the rest of Michigan, rates were stable over the study’s time period.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“As a pediatrician, there is no outcome more important than babies surviving,” says Mona Hanna of the Michigan State University College of Human Medicine in Flint, who is also the founder and director of Rx Kids. “These early findings suggest that something as simple as providing families with financial support during pregnancy and infancy may help save babies’ lives.”

Income tends to drop and expenses rise in the months before and after a birth, making the perinatal period especially difficult financially for many families. Economic precarity can expose moms and babies to health harms. For example, housing instability and homelessness is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight.

Backed by public and private funds, Rx Kids got started in Flint, a city with a high rate of child poverty that has been dealing with the public health fallout of lead contamination in the water distribution system. Nearly 100 percent of the community participates in the program. Flint families receive $1,500 once during pregnancy and $500 per month in the baby’s first year. Anyone who is a resident, at least 16 weeks pregnant or with a newborn up to six months old can enroll. Families have put the extra cash toward diapers, transportation, housing and safe places for their babies to sleep, Hanna says.

“Every day, we hear from moms who tell us, ‘I can breathe’ or ‘A weight has been lifted off my shoulders.’ They tell us they feel less stressed, more hopeful, more supported and more loved,” Hanna says.

The support has had a measurable health impact, with studies linking the program to more access to prenatal care, a decrease in the preterm birth rate and in low-weight births and fewer neonatal intensive care admissions.

Rx Kids has now expanded to dozens of communities in Michigan and Ohio.

#6409. Before a baby is born, a mother’s brain holds clues to their bond

A small study links bonding with an unborn baby to more coordinated activity in specific brain regions of mothers.

A pregnant woman may imagine what her baby looks like or pause to enjoy the feeling of the baby moving.

Researchers have studied this early bond for decades, yet relatively little is known about what’s happening in the mother’s brain as it forms.

Late in pregnancy, women who reported more anticipation of and interaction with their baby had more closely matched electrical rhythms between certain parts of the brain.

The new study suggests that parts of the bond are already reflected in the brain before birth.

Kathy Ayala of Yale’s Interdepartmental Neuroscience Program conducted the study with colleagues.

The senior researcher was Helena Rutherford, an associate professor in the Yale Child Study Center.

The team recorded brain activity once in each of 35 women in their third trimester. The results show a link at one moment in pregnancy, not proof that one thing causes the other.

Researchers call this early connection maternal-fetal attachment, though the word attachment is debated.

Classic attachment theory uses it for a child seeking care from another person, while here it means the mother’s one-way emotional bond with the fetus.

Earlier studies have linked a stronger bond during pregnancy to more sensitive caregiving after birth and to more responsive interactions between mothers and babies.

Each woman rated 18 statements from “almost never” to “almost always.”

Six covered anticipation, such as “I wonder what the baby looks like now,” and six covered interaction, such as “I enjoy feeling the baby move.”

The last six covered differentiation, a mother’s sense of the baby as a separate person, such as “I think the baby already has a personality.”

Each six-statement part had a top score of 24 points, and the group’s averages ran from about 18.7 to 19.6 points.

The volunteers were recruited through flyers and word of mouth around New Haven, Connecticut.

They were 28 years old on average and nearly 37 weeks pregnant, and 22 of them had never given birth before.

Each woman wore a net of 128 sensors, soaked beforehand in a warm salt solution.

In a dim, quiet room, she spent three 30-second stretches with her eyes closed, alternating with three with her eyes open.

The sensors recorded an EEG, the brain’s electrical activity as picked up from the scalp. Only the eyes-closed recordings were analyzed, because earlier work found them steadier.

The team focused on alpha waves, a rhythm that rises and falls 8 to 13 times per second. Alpha activity has been tied to attention, memory, and holding back unwanted responses.

The researchers measured coherence: how closely the alpha rhythm at one spot on the scalp rises and falls with the rhythm at another spot. It’s like checking whether two people clapping keep the same beat.

Four pairs of spots were compared. Two ran across the head, at the front and near the top and back, and two ran from front to back on each side.

Two of those pairs showed links with the questionnaire.

Women whose alpha rhythms over the left front and left back of the head were more closely in step scored higher on anticipation and on interaction.

So did women whose rhythms over the left and right front of the head were more closely in step.

The links held after the researchers accounted for how far along each woman was and whether she had given birth before.

The pair across the back of the head and the pair on the right side showed no link with either score.

Each of these positive associations met the threshold for statistical significance, though only narrowly.

Women who scored high on one part of the questionnaire tended to score high on all three. Yet differentiation showed only weak links with the brain measures, and none passed that test.

A 2022 study offers one possible explanation.

It measured women’s brains before and after pregnancy and found that increases in coordination within a large set of connected regions, called the default mode network, were linked to differentiation.

The 2022 study tracked changes across a whole pregnancy, while the new one measured each brain once.

Ayala’s team suggested that differentiation may depend on longer-term brain changes, while alpha coherence may reflect a woman’s engagement with the fetus in the moment.

Or, the authors wrote, 35 women may have been too few to detect a link with differentiation.

A 2023 study that Rutherford co-authored found that alpha coherence between the left front and left back of the head falls from pregnancy to the period after birth.

Its authors read the drop as a loosening of the brain’s tendency to hold back responses, which may help new mothers react to a baby’s signals.

If lower coherence after birth helps mothers respond, is higher coherence during pregnancy a problem?

According to Ayala’s team, not necessarily. Pregnancy changes the brain in large ways.

A 2025 study found that gray matter, the tissue that holds the bodies of nerve cells, shrinks during pregnancy and partly recovers after birth.

The steepest declines came in the default mode network and in networks linking the front and top of the brain. Ayala’s team described any tie between those changes and its own results as speculative.

Still, the authors suggest that higher coherence during pregnancy may reflect a brain state suited to preparing for parenthood.

The later drop may support a different job, responding to the infant.

The study was small, and it captured each woman at a single point late in pregnancy.

The authors found it surprising that the links didn’t differ between first-time mothers and women who had given birth before.

Earlier work had found that first-time mothers report a stronger bond during pregnancy.

With only 22 women in one group and 13 in the other, the study may have been too small to detect a difference.

Future studies should also measure mental health, including depression and anxiety, the authors wrote.

Because the women weren’t followed past birth, the study can’t say whether those with the most closely matched rhythms cared for their newborns differently.

The researchers want future studies to follow women from before conception into the period after birth, which could show whether the bond or the brain rhythms change first.

The full study was published in the Journal of Neuroendocrinology.

#6408. The 8 Best Cordless Stick Vacuums Are Convenient, Versatile, and Work Well on Carpets Too

These lightweight, easy-to-store models get the job done with multiple attachments and powerful motors.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

A cordless stick vacuum has the potential to be one of the most convenient cleaning tools in your home. These lightweight machines make it easy to clean up pet hair from area rugs and hidden dust along baseboards, without having to haul out an upright vacuum or wrestling with a power cord. Most models also convert into handheld vacuums, giving you more flexibility to clean furniture, stairs, and other hard-to-reach spots.

Suction power, battery life, maneuverability, and dustbin capacities vary between models, so the right cordless stick vacuum ultimately depends on your home’s flooring, how much debris you’re dealing with, and the features that will actually make your cleaning routine easier.

We’ve rounded up the best cordless stick vacuums worth considering based on our hands-on experience, with options for everything from everyday maintenance to deeper carpet cleaning.

🔎 Looking for more ways to keep your floors and furniture clean? Check out our stories on the best robot vacuums, the best vacuums for pet hair, the best vacuums for hardwood floors, and the best handheld vacuums.

I’ve spent considerable time researching, testing, and vetting all types of vacuums, so I’ve developed a pretty good understanding of what separates a genuinely useful appliance from one that is just going to take up space in your storage closet. I’ve evaluated a wide range of models, including full-size uprights, canister vacuums, robot, and handheld models vacuums, paying close attention to performance, ease of use, and features that can really make a difference in a your regular cleaning routine.

When testing cordless stick vacuums, we assessed how well each model could handle common household debris, its ability to transition between carpet and hardwood floors, and how easy it was to move around furniture and into tighter spaces. We also looked at the practical considerations like battery life, suction power, dustbin capacity, weight, filtration, and included attachments.

Beyond just how the vacuum cleans, we also considered the overall experience for an owner. Removable batteries, self-cleaning docking stations, washable filters, and easy-to-empty dustbins can also make daily vacuuming less of a drag. The below recommendations are both powerful and dependable for a wide range of cleaning needs and surface types.

The Dyson V15 Detect is the most expensive stick vacuum in our lineup, but if you can stomach the price tag, you’ll get a cordless stick vacuum that (quite literally) leaves the competition in the dust across the board. It delivers top-notch performance on floors and carpets to tackle everything from fine dust and pet dander to larger debris.

Its motor spins up to 125,000 rpm and it comes with two cleaning heads, including an upgraded version of the brand’s “fluffy” head that features a green laser headlight to detect fine dust. During testing, we found that being able to switch from cordless to handheld made it easier to transition from tackling small messes to deeper cleaning sessions.

The auto mode is a nice feature for conserving battery life, as this model only runs for about an hour off one charge. Another highlight is the motorized pet tool.

Full Dyson V15 Detect Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

The PowerClean FurFinder is a more affordable alternative to the PowerClean FurGuard we recommend, but that doesn’t mean you have to give up useful features.

This cordless stick vacuum is intended for use on a variety of floor types, and the flat-lay construction makes cleaning under furniture much more accessible. The vacuum also stands up on its own which leads to fewer interruptions during a cleaning session.

We love that both the main vacuum head and pet hair attachment come with headlights because it makes it a lot easier to see hidden dirt and debris. The brush roll is a tangle-free design, and the FurFinder is equipped with a HEPA filter for trapping small particles and allergens.

The motor on this vacuum is less powerful than the PowerClean, but it still provides plenty of suction for daily household cleaning.

Full Bissell PowerClean FurFinder Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

Since we’re big fans of the Shark AZ2002 Vertex upright vacuum for deep and thorough cleans, it’s no surprise that we like the cordless model in this lineup, too. The brush roll is excellent at pulling hair and large debris from carpets, as well as polishing up your hardwood floors. The cordless stick vacuum features an advertised runtime of 60 minutes.

It also offers a HEPA filtration system and converts to a hand vac, and it also bends at the center of the wand to get around and under furniture. The Vertex comes with plenty of accessories for cleaning a variety of spaces. However, this may not be the best choice if you regularly clean stairs, as the cordless vacuum weighs roughly nine pounds—significantly more than other vacuums we cover.

I have two cats and live with my partner, which means there is plenty of mess to go around, from pet hair and dust to tracked-in dirt. I appreciate all the thoughtful features of the Tineco Station 5 because they make daily maintenance much easier.

Automatic suction adjustment has proved useful on my laminate and tile floors. I can hear when the motor gets a boost of power in a particularly dirty area, and it helps on carpets and area rugs where crumbs and debris tends to get trapped between the fibers. Add to that a green laser light for dust detection and you’ll hardly ever miss a spot.

I particularly like the base station. It has a 2.5-liter capacity, and after two months of using the Station 5, I still haven’t had to empty it. When I dock the vacuum onto the base, it automatically empties the onboard dustbin, cleans the floorhead brush roll, and charges the vacuum. Combined, these intuitive features make for a cleaning routine that is virtually hands-free.

Full Tineco Pure ONE Station 5 Pro Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

Even though the Dyson V11 Origin came out several years ago, that doesn’t mean this model has stopped being useful.

The motorbar cleaner head works exceptionally well on carpet, successfully agitating fibers to pull up embedded dirt, dander, and hair. Suction is equally impressive, and there are three power modes depending on the level of cleaning you need. I ran the vacuum on medium most of the time, but I used boost occasionally whenever an area needed the extra attention.

This model doesn’t come with a soft roller brush vacuum head, and while it does work on all floor types, it can be loud on hardwood and laminate. But if your home is mostly carpet, this is a cordless stick vacuum I would reach for.

Full Dyson V11 Origin Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

Our tester has a busy household six pets, so there’s no question that she’s regularly cleaning up after her animals. Pulling out the upright vacuum daily isn’t convenient, so she turned to the Levoit LVAC-300 to fill the gap.

This cordless stick vacuum has three different cleaning modes—eco, medium, and max—and she was able to cycle through each right from the handle depending on how much suction power she needed. She found that the vacuum was able to pick up litter and sand on different surfaces and between thresholds with ease.

The attachments are useful for cleaning curtains, cushions, and staircases, but she was disappointed that there’s nowhere to store these tools on the vacuum itself. The LVAC-300 runs for up to 60 minutes depending on what mode you’re using, and the HEPA filter is a great feature if you have animals.

Full Levoit LVAC-300 Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

I used the Bissell PowerClean FurGuard across my apartment to clean laminate floors, area rugs, carpeting, and upholstery, and I fell in love with several features.

The vacuum lays completely flat, making it really easy to get underneath furniture, and the swivel steering helps guide the FurGuard around tight spaces. Being a pet owner, I appreciate that the brush roll is tangle-free, so I don’t have to cut hair loose as often as I would with a standard, bristled brush roll.

Other highlights were lights on the main vacuum head and pet hair attachment. I was able to see collected dirt and debris that I would normally miss on hardwood flooring, carpet, and furniture. I also like that this model is designed to be self-standing.

It’s hard to come by a cordless stick vacuum that you don’t have to re-mount or set on the ground during your cleaning session. With this model, I was able to stop and start with ease.

Full Bissell PowerClean FurGuard Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

We recently got our hands on one of the latest cordless stick vacuums from Shark, and we were impressed by the PowerDetect’s construction. The pole has a hinge in the center and when you release it, the vacuum bends to extend under furniture and hard-to-reach places. Our tester didn’t have to kneel down or adjust angles while he was cleaning thanks to the intuitive design.

Beyond that, the PowerDetect vacuum uses sensors on the bottom of the floor head to discern between surface types, and adjusts suction power when needed. During testing, the motor could be heard transitioning speeds when used on hardwood and shag carpet.

This vacuum also comes with a docking station, which automates the process of emptying out the dustbin. The vacuum itself can’t hold that much debris onboard, so it’s nice having a one-stop-shop for clearing out the bagless canister during a cleaning session. It’s a little heavy for a cordless stick vacuum, but it still gets the job done.

Full Shark PowerDetect Cordless Stick Vacuum Review

Not every cordless stick vacuum we test ends up in this roundup. However, these other models still perform well and are reliable recommendations:

Levoit Aero Cordless Vacuum Cleaner: The Tineco we’ve included above has more raw suction power, reaching up to 27,000Pa versus the 14,000Pa of the Levoit. However, one of the highlights of the Aero is the 3.5-liter-capacity dust bag in the docking station. Depending on your cleaning frequency, you could potentially go months without having to empty and replace it, and this design is better for keeping dust and dander from being expelled back into the air.

Dyson Gen5Detect Cordless Stick Vacuum: This cordless stick vacuum certainly commands a premium price, and you get a lot of the same features as the Dyson V15 Detect we recommend above, such as an LCD display screen, the Fluffy Optic cleaner head, and pet hair attachments. If you’re an allergy sufferer, you may prefer the Gen5Detect because its filtration system captures particles down to 0.1 microns, while the V15 filters down to just 0.3 microns. Plus, runtime is slightly longer on the Gen5Detect.

The main advantages of owning a cordless stick vacuum are easy portability and storage. But what you trade for the convenience is battery life and runtime. Most models clean from 30 to 60 minutes, but that’s also dependent on what setting you’re using. If you’re running the vacuum on its highest speed the entire time, it might die faster. Be wary of manufacturers’ advertised total runtime because it may represent performance on the lowest setting or using two fully charged batteries, for instance. Battery charging should also be factored in, so plan your cleaning session accordingly so you don’t lose power in the middle of a floor swipe.

Like we mentioned earlier, the dustbins on cordless stick vacuums are significantly smaller than those of an upright or canister unit. You should consider your cleaning habits and the spaces you usually vacuum to find a model that aligns with your needs. If you live in an apartment or are using the cordless vac to supplement your other cleaning supplies, then a dustbin with at least half a liter capacity should do. Some of the models we recommend hold up to one liter of debris, which helps limit the number of trips to the trash can.

Although not a necessity, having a good amount of attachments with your vacuum is especially helpful for cleaning hard-to-reach places or targeting specific issues. Crevice tools pick up dirt and dander from corners and couch cushions, while bristled brushes and motorized pet tools agitate and lift hair and fur that’s been embedded into upholstery.

A good filtration system helps combat allergens such as dust and pet dander that are being kicked up by a vacuum. The best option is a HEPA filter, or “high-efficiency particulate air” filter, which traps 99.97 percent of particles that are 0.3 microns or larger in size. A fully sealed or multi-step filtration system also has the potential to trap a wide variety of airborne allergens without releasing them back into your home.

Cordless vacuums are very effective at picking up pet hair, especially models designed with high suction power and specialized brush rolls. Some of the models we recommend include motorized attachments that lift embedded hair from upholstery and carpets. Anti-tangle vacuum heads are also a key feature that helps prevent hair from wrapping around the brush roll. While not all models perform equally, a high-quality cordless stick vacuum is able to handle pet hair just as well as traditional versions.

The lifespan of these vacuums typically lasts from three to five years, depending on usage, build quality, and maintenance. Battery performance plays a major role, since lithium-ion batteries start to lose capacity over time.

Avoiding overcharging and storing the vacuum properly could help extend the battery life significantly. Running regular maintenance like cleaning the vacuum filters and emptying the dustbin completely preserves suction and functionality. Higher-end models often last longer due to better materials and replaceable parts, but either price point has potential to last for years with proper care.

Modern designs are increasingly more effective at cleaning many surface types, including rugs and carpets. Advances in battery tech and general efficiency have allowed for strong suction performance that is comparable to corded models. Adjustable power modes allow for deeper cleaning on thicker carpets, and multi-roller and motorized brush heads agitate fibers to loosen dirt and debris.

Performance may vary depending on the type of flooring. Some vacuums are designed to work on low-to-medium pile carpets, while others are able to handle high-pile. It’s best to consult the listed features and specs of the model you’re considering to ensure it aligns with the flooring types in your home.

Amber is a Reviews Editor with bylines on Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, and Best Products sites. Specializing in kitchen gadgets, small appliances, lifestyle, and consumer tech, she brings hands-on testing and a detail-oriented approach to every review. #6407. What makes people pay more for sustainable products? Study identifies a key factor

Why don’t green values always lead to greener purchases? A new study explores how enjoyment and practicality shape willingness to pay more.

Here’s a paradox that should keep sustainability marketers awake at night. Consumers who genuinely care about the environment and say they’d happily pay extra for eco-friendly products often don’t.

They walk past the biofuel, ignore the recycled-fiber T-shirt, and go home with whatever was cheapest and most practical.

The gap between what people believe and what they actually buy is called the sustainability value-behavior gap. A new study may have now found one of its key mechanisms.

Whether a product feels enjoyable or primarily functional may help explain the gap.

Researchers at the University of Eastern Finland found that hedonic attitudes – the sense that a sustainable product is fun, exciting, or delightful – act as a bridge between people’s green values and their wallets.

Utilitarian attitudes – the cold calculus of price, efficiency, and practicality – do the opposite. They widen the gap.

The research team, led by Jani Holopainen and doctoral researcher Jyri Hoffrén, ran three studies using a demographically representative panel of Finnish and Dutch citizens.

The first tested their theoretical model on 461 participants. The results were clear: sustainable consumption values strongly predicted willingness to pay a premium for green products.

But when hedonic attitudes entered the picture that relationship got even stronger.

“Consumers who value sustainable consumption are more willing to pay a premium, particularly when a product offers positive emotional and user experiences. Enjoyment helps translate sustainability values into actual consumption behavior,” Hoffrén said.

In the base model, sustainable values alone explained 47 percent of the variance in willingness to pay a premium.

Adding hedonic and utilitarian attitudes as moderators nudged the model’s explanatory power to nearly 48 percent.

That’s not a dramatic gain in raw statistical terms. Still, the interaction effects were significant and, more importantly, pointed in opposite directions.

The second study asked whether this was just a snapshot or something durable.

The researchers followed 239 participants over two years, measuring their sustainable consumption values and attitudes at one point and their actual purchasing behavior two years later.

The pattern held. Values predicted behavior across the two-year gap, and hedonic attitudes strengthened that link while utilitarian attitudes weakened it.

Values tend to be stable, but attitudes fluctuate. The fact that hedonic attitudes measured at time one still amplified the values-to-behavior connection at time two suggests something deeper than a fleeting mood.

The results suggest that enjoyment may help people act on their sustainability values, while a stronger focus on practical considerations may weaken that connection.

The third study broke the question apart across three wood-based bioproducts that sit at different points on the pleasure-to-practicality spectrum: a bioplastic water bottle, a T-shirt made from wood-based fabric, and a wood-based biofuel.

The bioplastic bottle was the star. Both effects showed up clearly – hedonic attitudes boosted willingness to pay, utilitarian attitudes dragged it down.

This aligns with earlier research suggesting that ecological packaging is inherently perceived as hedonic. People find it appealing, novel, and satisfying to hold. That emotional connection does real commercial work.

The T-shirt fell in the middle. Utilitarian attitudes still suppressed willingness to pay, but the hedonic boost disappeared.

The biofuel landed at the utilitarian extreme, and the results were stark. The negative utilitarian interaction was the strongest across all three products.

People who evaluated biofuel through the lens of price and efficiency were significantly less likely to pay a premium, even when they held strong sustainability values. The hedonic interaction was not even statistically significant.

The findings also raise a potential concern about greenwashing. The researchers suggest that emphasizing enjoyment could make consumers less critical of environmental claims.

“Companies should consider sustainability as part of a product’s overall value. If product marketing emphasizes enjoyment without genuine experiential benefits, it may lose credibility,” Hoffrén said.

“For utilitarian products, consumers are also quick to scrutinise whether the environmental benefits are genuine.”

Enjoyment may help legitimate sustainable products attract buyers, but it could also give misleading environmental claims an advantage.

Policymakers eyeing greenwashing regulations might want to pay particular attention to products marketed at the intersection of sustainability and pleasure.

The study was published in a forestry economics journal for a reason.

Wood-based bioproducts – an expanding category that includes bioplastics, textiles, and biofuels – face exactly this dilemma.

For the bioplastic bottle, enjoyment strengthened the link between sustainability values and willingness to pay extra. For biofuel, practical considerations weakened that link most strongly.

For the wood products industry, the lesson is that environmental credentials alone won’t move units. The product has to feel good in someone’s hand, or on their body, or in their daily routine.

“This finding helps explain the value-behavior gap. Consumers may consider sustainability important but decide not to buy a product if its price, practicality, or perceived benefits fail to meet their expectations,” Hoffrén concluded.

The study is published in the journal Forest Policy and Economics.

A new mom experienced intense feelings of sadness whenever she breastfed.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The symptoms: About two weeks after her baby's birth, the woman began experiencing intensely negative emotions at every breastfeeding session. These feelings of "extreme unhappiness" would start just before her milk ejection reflex (during which milk moves from the breast ducts to the nipples) and last up to two minutes.

The feelings would end abruptly when she finished breastfeeding and then appear again the next time she was about to release milk, according to a report of the case, which the patient co-authored. The patient was a breastfeeding counselor for the United States Department of Agriculture Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) Program.

Until the baby was about 18 months old, this phenomenon would happen every time the woman breastfed — about five times per day, on average. Unlike postpartum depression,‬ which can cause persistent feelings of despondency, anxiety and mood swings in new parents,‬ the woman felt "helpless, hopeless, [and] worthless" only during her milk release. She reported that she otherwise felt happy and bonded with her new baby.

What happened next: When her baby was 7 months old, the woman began meeting with a lactation consultant, who later co-authored the case report. They worked together to track the mother's symptoms over time, noting when negative feelings began and if any intervention made them subside or worsen.

The diagnosis: Because the woman's condition did not have a formal name at the time, she began calling it "dysphoric milk ejection reflex," or D-MER.

The case report authors initially suspected that fluctuations in the woman's oxytocin levels might be causing D-MER, since the hormone is released into the bloodstream prior to the milk ejection reflex during breastfeeding. However, external factors that are known to affect oxytocin levels, such as tobacco use, did not always trigger the woman's symptoms.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Next, they looked at dopamine. The chemical messenger's fluctuations during breastfeeding are less studied than those of oxytocin and prolactin, another hormone linked to lactation. However, dopamine levels have otherwise been connected to strong emotional responses. Activities that seemed to ease the patient's D-MER symptoms — such as taking the cold medication pseudoephedrine, smoking cigarettes or binging on chocolate ice cream — are also known to increase dopamine levels. Meanwhile, acute stress, which reduces dopamine, worsened her symptoms.

The authors hypothesized that an abrupt drop in dopamine prior to milk release might be a trigger for D-MER.

D-MER differs from postpartum depression in that the feelings of sadness are very specific to lactation.

The treatment: The woman began taking bupropion (better known by the brand name Wellbutrin), an antidepressant that increases the amount of dopamine in the brain. She saw a dramatic reduction in her D-MER symptoms within a day, and five days later, her symptoms were almost entirely gone.

However, she stopped taking the drug after a few weeks due to unwanted side effects (which aren't described in the report), and the symptoms came back. She then tried an herbal remedy containing roseroot (Rhodiola rosea), a plant historically used in some places to manage depression. Some recent studies suggest that compounds in R. rosea interact with receptors for chemical messengers in the brain; however, there is little reliable evidence demonstrating its purported therapeutic benefits, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health.

She took R. rosea three to four times per day, reporting that her symptoms became "much milder" but returned if she skipped a day. As her daughter grew older and the woman breastfed less often, the woman stopped taking the supplement. When the child was 3 years old and no longer breastfeeding, the woman's D-MER symptoms went away entirely.

What makes the case unique: Prior to this report, published in 2011, D-MER was not widely recognized or documented in the scientific literature, and there was no research into its causes or treatment.

The patient and co-author of the report created the website D-MER.org in 2007 to share information about the condition more widely. She hoped to raise awareness among medical professionals and to help breastfeeding people who experience this condition by providing resources and support and encouraging them to understand that what they were feeling was a physiological side effect of nursing. Since the site's launch, hundreds of visitors have described having negative feelings while breastfeeding, according to the report.

Over the past two decades, more case reports describing the condition have been published. In a 2025 paper in the European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology, researchers estimated that roughly 14.2% of lactating parents experience D-MER and that 1 in 6 stop breastfeeding as a result. Dopamine is thought to play a part, but the exact cause of D-MER has not been definitively established in peer-reviewed research yet.

There is no definitive treatment for D-MER, although some have anecdotally found relief through techniques for stress reduction, such as meditation and breathing exercises, and by seeking support from partners, friends and breastfeeding groups online.

Short-lived negative feelings resembling D-MER have also been reported in people who are not lactating. These anecdotal accounts describe intense, negative feelings brought on by nipple stimulation. One online discussion group referred to this phenomenon as "sad nipple syndrome," according to the authors of the case report. As with D-MER, dopamine may play a part, but the overall neurochemistry underlying that emotional response is unknown.

Breastfeeding and parenthood can be an emotional roller coaster even under the best circumstances, the authors noted. In that sense, they explained, people with D-MER have "the same emotional peaks and valleys" as all new parents do. Yet the negative feelings that accompany D-MER are nonetheless different from the normal range of emotions in the parents of newborns, and they can cause extreme distress if they are not correctly identified and addressed as being specific to breastfeeding.

People with D-MER, the authors concluded, "serve as a reminder to us all that we do not yet have a complete understanding of human lactation."

#6405. A lost sea channel shaped this striking corner of Cyprus

A satellite image of Cyprus reveals how ancient islands joined to form the Akrotiri Peninsula, enclosing a salt lake once open to the sea.

A shallow salt lake at the southern edge of Cyprus marks a place where the Mediterranean once flowed between two islands.

Today, strips of land join those islands together, leaving a coastal landscape that still carries the outline of its watery past.

The Akrotiri Peninsula offers a striking reminder that even an island’s shape is temporary.

Rivers, shifting shorelines, and rising rock helped build this southern tip of Cyprus, connecting land that once stood apart.

On October 10, 2026, Landsat 8 captured images of the peninsula’s sandy margins and the lake enclosed between them.

Behind that modern view lies a story spanning ancient ocean floors, migrating flamingos, and a cape whose name recalls a legendary arrival of cats.

Akrotiri Salt Lake occupies a former arm of the Mediterranean.

Its enclosure happened gradually, as sediment accumulated along two routes between Cyprus and a smaller island to the south.

These natural connections are known as tombolos: deposits of sand, gravel, or other sediment that link an island to another landmass.

At Akrotiri, two such bridges helped turn separate islands into a single peninsula.

The western connection formed first. About 50,000 years ago, gravel and sand delivered by the Kouris River began building the tombolo on that side.

The eastern connection developed later, extending south from Cyprus.

Geologists place the final separation of the lagoon from the open Mediterranean within the past 2,000 years.

That difference in timing gives the landscape an unusual perspective.

Although the rocks beneath Cyprus record tens of millions of years, the closure that helped define this lake occurred within human history.

The two land bridges also explain why the lake sits where it does. Rather than forming in an isolated inland basin, it occupies space left between growing coastal connections.

Its position preserves evidence of the channel even though the surrounding land now provides an unbroken route onto the peninsula.

Long before those sediment bridges formed, the material that would become Cyprus was taking shape underwater.

About 90 million years ago, during the Late Cretaceous, molten rock emerged from the seafloor and cooled into new oceanic crust.

Tectonic forces eventually pushed portions of that crust upward, bringing formerly submerged rock above the waves.

The Troodos Mountains preserve remnants of this ancient oceanic material.

Geologists call the rock assemblage an ophiolite, a term associated with the snakelike appearance of some of its mottled green rocks.

The peninsula’s southern portion has a different geological background.

During the much later Miocene epoch, marine deposits accumulated around the emerging island, including chalk, limestone, and marl.

Later uplift raised some of this younger material into a smaller island offshore.

River sediment and marine deposits eventually filled parts of the intervening channel, creating the connections visible in the peninsula’s present shape.

The lake now follows a seasonal rhythm. Water typically returns in late autumn and winter, while summer brings drying.

Those winter waters have historically supported large gatherings of flamingos, with overwintering numbers averaging about 4,000 birds.

The birds come to feed on small creatures such as fairy shrimp. These shrimp contain carotenoids, pigments that contribute to the flamingos’ familiar pink coloration.

Recent counts offer a more sobering picture. News reports put the lake’s wintering flamingo population at just 30 birds in 2025, a sharp departure from its historical abundance.

The satellite scene captures the setting for this seasonal gathering.

The birds themselves, and the changes in their numbers, belong to a smaller scale of observation that adds another layer to the landscape’s story.

On the southeastern peninsula, Cape Gata introduces a different animal connection. Its name means Cape Cat in Greek.

According to legend, a severe fourth-century drought left Cyprus struggling with snakes. Empress Helena, the mother of Constantine the Great, responded by arranging for cats to arrive from Egypt.

The story places some of those cats near what became the Holy Monastery of St. Nicholas of the Cats, where monks supposedly encouraged them to hunt snakes.

The tale survives alongside a continuing tradition of caring for cats at the monastery.

Seen together, the lake, land bridges, and cape reveal several histories sharing one small stretch of coast.

Ancient seabed became an island, sediment closed a channel, and people attached stories to the land that emerged.

The shoreline in this image is the latest chapter in a landscape still shaped by water.

Image Credit: NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison

#6404. Menopause leaves clues in the blood about women’s future brain health

Blood protein changes around menopause may offer clues to later brain aging and Alzheimer’s risk, a new study suggests.

Menopause marks the end of a woman’s menstrual periods, often accompanied by hot flashes and disrupted sleep.

Changes in blood proteins may also offer clues to brain health decades later.

Compared with women who hadn’t reached menopause, those past it had more of certain proteins tied to inflammation, brain cell signaling, and Alzheimer’s disease.

That difference followed hormone levels more closely than age.

The same protein pattern appeared again in older women. Those whose blood showed it more strongly tended to decline faster on memory and thinking tests.

In the largest group, they also had a modestly higher risk of Alzheimer’s dementia.

Menopause may be a window for spotting the earliest signs of brain aging, years before memory problems usually appear.

The work was led by Madeline Wood Alexander at Sunnybrook Research Institute in Toronto, with Rowan Saloner and Kaitlin Casaletto at the University of California, San Francisco.

Because the findings come from blood samples and health records, they link these proteins to brain aging without showing that one causes the other.

“Menopause is not an isolated reproductive event,” said Emily Jacobs, a professor of psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara, whose lab runs the study that supplied the midlife volunteers.

“It is a whole-body biological transition. Now we can begin to see a molecular fingerprint of that transition in the blood and ask how it relates to brain health decades later.”

Menopause arrives around age 51 on average, more than two decades before dementia symptoms usually show up.

But the brain changes behind Alzheimer’s seem to start long before symptoms do, possibly around the same years as menopause.

The midlife part of the study included 80 healthy women aged 43 to 58. Thirty of them hadn’t reached menopause, 26 were in the transition often called perimenopause, and 24 had already passed through it.

In blood drawn after an eight-hour fast, the team measured about 120 proteins thought to be involved in brain aging. Sixteen of them were higher in women past menopause than in women who hadn’t reached it.

Eight of those 16 are involved in inflammation, four in the connections between nerve cells, and two in metabolism. The remaining two are tied to Alzheimer’s.

One is p-tau231, a form of tau, the protein that forms tangles inside brain cells in Alzheimer’s. The other is BACE1, an enzyme that helps make amyloid, the sticky protein in Alzheimer’s plaques.

The team also checked six standard Alzheimer’s blood markers. Once age was taken into account, p-tau231 was the only one that differed between women before and after menopause.

Next, the researchers combined the 16 proteins into a single score. It was lowest in women before menopause, higher in women in the transition, and highest in women past it.

Older women in the midlife group also had higher scores. That link disappeared once menopause stage was taken into account.

Thirty-six men of similar ages also gave blood, and in them the score didn’t rise with age at all.

Estradiol, the main form of estrogen, was about one-tenth as high in women past menopause as in women who hadn’t reached it.

Follicle-stimulating hormone, or FSH, was about nine times higher. The pituitary gland at the base of the brain releases FSH to signal the ovaries.

When estradiol, FSH, and progesterone were analyzed together, FSH was the only one still tied to the protein score.

Higher FSH was associated with higher levels of BACE1 and two proteins tied to nerve cell connections, while lower estradiol was associated with higher levels of four inflammation proteins.

The authors wrote that FSH receptors are common in brain regions that Alzheimer’s damages. In experiments on mice, FSH can trigger Alzheimer’s-like brain changes and thinking problems.

To check the results, the team turned to the UK Biobank, which holds health data from about half a million volunteers in the United Kingdom.

They compared 1,407 women past menopause with 1,407 women who hadn’t reached it, all aged 45 to 60 and matched closely on age.

In those women, a different lab method measured 2,923 proteins, and about 44% of them differed between the two groups.

The larger analysis measured 13 of the original 16 proteins. Nine showed differences in the same direction as in the midlife volunteers.

The team also used aging clocks, computer models that estimate how old an organ looks from blood proteins tied to that organ.

On 11 of 13 organ measures, women past menopause looked biologically older than women of the same age who hadn’t reached it.

The arteries, brain, and intestine showed some of the largest differences.

Among the midlife women in or past the transition, those who’d had night sweats in the previous two weeks had higher protein scores. They also had higher levels of four inflammation proteins.

Hot flashes, the sudden waves of heat many women feel around menopause, weren’t linked to the score in this group.

Women with vaginal dryness had lower scores, and the authors wrote that the meaning of that result is unclear.

Next came 89 older women, around 69 years old on average, from the Wisconsin Registry for Alzheimer’s Prevention, which enrolls many people with a parent who had Alzheimer’s.

Those who reported a history of hot flashes or sleep problems had higher protein scores years after menopause.

One inflammation protein, CCL2, was tied to heat symptoms in both groups: night sweats in the midlife women and hot flashes in the older ones.

CCL2 helps call immune cells to sites of inflammation, and the authors wrote that its link to heat symptoms may last into later life.

The team then calculated the protein score for 11,925 older women in four separate groups, with average ages between about 61 and 72.

In a long-running Alzheimer’s study, 673 women around 71 years old were followed for about five years. Those with higher scores declined faster on memory and thinking tests.

The same was true in a smaller San Francisco study that followed 100 women for nearly six years.

The two groups started out very differently. More than half the women in the first study already had mild thinking problems or dementia at the start. Almost none in the San Francisco group did.

In the Wisconsin group, women with higher scores did worse on thinking tests taken at a single visit.

The UK Biobank group was the largest, with 11,059 women followed for nearly 16 years.

During that time, 219 of them developed Alzheimer’s dementia, and women with higher scores had a modestly higher risk of it. The scores weren’t linked to dementia of all types combined.

“Midlife is a critical window for both men and women where we can really set up the brain to be more resilient or more vulnerable to dementia in later life,” said Casaletto, one of the study’s senior authors.

“For women, menopause may be this especially powerful time to intervene.”

“The findings do not mean that menopause causes Alzheimer’s disease,” Casaletto said.

Most women don’t develop Alzheimer’s, she added, and it’s still unclear what small midlife rises in Alzheimer’s-linked proteins mean for any one person.

The authors described the link to Alzheimer’s dementia as relatively small.

The individual proteins most strongly associated with cognitive performance also varied across the groups of older women.

The authors wrote that the overall pattern may matter more than any one protein.

The midlife group was small and mostly White, and symptoms were self-reported. Proteins in the blood can also come from organs throughout the body, not only the brain.

“Women spend roughly one third of their lives after the menopause transition, yet we know remarkably little about the biology connecting menopause to later-life brain health,” Jacobs said.

Each midlife volunteer gave blood only once, so the study compared different women at different stages.

The authors wrote that confirming these shifts will mean following the same women from before menopause to years after it.

Those studies would track hormones, proteins, symptoms, and thinking along the way.

They could also separate the part of the change that comes from hormones from the part that comes with age.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Medicine.

#6403. The Next Ice Age Began 2,000 Years Ago. Then, in 1960, Humans Abruptly Ended It.

Ancient moss frozen beneath Baffin Island’s ice tells the story of a glaciation humans snuffed out.

Researchers at Columbia University have pinpointed the summer of 1960 as the moment when a new glacial period, which had already begun, started melting away. They said the blame rests squarely on humans and the surge in greenhouse gases.

In a new study published in the journal Science, the researchers wrote that the newest glacial period (often colloquially called an ice age) began 2,000 years ago, even though it would have taken about 30,000 years for anyone to really notice. Human activity cut it short in 1960.

“It was just getting started, everything was normal, the next glaciation was about to happen—and yet it stopped,” Nicolas Young, a geochemist at the Columbia Climate School, said in a statement from Columbia University. “It’s a very powerful example of how we have jolted the system.”

To gather their data, the team studied what remains of the Laurentide Ice Sheet. At its peak roughly 20,000 years ago, the ice sheet stretched from the Arctic Circle down to Illinois and was two miles thick in places. It shrank to its smallest size about 3,000 years ago, then started growing again about 2,000 years ago.

“People always say that it disappeared, but that’s not true,” Young said of the ice sheet. He noted that a piece of it survives today as the Barnes Ice Cap on Baffin Island in the Canadian territory of Nunavut, and that this remnant is still about the size of Delaware. Because the ice cap is frozen directly to the bedrock beneath it, it doesn’t slide, so it preserves the vegetation underneath instead of scraping it away. When the ice expands, it entombs the plants it covers. When it recedes, it exposes them again, allowing the team to sample the moss and date it using radiocarbon dating.

“If you do this enough times, you can actually develop a timeline of that ice margin systematically advancing over plants,” Young said. “You’re actually tracking the expansion of that ice margin.”

That timeline is critical, according to Joerg Schaefer, also a Columbia climate geochemist. “We have a decent understanding of how this enormous ice sheet grew and disappeared over thousands of years from proxy records, but catching the start of this process with direct observations is new,” Schaefer said. “Our approach helped us see the first steps of ice-sheet growth preserved in the landscape. It gave us a rare opportunity to understand how re-glaciation begins and how the Laurentide Ice Sheet reforms.”

Technically, Earth has been in the Late Cenozoic Ice Age for about 34 million years, the researchers said. Within that span, the planet swings between glacial periods and warmer interglacial periods, and conventionally we have been in an interglacial since the last glacial period ended roughly 11,700 years ago. The new research challenges that framework by arguing that the first renewed growth of an ice sheet equals the start of a glacial period, “marking the onset of the next glaciation.” That period didn’t last long, however. The ice cap reached its maximum extent around 1960, when summer warming caused a “negative mass balance, ice margin recession, and the termination of the next glaciation.”

In other words, Earth’s climate had warmed enough that the Barnes Ice Cap lost more ice in the summer of 1960 than it gained the previous winter, effectively ending the next glaciation. “The demise of the next glaciation, despite the ongoing decline in summer insolation, illustrates the influence of anomalous greenhouse gas forcing on climate,” the authors wrote.

The team expects the ice cap to vanish within a few centuries. Without that icy foundation, it will be harder for new ice to build up. As a result, scientists can’t say when (or where) the next glaciation might occur, especially while greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere remain high.

Young described what the ice cap’s loss will mean: “That will be the true very last remains of the Laurentide, disappearing for good,” he said. “What has been an extremely natural and predictable phenomenon is now gone.”
